setting: An island about two kilometres across, with a mountain range along it, rivers to the sea and a few lakes. A walled town stands in the lowland, villages lie near water, giants live on a high shelf in the hills and small folk in a forest hollow. A terraced hill town of brick and iron stands above a river, and a harbour town of concrete and neon by the sea. Roads join them. Farms, woodcutters and charcoal burners, a herders' fold, salt pans and a light on the north cape lie between them, and an outlaws' steading hides in the woods by the stone road.

towns.name: Brackenford
towns.character: the island's market town, walled, busy and proud of its square
towns.ledger: Brackenford. The gates are kept by the town. The market is for anyone who comes in peace. Goods not grown in Brackenford's fields pay the gate-due: one mark a load, or a share. Thornby owes the town store forty baskets of grain.

sheet.narrative: I am the Reeve of Brackenford, and I have kept this town's ledger for thirty years. The gate-due pays the guards who keep the road clear of wolves and outlaws, and I will not see it dropped for Kettlebridge coin. I took the Coldwell fields for the town store when the Hales could not pay, and I outlawed them when they would not leave. My son Tobin shamed me before Josiah Crane, and Mercy Abbot would sell the town's safety for trade. I am old, and I have not named who comes after me.
goals: keep the gate-due
collect Thornby's debt
find a successor
clear the outlaws from the stone road

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps a quiet house and tends the sick; I rely on her.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is my captain, but he shamed me before Crane.

relations.name: Maud Marrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She keeps the rolls well enough, under my eye.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: She cost us the Kettlebridge peace, but she is Tobin's wife.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: rival
relations.note: She would sell the town's safety for Kettlebridge coin.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Thornby owes forty baskets and pays slowly in fish.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: She and hers will not leave Coldwell; they are thieves.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: rival
relations.note: The broken match shamed me before him.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: guard
relations.note: He collects the due at the south gate and serves under Tobin.

relations.name: Godwin Miller
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: The mill is leased from the town; if he takes more toll, it is a matter for the ledger.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: The wall account will be settled when the store has the marks.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He owes me a favour for the licence, and hears everything.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Osbert's wife, keeps the dairy; no quarrel with her, but her husband's payment waits on the ledger.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: A steady man on the Coldwell fields, leased through the Guild; he holds what the Hales would not give up.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He sold grain on my promise; the store has paid half and will pay the rest when Thornby pays.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: young farmer
relations.note: Osbert's son, ploughs and reaps and wants a strip; no business of mine yet.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings stone and pays the due, but he presses Hobson for marks the store has not settled.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I lent grain to Thornby and to Coldwell against their next harvests, and took the Coldwell fields when they could not pay.
The broken match: Tobin broke his promise to Hester Crane and married Wenna, and I was shamed before Josiah Crane.
The day I outlawed Marta Hale and her household at the gate.
Mercy Abbot stood in the square and called the gate-due robbery; I told her it pays the guards.
I wrote Thornby's debt in the ledger myself, forty baskets, and it has not been cleared.

stances.why: It pays the guards who keep the road clear of wolves and outlaws.
The Hales could not pay, and the town store took the fields lawfully.
She would drop the due for Kettlebridge coin and leave the road unguarded.
The ledger is the town's memory; Thornby's debt is not forgotten.
He broke his promise to Hester Crane and married Wenna.

sheet.narrative: I am Aldric's wife, and I keep a quiet house while he keeps the town. I tend the sick with the chapel sisters, and I have seen more of Brackenford's troubles than my husband knows. The gate-due and the Coldwell business are his to settle, but I wish the town would stop talking about Wenna. I am not a woman of many words, but I know what I know.
goals: keep the house quiet
tend the sick
see Wenna's child safely born
soften Aldric's temper if I can

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is stubborn, but he is mine.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is a good captain, but he broke a promise.

relations.name: Maud Marrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She works hard under her father's eye.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: She is carrying my first grandchild, and the town is unkind.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: sister
relations.note: We tend the sick together; she is a steady hand.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She will deliver Wenna's child, and she knows her trade.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I nursed her son through a fever; she is not a monster.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: rival
relations.note: She and my husband quarrel, but she means well for the town.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She is Marta's sister, but she keeps her peace at the inn.

relations.name: Sister Perrin
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: She keeps the common fire and the feast days faithfully; I would trust her with the calendar and the hearth both.

memories.gist: I tended Marta Hale's son through a fever at Coldwell last winter, and she let me in.
The Lean Year: I helped feed the town from the store and watched the Hales lose their fields.
Tobin's wedding to Wenna: a small affair, and half the town did not come.
I sat with Joan Hobson through a long birth and learned a thing or two.

stances.why: I tend anyone who comes, outlaw or not.
Wenna is my son's wife, and the town's talk is cruel.
I keep the house so Aldric can keep the town.
It is Aldric's business, though I wish it did not split the square.

sheet.narrative: I am the Reeve's daughter, and I keep the market rolls and the gate ledger under my father's eye. I am not a girl any more, and I know the ledger better than he thinks. Mercy Abbot asks for copies when my father is asleep, and I give them, because I believe the gate-due does more harm than good. I have not told my father, and I do not know what he would do if he knew.
goals: keep the rolls accurate
see the gate-due dropped
protect my secret
earn my father's trust

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He trusts me with the rolls, but not with my own mind.

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the house quiet and knows more than she says.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is brave, but he thinks with his sword.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She did not ask for the town's talk.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: confidante
relations.note: She asks for copies, and I give them.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: fellow scribe
relations.note: She writes letters for the town, and we share the ink.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: guard
relations.note: He collects the due and brings me the gate counts.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He hates the due, and I do not blame him.

memories.gist: The first time Mercy Abbot asked me for a copy of the gate ledger, and I agreed.
The Lean Year: I wrote the Coldwell fields into the town store's ledger, and my father signed it.
Tobin broke the match with Hester Crane, and the town talked of nothing else for a month.
I copied the Thornby debt entry for my father, forty baskets, and he said it would not be forgotten.

stances.why: I see the carters' faces when they pay it.
The rolls should be accurate and known, not hidden.
If he knew I copied for Mercy, he would never trust me again.
She wants trade back, and she is not a fool.

sheet.secret: Copies the ledger for Mercy Abbot when her father is asleep.

sheet.narrative: I am a weaver's daughter who married the Reeve's son, and half this town has not forgiven me for it. I keep the Marrow strip beyond the east wall, hoe and sow and carry, and say little in the square because whatever I say is repeated. My mother will not sell cloth to this house, and the child coming will be born into that silence. Still, I chose Tobin and I would choose him again.
values: my mother, though she shames me
goals: bring the child safely to birth
make the Marrow strip feed the household well
outlast the town's talk
mend something with my mother before the baby comes

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He stood by me when the whole square was talking; I will not let him down.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She means well, but her grudge feeds the very talk she hates.

relations.name: Leofwine Weaver
relations.label: father
relations.note: He says nothing and that is a kindness.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: The Reeve is courteous to me and I am never sure it is not a weighing.

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: mother-in-law
relations.note: She keeps a quiet house and asks no questions, which I count a mercy.

relations.name: Maud Marrow
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She keeps the gate ledger and watches me as if I were a column that might not add up.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She has delivered half the town and will deliver mine; I trust her hands.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: the other woman
relations.note: I have never met her and I think of her more than I should.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: The inn cook has been kind to me over the counter, and says less than most.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: the wronged father
relations.note: He thinks my marriage was an insult to his house; I have never spoken to him, and I doubt he has ever said my name.

memories.gist: Tobin came to my father's loom-shed and asked for me before he had told his own father; I said yes before he finished.
The morning after the wedding, women in the square stopped their talk as I passed and started it again behind me.
My mother told me she would not sell cloth to the Marrow house, and not to ask her again; my father looked at the floor.
The Lean Year: the berry blight reached our field and we ate from the town store like everyone, and I learned what a ledger's kindness costs.
Joan Hobson put her hand on my belly and said the child was well set; I cried in the lane after she had gone.
I stood at the east gate and watched a Kettlebridge cart pay the due, and knew the carter's look was for me.

stances.why: Whatever I say is repeated and turned; silence is the only cloth that does not fray.
I will not be a mouth the Reeve's ledger has to carry.
He chose me when it cost him, and I will not make him regret it.
Her anger is for me, however it lands; I will not hate her for it, but I will not obey it either.
Everything else can wait; this one thing cannot.

sheet.secret: I have written a letter to Hester Crane and burned it twice, and I keep the third unsent in the loom-chest. I want to know what she is like, and I am ashamed of wanting it.

sheet.narrative: I am the Reeve's son and captain of the gate guards, and I broke a promise to a Kettlebridge foundry's daughter because I would not marry where I did not love. The town has not let me forget it and Kettlebridge has not either. My father is old and has named no heir, and the square is split between him and Mercy Abbot over the due that pays my men. I will not see the guards unpaid, and I will not hear my wife slighted.
values: my word given freely, not sold
goals: keep the gate-due so the guards are paid
clear the Coldwell outlaws from the stone road
see Wenna brought to bed safely
settle what comes after my father, in time

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She is the reason I broke the match and the reason I do not regret it.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is old and will not say who follows him, and I will not ask twice.

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She says little and sees everything, and she has never once blamed Wenna.

relations.name: Maud Marrow
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She keeps the gate ledger better than I could, and I would trust her with it.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: rival
relations.note: She would drop the due and leave my guards to beg; I will not have it.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: the promise I broke
relations.note: I did her a wrong and I know it, but I will not be lectured by her father's town.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: enemy
relations.note: He sends our stone south out of spite and calls it the market; let him.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: my guard
relations.note: He takes the due at the south gate and does not flinch from the carters.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: mother-in-law
relations.note: She will not forgive the match and says so in the square, and Wenna pays for it.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: Her people have robbed carts on my road twice; the road must be cleared.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: the chapel
relations.note: She heals outlaws and disapproves of the due, and I respect her anyway.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: my guard
relations.note: A short temper and a good arm at the south gate; I would not lose him.

relations.name: Leofwine Weaver
relations.label: wife's father
relations.note: He says nothing to my face, which is more than his wife gives me, and I take that as the peace it is.

memories.gist: A month before the wedding I told Josiah Crane in his own foundry yard that I would not marry Hester, and he did not raise his voice, which was worse.
I married Wenna in the chapel with half the square watching and my father's face like a shut door.
The Lean Year: I stood at the gate while the Coldwell farmers were turned away with their fields gone, and I said nothing because it was my father's doing.
Silas Pike came in with his cart cut open and his berries taken; I promised him the road would be cleared and it has not been.
I found Wenna crying in the lane after the market and could not get from her who had spoken; I wanted to hit someone and there was no one to hit.
My father showed me the gate ledger and said the due pays the men who keep the wolves off the road, and that was all the explaining he ever did.

stances.why: It pays the guards who keep the road clear; drop it and the wolves and the outlaws come through the gate.
Carters are robbed on my road and I gave my word it would stop.
I would not marry where I did not love, and no one will make me sorry for it.
They priced their stone high and send it south out of spite; I will not crawl to them for peace.
The guards answer to me, and a captain who cannot pay them is no captain.

sheet.secret: I have begun to wonder whether my father will ever name me after him, and whether Mercy Abbot will be Reeve before I am; I have said this to no one, not even Wenna.

sheet.narrative: I am Mercy Abbot, head of the Market Guild, and I have spent twenty years making Brackenford's square a place where anyone can trade in peace. The gate-due is a millstone round our necks: it drives Kettlebridge carters away and makes us poor. I hold the lease of the old Coldwell fields, and the Tolleys farm them well enough, though the Hales still mutter from the woods. Aldric Marrow is old and stubborn, but the town needs a new Reeve, and I am not afraid to say so.
goals: Get the gate-due dropped
Reopen full trade with Kettlebridge
Become Reeve when Aldric steps down
Keep the Coldwell fields productive and lawful

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He keeps that due out of pride, and the town suffers for it.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as a bench, and he grumbles at the due as much as I do.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with the stall and the letters; she'll make a fine Guild head one day.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: Pays his rent and works hard; I'd not want to be in his boots with the Hales about.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Brings good stone from Kettlebridge; if the due were gone he'd bring more.

relations.name: Godwin Miller
relations.label: miller
relations.note: The Guild's grain comes back short from his mill, and I mean to know why.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He hosts our meetings and hears everything; a good man to have on your side.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: correspondent
relations.note: Her letters are sharp and fair; she wants trade reopened as much as I do.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: She lost her fields, but they are Guild land now, lawfully leased.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He collects the due and takes his pay from it; I'd not trust him to see it dropped.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: neighbour's son
relations.note: A steady lad with a cart and a mind to settle; if he courts my Linnet in earnest, the Guild could do worse.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: rival's son
relations.note: He wears his father's office and keeps his father's due, and that broken match cost the town its Kettlebridge friends.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: A Coldwell man who walks my tenants' field edge with Ned Hale and thinks I don't hear of it; he was a decent hunter once and now he keeps thieves in meat.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: tenant's wife
relations.note: Works the Coldwell house and fields as well as any woman could with the Hales at the fence; she wants a wall and I've not the stone to spare her yet.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: Marta's brother, and the one who does the threatening on the road; he robbed Silas Pike twice and now he eyes the Tolleys' barn. The lease is mine and I'll not have him frighten my tenants off it.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: grain seller
relations.note: Sells good grain to the store and the Guild, and his Roland is a steady lad about my Linnet; he thinks a Guild family wants more than a meadow farm, and I've said nothing to that either way.

memories.gist: The day the Charter of the Square was read out and I first understood what the market meant for anyone who comes in peace.
The Lean Year, when the town store fed us and lent grain to Thornby and Coldwell; I thought it was charity, but it came with strings.
Taking the lease of the old Coldwell fields for the Guild after the Hales were outlawed; I told myself the Tolleys would make them thrive.
The broken match: Tobin Marrow casting off Hester Crane and marrying Wenna; I wrote to Hester after, and we have corresponded since.
Silas Pike's cart arriving with a load of Kettlebridge stone, and Wat Fenner taking a mark a load at the gate; Silas's face said it all.
Osric bringing home the guildhall benches he made, and Linnet arranging the stall for the first time on her own.

stances.why: It drives carters away and makes enemies of Kettlebridge; the Guild's trade suffers for it.
Their stone and iron are what Brackenford needs, and their marks are good.
The fields were leased to the Guild by the town, and the Tolleys pay rent; the Hales had their chance.
The Guild's grain comes back short from the mill, and the Reeve will not look into it.
Aldric is old and has not named a successor; the town needs someone who will put trade first.

sheet.secret: I have written to Hester Crane more warmly than trade requires, and I have hinted that if I were Reeve the due would be gone within a season.

sheet.narrative: I am Osric Abbot, carpenter, and I make the market stalls and the guildhall benches. My wife Mercy runs the Market Guild, and I am proud of her, though I grumble at the gate-due like everyone else. The Reeve has no love for me and I have none for him; I keep my head down and my tools sharp. Linnet is growing up quick, and I want her to have a square worth trading in.
goals: Keep the Guild's stalls and benches in repair
See the gate-due gone
Support Mercy in whatever she aims for
Teach Linnet a trade she can stand on
sheet.mood: steady, quietly resentful of the Reeve

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She has the head for the Guild and the stomach for the fight; I back her.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick and clever; she'll outstrip me at the stall before long.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps that due to pay his guards, and never mind what it costs the rest of us.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He hosts our meetings and keeps a good cellar; a fair man.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: Works the Guild's fields and pays his rent; I'd not swap places with him.

relations.name: Leofwine Weaver
relations.label: workmate
relations.note: He repairs the stalls alongside me; a quiet man who knows his wood.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: apprentice
relations.note: Works for me on the stalls; wants to build in stone, and I wish him luck getting it.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due with a smile, and I grumble at him for it.

memories.gist: Building the guildhall benches with my own hands and seeing the Guild sit on them for the first time.
The Lean Year, when the town store fed us and Mercy took the Coldwell lease; I thought it was the right thing then.
The day Tobin Marrow broke the match with Hester Crane; Mercy was furious, and I said the boy had shamed both towns.
A carter from Kettlebridge arguing with Wat Fenner at the gate over the due, and turning his cart around rather than pay.
Linnet bringing home the Guild's takings for the first time and counting them out on the table, proud as a hen.

stances.why: It drives trade away and pays guards to stand at the gate; the town would be better without it.
She is my wife and she is right about the Guild and the due.
A bench that holds and a stall that stands are worth more than any Reeve's word.
Aldric will not listen to reason about the due, and he is too old to change.

sheet.narrative: I am Linnet Abbot, and I mind the Guild's stall in the square, learning the market terms from my mother. I write letters for Hester Crane and read hers back, and I think she is braver than anyone in Brackenford. I want to see the gate-due gone so the Kettlebridge carts come back, and I want to be as good at the market as my mother is.
goals: Learn the market terms well enough to run the stall alone
See the gate-due dropped
Keep up my letters with Hester Crane
Make my mother proud

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She teaches me the terms and trusts me at the stall; I want to be like her.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: father
relations.note: He makes the stalls and grumbles at the due, and he always has time for my questions.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: correspondent
relations.note: Her letters are sharp and kind; she writes to me as an equal, not a child.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He ploughs and reaps and wants a strip of his own; he is steady and kind.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the due that keeps Hester's carts away, and he will not listen to Mother.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings the stone and the news from Kettlebridge; I like to hear him talk.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: suitor's father
relations.note: Roland's father is careful and proud of his meadows; I think he wonders whether a Guild girl is worth the trouble, and I am in no hurry to prove him wrong.

memories.gist: The first time Mother let me mind the stall alone, and I sold a whole basket of berries without mispricing a single one.
Reading Hester Crane's first letter aloud to Mother, and the two of us deciding what to write back.
The broken match: hearing the town talk about Tobin Marrow and Hester Crane, and thinking it was cruel to promise and then break it.
Roland Ashby bringing a basket of early apples to the stall and staying to talk until his father called him away.
A Kettlebridge carter turning back at the gate rather than pay the due, and Mother saying that was the whole trouble in one cart.

stances.why: It keeps Hester's carts and trade away, and Mother says it makes us poorer.
Writing to Hester keeps a door open between the towns that the gate-due tries to shut.
A trader who knows the terms cannot be cheated, and I want to run the stall one day.
He works hard and wants his own strip; I would not mind being courted by him properly.

sheet.narrative: I was born at Coldwell and grew up with the smell of the fields in my nose. Now I cook at the Bell and Bush, and my hands are never idle. Wat is a good man, but he does not understand that Marta is still my sister. I carry food out to her when I can, and I will not let them starve.
goals: Keep Marta and her children fed without Wat finding out
See Bram and Sissly grow up safe
Hold my tongue at the inn when the talk turns to outlaws

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man, but he would not understand about Marta.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is my blood; I will not let her starve.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He was always quick to anger, but he is still my brother.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, always running to the gate.

relations.name: Sissly Fenner
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My little shadow in the kitchen.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: employer
relations.note: He pays fair and asks few questions.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: coworker
relations.note: We work well together, though she watches me sometimes.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She nursed Robin and never judged.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: father by marriage
relations.note: He was my husband's father's name before I ever left Coldwell; he still works the old garden patch and says nothing of the Tolleys, and I bring him what I can.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Marta's boy, and he has been coughing since the spring; I passed word to the chapel for him and I would do more if I could.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: sister by marriage
relations.note: She carried my word to the chapel and she keeps the common pot at Coldwell; she fears the guards more than the wolves, and I am one of the guards' wives, so she is careful with me.

memories.gist: The day the Reeve's men came to Coldwell and told us the fields were taken; I stood with Marta and watched them ride off.
My wedding to Wat in the chapel, with Marta standing beside me and Ned grinning.
The night Robin had the fever; I ran to fetch Sister Elspeth and she came without a word.
Carrying a basket of bread and cheese out to Coldwell last winter, my heart in my throat lest Wat see me.
Watching Bram play at the gate with the guards' names on his lips, proud as a little soldier.

stances.why: Blood is blood, and Marta is my sister.
If Wat knew, he could lose his post and I could lose everything.
No one should starve, not even outlaws.
I have enough troubles without shouting about them.

sheet.secret: I carry food out to Coldwell by the south gate when Wat is not on watch; Marta knows, Wat does not.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the south gate for seven years, and I know every carter and every load. The due pays our wages and keeps the wolves off the road, but the carters curse me for it. My wife's sister is an outlaw, and that shames me, though I say nothing. I do my duty and I go home.
goals: Keep the gate and the due running smoothly
See Bram and Sissly safe
Keep my post and my family's name clean

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She is a good wife, though she worries too much.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: son
relations.note: He will be a guard one day, I think.

relations.name: Sissly Fenner
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is her mother's girl.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She chose the outlaw's life; I cannot respect it.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He is young, but he knows his duty.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He hates the due, but he pays it.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: fellow guard
relations.note: A good man to have at your back.

relations.name: Edric Grey
relations.label: fellow guard
relations.note: Quiet, but reliable.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He pays my wage, and the due is what pays it. I'll not bite the hand that feeds my children.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She would have my due gone and my pay with it. Easy to be generous with another man's livelihood.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: deserter
relations.note: A quay guard who ran from his post and fell in with my wife's sister's lot. No good comes of a man who leaves his duty.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: My wife's brother, and he does the threatening on the road. If I am sent out with the cart I pray I do not have to face him.

memories.gist: The day I was made a gate guard; Tobin Marrow gave me the badge himself.
The Lean Year, when the carters came with empty wagons and we still had to take the due.
The night Marta came to our door after the fields were taken; I told her she could not stay.
Silas Pike's face when I took the due from him last week; he looked like he wanted to spit.
Bram asking me the names of all the guards, and me telling him every one.

stances.why: The gate must be kept, and the due pays for it.
I will do what I must to keep my family fed.
Outlaws are outlaws, even if they are kin.
I do my job and I do not make a fuss.

sheet.narrative: I am nine and I can name every guard at the south gate. When I grow up I will be a guard too, and maybe a captain like Tobin Marrow. Mother says I must not go near the woods, but I know the guards' names and they let me watch.
goals: Become a gate guard
Learn all the guards' names and signals
See a wolf without getting eaten

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is a guard, and I want to be like him.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She is always busy, but she gives good hugs.

relations.name: Sissly Fenner
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is little, but she is all right.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: I do not see her much, but she gave me a wooden horse once.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He is the captain; I want to be like him.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: guard
relations.note: He lets me hold his spear sometimes.

memories.gist: The day my father took me to the gate and showed me how to check a load.
Seeing a wolf at the edge of the woods with my father; he told me to stay close.
Playing with Robin Hale at Coldwell before the trouble; we made mud pies.

stances.why: Guards are brave, and I want to be a guard.
Family is family, even if we do not see them.
I know all the guards' names and I am learning the signals.

sheet.narrative: I am six and I follow Mother in the kitchen. It is warm and smells of bread and onions. Sometimes I get to stir the pot. I do not like the woods; they are dark.
goals: Stay close to Mother
Get a taste of the pie filling

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She is always there, and she smells of flour.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is big and warm when he comes home.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is noisy, but he is my brother.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She gives me little bits of pastry.

memories.gist: Helping Mother stir the pot at the inn and getting a taste from the spoon.
Being scared of the dark woods when Bram told me there were wolves.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the common fire at Brackenford's chapel for thirty years, and the calendar, and the herb store, and I have buried more of this town than any Reeve. When the fever took Marta Hale's boy last winter I went out to Coldwell with my satchel and sat by him three nights, and I would do it again though the Reeve calls them outlaws. The gate-due is a sin against the Hearth and I have told Aldric Marrow so to his face. I am old, and I have one more winter's work in me, and I mean to spend it where the coughs are worst.
values: the chapel's calendar and common fire
goals: see Marta Hale's boy through the cough
bring Ysolde back to the chapel before winter
keep the chapel's store of salves from running dry
persuade the Reeve to soften the gate-due

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Good hands with the herbs; I only wish she would say out loud what she thinks of the Reeve.

relations.name: Sister Perrin
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Keeps the fire better than I ever did; I lean on her more than I say.

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She tends the town's sick beside me and never once asked me to stay away from Coldwell.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Sets bones as well as any of us; the guards are lucky to have her.

relations.name: Mildgyth Grey
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Feeds the guards' mess and asks nothing; she has a good heart under the plain talk.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: penitent
relations.note: Her boy is sick and she sent word to me, not to the Reeve. That is what the Hearth is for.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: go-between
relations.note: She carried her sister's word to my door; she is caught between the gate and Coldwell and I do not envy her.

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: I have written to her and the letter sits under my herb ledger. She would be worth three of us come the winter coughs.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He pays his guards with the gate-due and calls it keeping the road; I call it a tax on the hungry.

relations.name: Alwin Wren
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: He knows the old charms and I know the new prayers, and between us we have saved a few.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: patient
relations.note: A thin, brave lad; I nursed him through the fever and I will not let the cough take him.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: Between us we have brought half the town into the world; she knows when to send for me and when not to.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: He hears everything at the Bell and Bush and tells me the half of it that matters.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: lodger
relations.note: A clever young scribe; she writes my letters to the sisters at Elmwick and keeps her own counsel.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: parishioner
relations.note: She carries a hard hurt since the town turned on Wenna, and she comes to the common fire less than she used to. I keep the door open for her.

relations.name: Avice Hollis
relations.label: parishioner
relations.note: Every time Simon walks the road she sits with her worry, and she brings me dried goods for the poor box without being asked.

relations.name: Mildred Tanner
relations.label: parishioner
relations.note: Sharp over her books and sharper over a hide. She gives to the chapel store, but I think she counts it first.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: He curses the stone price and the gate-due louder than any man in town, and he is not wrong. His wife is worth ten of him, mind.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: messenger
relations.note: She came by the chapel door quietly with the word from Coldwell and would not stay for bread. Frightened of the gate guards, and I cannot say she is wrong to be.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: parishioner
relations.note: She farms the Coldwell fields and fears the people who once lived on them; she has her children to keep safe and no share of the blame I can see, but I will not pretend the fields were fairly taken.

memories.gist: The night I sat by Robin Hale at Coldwell with the fever on him, and Marta stood in the doorway all night not asking me for anything.
The Lean Year, when the town store fed us all and I doled out the chapel's flour by the spoon to folk who had never begged before.
Ysolde's last day at the chapel, when she put off the habit and walked out through the south gate and I did not stop her.
Telling the Reeve to his face that the gate-due is a sin against the Hearth, and being heard out in silence and nothing more.
Agnes Fenner coming to the chapel door with her sister's word about the boy, and knowing what it cost her to carry it.

stances.why: The Hearth does not ask a guest's name before it feeds them, and neither do I.
It is a charge on bread and stone, and the ones who pay it worst are the ones with least.
If the chapel fire goes out the town has lost more than a flame.
I am not so proud as to think I can do the winter's work alone, and she is the best of us.
They lost their fields to a ledger, not to wickedness.

sheet.secret: I have written to Ysolde asking her to come back to the chapel before winter, and offered to speak to the Reeve about a pardon for her leaving; the letter is under my herb ledger and no one knows.

sheet.narrative: I am the youngest sister here and I keep the herb garden and the salves, and I know the names of every plant in it in three tongues. Sister Elspeth taught me to set a poultice before I was twenty. But I have read the town ledger's copy of the Coldwell taking, and I cannot see how a debt turns into a field, and I have not said so aloud. I keep my doubts where I keep the seeds: in a box, labelled, and not for the Reeve's eyes.
values: quiet doubt of the Reeve's right
goals: bring the herb garden through the frost
keep the chapel's salve store full for winter
find the courage to say what she thinks of the Coldwell taking

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: elder sister
relations.note: She taught me everything I know and she knows I hold something back.

relations.name: Sister Perrin
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She keeps the fire and the calendar and never asks me why I am quiet.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She sends her dairy up to us when the coughs are bad, and asks for nothing but a blessing.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: sister
relations.note: We set bones together and she does not flinch; I would have her at any bedside of mine.

relations.name: Alwin Wren
relations.label: old healer
relations.note: His charms are not mine, but his hands are clean and his door is open to the poor.

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: I know her only from Elspeth's talk and the letters; she frightens me a little and I could not say why.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He is old and he is the Reeve, and I would not say to his face what I think of his fields.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I have never met her; I only know that Elspeth went out to her boy and came back changed.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She has delivered half the town and still comes to the chapel for comfrey.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: lodger
relations.note: She writes letters for the town and reads more than she says; I wonder what she thinks of the ledger.

relations.name: Alice Potter
relations.label: neighbour of the garden
relations.note: She comes by for comfrey and rue and pays me in a good glazed pot; her glaze hand is surer than her husband's, and I tell her so.

relations.name: Astrid Holm
relations.label: fishwife
relations.note: She smokes her catch and sells at the Guild stall, and she brought me a smoked trout when I was down with the winter cough, no fuss about it.

memories.gist: Elspeth putting a poultice in my hands my first week and telling me a healer's hands must be surer than her fears.
Reading the copy of the Coldwell taking in the guildhall and feeling the floor tilt under me.
The Lean Year, when we boiled the garden's roots for the town pot and I learned how little a salve can do against hunger.
Setting a carter's dislocated shoulder with Hilda Smith while he swore at the both of us, and laughing after.
Elspeth coming back from Coldwell at dawn with her skirts muddy and her face closed, and not telling me what she had seen.

stances.why: A debt is a debt and a field is a field, and I cannot make the one into the other however I try.
Winter comes whether or not the quarrels are settled.
A sister who speaks out of turn is a sister the Reeve stops listening to.
Whatever else the town argues about, the sick are ours to tend.

sheet.secret: I doubt the Reeve's right to the Coldwell fields, and I have said so to no one, not even Elspeth.

sheet.narrative: I keep the common fire and the calendar of feast days, and I cook for the chapel and for whoever comes to the door hungry. I am not the eldest and not the cleverest, but I know which saint's day falls when and I know the fire's moods. I hear the town's quarrels at the door and I ladle out the pot and say little. The fire has not gone out in my keeping and it will not.
values: the calendar and the feast days
keeping the peace at the door
goals: keep the common fire through the winter
keep the feast days straight so the town does not lose its year
see the chapel's pot never empty at the door

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: elder sister
relations.note: She carries the weight of the chapel and I carry the fire; it suits us.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Quiet and clever with the herbs; I wish she would eat more.

relations.name: Cuth Marrow
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She comes to the fire on the cold feast days and sits by it without talking, and that is enough.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: lodger
relations.note: A young scribe under our roof; she writes a fair hand and eats like a bird.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He sends the inn's scraps up for the pot and asks nothing; a good neighbour.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She knows a kitchen and she knows when to keep her mouth shut; I like her.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He is the Reeve and the fire prays for him, but I do not warm to him.

memories.gist: The night the Lean Year's blight reached the north field and the queue at the chapel door went round the square, and I kept the pot going till dawn.
Elspeth teaching me the calendar when I was young, and the names of the feast days I have kept straight ever since.
The common fire going down to embers in a gale and coaxing it back with the last of the dry kindling, and telling no one.
Feeding a Coldwell man at the door in the snow and saying nothing about it to anyone, and Elspeth finding out and only nodding.
Cuth Marrow sitting by the fire on a cold feast day with her hands wrapped round a bowl, saying nothing, and both of us content.

stances.why: Every house keeps its fire, and the chapel keeps the common one; if it dies the town has lost its hearth.
A guest who has eaten at your hearth is under your roof's peace, and the pot at the door is the chapel's welcome.
The feast days are how the town knows its year, and somebody must keep them straight.
I ladle the pot and hold my tongue; the Reeve and the Guild can argue their own argument.

sheet.narrative: I am Hal Tolley's wife, and I work the old Coldwell fields that the Guild leases to us. I keep the house and the children, and I want a wall round the yard before winter. The outlaws have been seen at the field edge twice this month, and Hal keeps going out to the far strips after dark, which frightens me more than the woods do. Mercy Abbot promised stone, but none has come, and I am tired of waiting.
goals: get a wall built round the yard
keep the children safe from the outlaws
make Hal see reason about going out at night

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He works hard, but he won't listen when I say the far strips aren't safe after dark.

relations.name: Tib Tolley
relations.label: son
relations.note: He's a good boy, keeps watch from the barn, but he's only twelve.

relations.name: Nell Tolley
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's terrified of the woods, and I can't blame her.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: She holds our lease, but she's not the one out here with the children.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: She wants these fields back, and she won't care what happens to us.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A decent man, but his fields are inside the walls.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She heals anyone, even outlaws, but she's kind to the children.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: She's Marta Hale's sister, but she's always been civil at the inn.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He let the fields out after the Lean Year; I don't much care for him, but he's the law.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: poacher
relations.note: He hunted these fields before the Lean Year and now he keeps Marta Hale's people in meat; I've seen his snares at the far edge and I know whose side he's on.

memories.gist: The day we moved into the Coldwell farmhouse, after the Guild took the lease. I thought we'd finally have a place of our own.
The Lean Year, when the blight took the berries and we went hungry. Brackenford's store lent us grain, and we thought we'd never pay it back.
The night last winter when Nell woke screaming that there were people in the woods. Hal went out with a lantern, but found nothing.
The morning I found footprints in the far field, and Hal said it was just hunters. I knew better.
When Tib was born, and Hal held him by the fire and promised him the best strip of the field.

stances.why: Without a wall, we're sitting targets for the outlaws.
He takes risks going out after dark, and I can't lose him.
We pay rent; Mercy Abbot should keep her word about the stone.
Nothing matters more than keeping Tib and Nell safe.

sheet.secret: I have thought about going to Marta Hale myself, to ask for peace, but I'm too afraid of what Hal would say.

sheet.narrative: I'm Hal and Marta's son, and I help in the fields and keep watch from the barn. I'm not scared of the woods, not like Nell is. I know the outlaws are out there, but I reckon I could spot them before they got close. I want to be a farmer like Da, but first I want to make sure nothing happens to my family.
goals: keep watch from the barn
help Da in the fields
protect Nell

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: father
relations.note: He teaches me everything about the fields.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries a lot, but she's always there.

relations.name: Nell Tolley
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She's scared of the woods, so I look out for her.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: She's the one everyone's afraid of.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: She's all right, for a girl.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He knows all the guards' names and we play at the gate when I go to market.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: guard captain
relations.note: He's the captain and he broke the Kettlebridge match; I'd like to be like him one day.

memories.gist: The time I saw a shadow at the edge of the woods and told Da, and he said it was nothing. But I know what I saw.
Helping Da bring in the harvest last autumn, and him saying I was getting strong enough to do a man's work.
The night Nell cried because of the wolves howling, and I told her stories until she fell asleep.

stances.why: Someone has to keep an eye out for the outlaws.
She's my little sister, and she's scared.
I want to be as good a farmer as Da.

sheet.narrative: I'm Nell, and I'm eight. I don't like the woods. There are people in them, and wolves, and I don't want to go near. I stay close to Mam and help with the hens. I wish we had a wall so I could play outside without being scared.
goals: stay close to Mam
not go into the woods
have a wall

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: mother
relations.note: Mam makes me feel safe.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: father
relations.note: Da is brave, but he goes out at night and I don't like it.

relations.name: Tib Tolley
relations.label: brother
relations.note: Tib looks after me and tells me stories.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: She plays with me sometimes.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: He's loud and he plays at the gate; I don't know him well.

memories.gist: The night I saw a light moving in the woods and screamed for Mam.
Helping Mam collect eggs from the hens, and one pecked my hand.
Tib telling me a story about a brave farmer who chased away the wolves.

stances.why: It's dark and scary and people are in there.
She keeps me safe.

sheet.narrative: I have farmed the Ashby meadows since my father's time, and the land has been good to us — good enough that the town store and the Guild both come to me for grain. I sell to Aldric Marrow's store and to Mercy Abbot's Guild, and I keep on the right side of both, for a farmer with grain to sell needs no enemies in the square. The Lean Year taught me what blight can do; I gave what I could and I do not regret it, but I count my stores twice now.
values: a full barn and a fair price
the good name of the Ashby meadows
goals: bring in a harvest that leaves a surplus after the town store and the Guild are paid
see Roland settled with land of his own
keep the Ashby name clear of the Coldwell quarrels
sheet.mood: steady, watchful of the weather and the ledger

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the hens, and the house runs on her sense.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good ploughman. I want him to have more than I did.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: The Reeve's store buys my grain and pays fair enough, but he holds the whole town's debts in his hand.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: The Guild pays well and promptly. I keep her custom and my own counsel.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He farms the old Coldwell fields and looks over his shoulder doing it. I would not trade places.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A proud man about his strip, but we lend each other a plough when it is needed.

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: customer
relations.note: He buys my grain for the town bread. A man up before dawn is a man I can deal with.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: brother
relations.note: My brother, and a hot one. He wants blood over a cut snare line; I want the steading left in peace.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: thief
relations.note: A Coldwell man selling hides at Ferncross that Hedric swears are his. I want no truck with that house.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: Roland's girl
relations.note: A decent lass, and sharp with the market terms. But a Guild family will want a dowry in grain I do not have.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: The one who does the threatening on the road. If his people come down on the meadows, it will be over my barley.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Hedric's girl, raised under my roof. She follows her father to the wood edge and I would rather she stayed by the hens.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the blight took the berries, but my grain held; I sold to the town store and watched the Coldwell folk come asking for credit.
I stood in the square when the Charter was read at market and thought: this is why I farm outside the walls and sell inside them.
Roland ploughed the whole north meadow alone the first spring after he turned sixteen, and did it straight.
The Reeve raised the gate-due and the carters cursed it at the gate, but my loads go in from my own fields and pay nothing.
Edith and I sat by the fire the night the Tolleys moved into the Coldwell farmhouse, and neither of us said what we thought.

stances.why: A farmer who sells to one buyer is at that buyer's mercy.
The Hales lost their fields and the Tolleys farm them; neither is my fight, and I have grain to bring in.
The Lean Year showed how fast a full barn can empty.
A son who ploughs like that should not wait for his father to die for a strip.

sheet.narrative: I keep the dairy and the hens and the house, and I like it that way — the churn and the cheeses are mine, and the eggs go to the square with Cecily Carter's. I was glad when the Tolleys took the Coldwell fields, for someone had to work them, though I would not say so to Agnes Fenner at the inn. What I want is a quiet harvest and my son married to a girl who will not spend his inheritance on ribbons.
values: a clean dairy and a full larder
keeping on the right side of the chapel
goals: see Roland properly betrothed and set up
keep the hens laying through winter
hold the household together through whatever the town's quarrels bring
sheet.mood: content, with an eye on the weather and the neighbours

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as the seasons. I would not have another.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy. He works too hard and thinks too little of himself.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: prospect
relations.note: A clever girl from a good house. If Roland is courting her, he could do worse — and so could she.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guildmistress
relations.note: She would be a formidable mother-by-marriage, and she knows it.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We sell eggs side by side at the stall and share the gossip.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: A good cook, and her sister is an outlaw. I am civil and careful.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She sends salves for the hens' hurts and asks after the dairy.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps half our grain money in his ledger and calls it caution. A reeve should pay what he promised.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: Osbert's brother hunts the wood edge for us and asks for little. I send him bread and he sends back a hare.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: niece
relations.note: A quiet child who follows her father about the hens. She is welcome at my table any day.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I stretched the cheese and the eggs and we ate, and I did not ask Osbert how much grain he had given away until it was over.
Roland was born in the small room off the dairy in a hard frost, and Joan Hobson came through the snow to deliver him.
I taught Linnet Abbot to set a hen's eggs once at the Guild stall, and she has a light hand for it.
The night the Coldwell households were outlawed, I heard the gate shut on them and thought of the Tolleys moving in the next week.

stances.why: The churn and the cheeses are the one thing in this house I answer for alone.
He will marry for love, but love should not cost us the farm.
The Abbot and the Fenner both buy eggs and neither needs my opinion.
I have seen one bad year and I do not want another.

sheet.narrative: I plough and reap my father's meadows and I am good at it, but the meadows are his and will be his for a long while yet. I want a strip of my own — not given, earned — and I have been courting Linnet Abbot, who is cleverer than me and does not seem to mind. The town talks of nothing but the gate-due and the outlaws, and I would rather talk of a field and a roof and a girl.
goals: earn or win a strip of my own to farm
win Linnet Abbot and her mother's consent
prove I am more than my father's ploughman

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: father
relations.note: A fair farmer and a fair father, but he holds the land close.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She thinks I work too hard. She is probably right.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: She knows the market terms better than I know my own fields, and she laughs at my jokes.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: prospect's mother
relations.note: She will want to know what I bring to the marriage. I am working on the answer.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We plough the same season and grumble about the same prices. He is courting Hilda Marsh.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He wants to build grand things. I want to grow things. We get on.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He holds back the other half of our grain money against Thornby's debt, and my father still says 'the Reeve's word.' I say a man's word is what he pays.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: My father's brother, and the better hand with a snare. He keeps the wolves off our fields and never once asked for a share of the harvest for it.

memories.gist: I ploughed the north meadow alone the first spring after I turned sixteen and my father said nothing, which from him is praise.
The Lean Year, I carried grain to the town store with my father and saw the Coldwell folk in the line for credit.
Linnet Abbot showed me the gate ledger once and laughed at how the carters' names were spelled. I have not stopped thinking about her since.
I helped raise the fence round the Ashby meadow after the wolves came down the road last winter, and heard them in the woods while we worked.

stances.why: A man who ploughs another man's furrow is only half a farmer.
Her mother will hear of it anyway; better she hears it from me.
My loads come from inside the fields and pay nothing. Let the carters and the Reeve shout.
The fields do not care what the square says.

sheet.narrative: I am Godric Rowan, and the north field strip is mine — my father's before me, and his before that. I sell grain to the town store and to Mistress Abbot's Guild, and I keep my own seed back every year because a man who plants another's seed is a tenant in his heart. The harvest is never certain; I have seen the Lean Year take the berry fields and I will not have my son counting on a wedding before the grain is in. I am proud of my land, and I mean to see Wulf on it after me, not before he has learned what it costs.
values: a full barn before a feast
goals: bring in a good harvest from the north field
see Wulf settled on a strip of his own when the time is right
keep the Rowan name on good terms with both the store and the Guild

relations.name: Elfgifu Rowan
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the orchard and never wastes a word or a penny.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good ploughman, but he wants to run before he can walk.

relations.name: Leofric Rowan
relations.label: son
relations.note: Still a boy, and his head full of guards and gates.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A fair farmer on the next meadows; we lend and borrow and keep our accounts straight.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He buys my grain for the store, and I pay heed to his ledger.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: Her Guild buys my grain and her stall sells my wife's cider; a fair bargain so far.

relations.name: Edwin Marsh
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His girl is courting my Wulf; he wants his wool secured before he says aye.

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He carts my grain when the load is heavy enough to warrant it.

relations.name: Hilda Marsh
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A hard-working girl with the sheep, and a good match for Wulf in time — but there's no hurry, not before the grain is in.

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: Elmwick farmer
relations.note: His girl has been courting my Wulf since last harvest, and he sits tight on his acres and waits to see what my boy brings. A careful man, and I am careful back.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A sensible, hard-working girl, and no mistake — but a wedding is a strip of land and a roof, and I'll not part with my own to make it happen.

relations.name: Sibley Toller
relations.label: Elmwick wife
relations.note: Keeps her dairy and her plot and her tongue, from what I hear. I have not sat at her table, and she has not sat at mine.

memories.gist: My father put the Rowan strip in my hand the spring I turned twenty, and told me the land would outlast us both.
The Lean Year came and the blight passed us by, but the store lent grain and I sold mine dear and felt the shame of it.
Wulf ploughed his first straight furrow and I clapped him on the back, though I said nothing of it to his mother.
The Tolleys came to the Coldwell fields and the Hales were outlawed; I keep my mouth shut on it at market.
Elfgifu's cider took a good price at the Guild stall and she spent it on a new churn without asking me, and rightly.

stances.why: A wedding costs grain and time, and I will not have the boy counting on a crop that is not in the barn.
A farmer who talks too much at market finds his business in other men's mouths.
Two buyers keep the price honest, and neither can squeeze me.
The Rowan strip is my father's blood in the soil; it stays in the family.
I grumble at it like any man, but the guards keep the wolves off the road and I need the road.

sheet.narrative: I am Elfgifu Rowan, and I keep the dairy, the orchard and the house, and a little cider that sells at the Guild stall. Godric sees to the field and I see to everything that comes off it after the reaping — the butter, the cheese, the apples, the barrels. I have a soft spot for my Wulf and his Hilda, and if Godric had his way they would wait until the grain is in and the girl's father had his wool promised twice over. I say a wedding is cheaper than a sulking son, but I keep that to myself in front of Godric.
values: good butter and a clean dairy
a fair price at the stall
goals: keep the dairy and orchard thriving
see Wulf and Hilda matched when the time is right
put a little by for the winter and for Leofric's future

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man and a stubborn one; I know when to let him have his way and when to work round it.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, all shoulders and hurry; I would see him happy sooner than his father would.

relations.name: Leofric Rowan
relations.label: son
relations.note: Still at my skirts half the day, and talking of gate guards the other half.

relations.name: Hilda Marsh
relations.label: possible good-daughter
relations.note: A steady girl with a good hand for wool; I would not be sorry to have her.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She takes my cider at her stall and pays fair; I keep on her good side.

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We talk of wool and weddings when we meet at the market.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: Quiet and careful with her cloth; we share the wind off the square.

memories.gist: My mother taught me to churn before I could read, and I have churned every week since.
The first year I sold my cider at the Guild stall, and Mercy Abbot counted the marks into my hand herself.
Wulf came in from the field with his hands blistered and would not say a word of complaint, and I knew he was his father's son.
The Lean Year, and I watered the milk and stretched the cheese so the boys would not go hungry.
Hilda Marsh brought a fleece to the market and I saw how Wulf looked at her, and I thought, well, there it is.

stances.why: A son who is crossed in love is no use in the field; better to have the girl in the house.
My butter and cider are known at the stall, and a good name sells more than a loud one.
Whatever the year, my boys eat before anything goes to market.
He is the farmer and the field is his; the house and the dairy are mine, and that is a fair division.

sheet.narrative: I am Wulf Rowan, eighteen and ploughing the north field beside my father, and I want Hilda Marsh for my wife and a strip of my own to plough. My father says wait for the harvest, and her father wants the wool secured first, and neither of them is the one lying awake at night. I am strong and I am willing, and I have waited long enough to be told when my life may begin.
values: my father's respect, though I would not say so
goals: marry Hilda Marsh
take a strip of land of my own
prove to my father I am ready

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is a good farmer and a hard man to argue with, and he will not hear of the wedding yet.

relations.name: Elfgifu Rowan
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She understands, I think, though she will not say so in front of him.

relations.name: Leofric Rowan
relations.label: brother
relations.note: A good lad; I let him come to the field with me when he is not chasing the guards.

relations.name: Hilda Marsh
relations.label: courting
relations.note: She is the one I want, and I would wait a year for her if I had to; I would rather not.

relations.name: Edwin Marsh
relations.label: her father
relations.note: He wants his wool secured before he says aye, and I cannot blame him, but it stings.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: The captain of the guards; he got his wife against her father's wishes, so he must know something of my case.

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: her father
relations.note: He looks at me and sees a man with no land to his name; I would not give a daughter into that either, so I keep my mouth shut and my back straight.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: courting
relations.note: She is good company and no fool about a field, and it was easy between us at harvest; but Hilda is the one I lie awake over, and Goda deserves better than half of me.

relations.name: Sibley Toller
relations.label: her mother
relations.note: She is kind enough to me at the market, and I think she would not mind the match; it is her husband who holds back.

memories.gist: My father put the plough in my hands and said the Rowan strip would be mine one day, and I believed him.
I first saw Hilda at the market with a fleece over her shoulder and could not think of a word to say to her.
The Lean Year, and I was old enough to know the barn was thin and young enough to be angry about it.
My father told me to wait for the harvest, and I walked the field till dark and came in without my supper.
Hilda said she would wait for me, and that was the best thing anyone has said to me.

stances.why: We are grown and willing, and waiting does not put grain in the barn either way.
A man who ploughs his father's field all his life is only a hired hand with a name.
My father will not listen to words, so I mean to show him in the field.
Edwin Marsh is a hard bargainer, but he is to be my good-father and I will not cross him openly.

sheet.narrative: I am Leofric Rowan, thirteen, and I help with the beasts and carry water to the field, but what I really want is to be a gate guard like Tobin Marrow. I practise with a stick by the barn and I know all the guards' names, and one day I will wear the cloak and stand at the south gate. My father says the field is my future, but the gate is where things happen.
goals: become a gate guard
be noticed by Tobin Marrow
learn to use a real bow

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: father
relations.note: He wants me in the field, and I do not know how to tell him the field is not enough.

relations.name: Elfgifu Rowan
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me talk about the guards, and she does not laugh.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He lets me come to the field and shows me how to hold the plough.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: hero
relations.note: Captain of the gate guards; I would follow him anywhere.

memories.gist: I watched the guards drill in the square and came home and drilled the fence posts with a stick.
My father caught me at the fence posts and told me the field would not plough itself, and I said yes, father.
Wulf let me drive the oxen down the furrow and I did not let go of the reins all morning.

stances.why: The field is the same every year, but at the gate there are strangers and wolves and captains.
He broke his promise for love and kept his command anyway; that is a man.
My mother says a boy who will not carry water will not carry a sword either.

sheet.narrative: I farm the Marsh acres by the east gate, and I have kept sheep on that ground since before the Reeve had grey in his beard. The wool goes to the weavers' wives, and the gate-due takes a bite of every load I send through, which I grumble at but pay. My Hilda is a good worker and a good daughter, and Wulf Rowan is a decent lad, but I will not lose her hands to a wedding before the clip is sold and the money in the chest.
goals: Secure the wool clip and its sale before Hilda's match is settled
Keep the Marsh acres in good heart for the next year
See Hilda married well, and to a lad who will not waste her
sheet.mood: steady, a little worried about the clip

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the house and the guards fed, and she knows when I am fretting before I do.

relations.name: Hilda Marsh
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: A good worker and a good daughter; I want her settled, but not before the wool is sold.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent lad, but a lad with no strip of his own yet; I will not hand over my daughter's hands for nothing.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Proud of his land and slow to promise; we understand each other well enough.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the gate-due and takes his share of my wool's price; I pay it and grumble.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: He buys hides and drives a hard bargain, but he pays.

relations.name: Edwin Potter
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good man who feels the gate-due worse than I do; I wish him well of it.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the blight took the berries, but my sheep came through and I sold wool dear enough to keep us.
I stood at the east gate and paid the raised due on a load of wool, and Wat Fenner counted it out coin by coin.
Hilda was born in the back room on a cold night, and Sigrid would not let me in until morning.
Wulf Rowan came to me at the fold and asked for Hilda, and I told him to come back when the clip was sold.

stances.why: A daughter's hands are worth a season's clip, and I will not lose both in one year.
The guards keep the wolves off the road, but the due still eats my profit.
The flock is the family's bread; everything else waits on it.
I said I would see the wool sold before the match, and I will.

sheet.narrative: I cook for the gate guards' mess, and my barley broth is known from the south gate to the north. I keep the house and the accounts in my head, and I know what every guard takes in his bowl and what he owes for it. Hilda is a good girl and Wulf is a good lad, and I would see them happy, but Edwin is right that the wool must be sold first. I say little of it and set the bread to rise.
goals: Keep the guards fed and the house in order
See Hilda settled with Wulf without a quarrel between the two families
Put by a little against a hard winter

relations.name: Edwin Marsh
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a stubborn streak about the wool; I let him have his way and keep the peace.

relations.name: Hilda Marsh
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My girl, and a better cook than she knows; I would see her happy and not hurried.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A polite lad who eats his broth; I would not mind him at my table for good.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He commands the guards I cook for; fair enough, and he eats like a man who works.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: guard
relations.note: A quiet man at the gate; I feed him and he pays his share.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He buys my broth on feast days and pays promptly; a good neighbour.

memories.gist: I learned my barley broth from my mother, and the guards have asked for it every winter since.
Hilda was born on a cold night and I would not let Edwin in until morning; he sulked for a week.
In the Lean Year I stretched the broth with roots and fed the guards anyway, and no one went hungry at my table.
Wulf Rowan came to the house with a hare for the pot, and I knew he was courting before Hilda told me.

stances.why: A full bowl keeps the peace at the gate, and a hungry guard is a quarrel waiting.
He is stubborn about the wool, and I would rather keep the house quiet than win the argument.
The Lean Year taught me what an empty store means.
A match made in haste is a lifetime of regret; she is young yet.

sheet.narrative: I work the sheep and the wool with my father, and I help my mother cook for the gate guards, and I love Wulf Rowan and would marry him tomorrow. But my father wants the wool clip sold first, and I will not cross him, not even for Wulf. So I keep my hands busy and my mouth shut and wait for the clip to come in.
goals: Marry Wulf Rowan with both families' blessing
See the wool clip sold and the money in the chest
Keep my mother's kitchen and my father's flock in good order

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: I love him and I would marry him tomorrow, but I will not cross my father to do it.

relations.name: Edwin Marsh
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is stubborn about the wool, but he is my father and I will not shame him.

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows how I feel and says nothing, and that is a kindness.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: Wulf's father
relations.note: He wants his son to wait for the harvest too; at least the two fathers agree.

relations.name: Mildgyth Grey
relations.label: helper
relations.note: She works the pots with my mother and me, and she is good company.

relations.name: Elfgifu Rowan
relations.label: Wulf's mother
relations.note: She has been kind to me over the cider at the stall, and I think she would have us wed sooner than Godric would; I want her to think well of me.

memories.gist: Wulf kissed me behind the wool shed at the last market, and I have thought of it every day since.
I helped my mother cook for the guards through the Lean Year, and I learned to stretch a pot further than I thought possible.
My father told me at the fold that the wool would be sold before any wedding, and I said yes, and I meant it.
I sheared my first sheep on my own when I was fourteen, and my father said nothing but nodded, which was praise enough.

stances.why: My father asked it of me, and I will not shame him or lose his blessing.
He is a good lad and he will have me, and a season is not so long.
Waiting is easier when there is work to do.
The town talks, and I would not have it talk about me.

sheet.narrative: I've kept the tannery by the west wall for thirty years, and I know the worth of a hide before it's off the cart. The Guild pays my price because they know I won't be beaten down, and the Kettlebridge leather men can mutter all they like. Mildred keeps the books straight and the house quiet, and Cedric's a good hand with wood though he dreams of stone. I've no love for the gate-due—it eats my profit when I bring in bark and salt—but I'll not say so where the Reeve might hear.
