values: keeping my word on a bargain
goals: keep the tannery profitable despite the gate-due
see Cedric settled in a trade that suits him
hold my ground against the Kettlebridge leather sellers

relations.name: Mildred Tanner
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the books and never misses a bad hide; I'd be lost without her.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good with his hands, but he wants to build in stone and there's none to be had.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She buys my leather at a fair price, but she'd have the gate-due gone and that suits me too.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His hides are sound and he delivers on time.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the gate-due and I pay it, but I don't have to like it.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings clay and stone from Kettlebridge, but his prices are sharp and the due makes them sharper.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival
relations.note: Kettlebridge leather undercuts mine, and Holt's quarry stone costs me dear.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: We both curse the stone price; he's a straight man.

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: customer
relations.note: He owes me for leather bindings, and I'll have my marks.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His wolf and deer hides come in rough but sound, and he doesn't haggle long; a hunter who knows what his skins are worth.

relations.name: Sigrun Beornson
relations.label: sharp trader
relations.note: She sells her man's hides at the stall and counts every mark twice — I'd rather deal with Beorn, but she's never cheated me outright.

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His saltings hides come west by the shore road and they're sound enough; he grumbles about the works' smoke souring his pans, but he pays his tally and doesn't waste my morning haggling.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: Cuthbert's boy brings cape bird and small-game skins down from Thornby — thin stuff, but honest, and I'll take a fair bundle of it when the price is right.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: blight took the berries, but hides still came in and I sold leather to the Guild at a good price. I kept my family fed and my store full.
The day the gate-due was raised: Silas Pike's cart came in loaded with clay, and Wat Fenner took a mark a load. Silas cursed, and I felt the pinch on my own bark and salt.
Cedric made his first barrel on his own, and I sold it to Baldwin Wade for the inn. I was proud, though I said only that it would do.
A Kettlebridge leather seller came to the square with cheap belts and gloves. I undercut him on the next stall and he went away. Mildred said I was a hard man, but I call it business.
Mildred caught a bad hide in a delivery from Osbert Ashby's farm and saved me from tanning it. I gave her a new ledger book for it.

stances.why: It's robbery, but the guards keep the wolves off the road and I need the road.
Mercy Abbot pays what leather is worth, and I'd rather sell to her than to strangers.
Mildred and Cedric are what I work for; the town can sort itself out.
A hard bargainer keeps his thoughts to himself until the price is named.

sheet.secret: I've quietly sold a few hides to a Kettlebridge leather man through Silas Pike, knowing the Guild would not like it. The marks were too good to refuse.

sheet.narrative: I keep the tannery books and the house, and I can spot a bad hide across the yard. Aethelred is a hard man in a bargain, but he's fair to me and Cedric, and I've no complaints. The gate-due eats into our profit and I write it down every time, but I don't say so in the square. Cedric wants to build in stone; I want him to have a roof and a wife and not worry about what the Kettlebridge men charge.
goals: keep the tannery books in order
see Cedric settled
make the house a comfort to Aethelred

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Hard in business, kind at home; I know his moods.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: son
relations.note: He's a good lad, but he dreams too big for what the town can give him.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She's sharp, and she pays on time; I'd not want to cross her.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His hides are mostly sound, but I always check.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: She's a good woman; I send her a little leather for the chapel's needs.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: inn cook
relations.note: She's Marta Hale's sister, and that worries me.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She's delivered half the town; I'd trust her with a birth.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: we had hides and leather to trade, and I kept the books balanced while Aethelred sold to the Guild. We were lucky.
Cedric's first cart frame: he brought it to me to check the joints, and I said it was fine work. He smiled like a boy.
A Kettlebridge leather man came to the square and Aethelred undercut him. I was proud and a little ashamed.
I found a bad hide in Osbert Ashby's delivery and saved us a week's work. Aethelred gave me a new ledger book.
The night the gate-due was raised, Aethelred came home angry and I wrote the new cost in the book. I said nothing, but I thought of the winter ahead.

stances.why: A false line in the book is a crack in the house.
The town's quarrels come and go; my family is what I have.
Marta Hale's people are dangerous, and Agnes Fenner is too close to them for comfort.
I keep the peace at home so Aethelred can do his work.

sheet.narrative: I make cart frames and barrels for Osric Abbot and my father's tannery, but what I want is to build houses in stone. The town is short of good stone and the Kettlebridge men charge dear for it, so I make do with wood. I'm friendly with Stephen Hobson, who's a mason's son, and we talk about what we'd build if we could. My father thinks I should stick to wood; my mother just wants me settled.
goals: learn stonework from the Kettlebridge masons
build something that lasts
earn enough to set up my own workshop

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's taught me a trade, but he doesn't see why I want stone.

relations.name: Mildred Tanner
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps me grounded and checks my work.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: employer
relations.note: He pays fair for cart frames and barrels.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk about building in stone; his father's a mason.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: He knows stone and curses the price; I'd learn from him if I could.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She might have work for a builder if I had stone.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings stone from Kettlebridge, but the gate-due makes it dear.

memories.gist: The day I made my first barrel on my own, my father sold it to Baldwin Wade for the inn. He said it would do, and I knew he was pleased.
Stephen Hobson showed me the chapel wall his father repaired, and I thought: I want to build something that lasts like that.
The Lean Year: there was little work for a carpenter, and I helped my father in the tannery. I don't want to go back to that.
A Kettlebridge carter brought a load of stone through the gate and Wat Fenner took a mark a load. I thought: that's why I can't build in stone.
I watched the masons at Kettlebridge from the road once, and their work was fine. I wanted to ask them to teach me, but I didn't.

stances.why: Wood rots and burns; stone lasts, and I want to build things that last.
The Kettlebridge masons know their trade, even if they're rivals.
Every mark the guards take is a mark I can't spend on stone.
My parents have given me a trade and a home; I won't forget it.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the Bell and Bush for thirty years, and I have learned that a man who talks in my common room learns more than one who drinks alone. I hear the Guild argue the gate-due and the Reeve's men count their pay, and I say little to either. The licence is the Reeve's to give, and I owe him for it, which sits poorly with an inn that must sell ale to both sides. Agnes cooks, Petra rules the kitchen, and my son drinks my profit at the corner table.
values: paying what I owe, in my own time
goals: keep the Bell and Bush the one roof where the town can argue without fists
see the licence renewed without bending further to Aldric
get Gareth to stand a sober watch and stop drinking the stock

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She runs the kitchen better than I run the rest, and her pies fill the room.

relations.name: Gareth Wade
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good lad with a spear and a bad thirst; I would have him keep the inn, not the gate.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Steady hands and a closed mouth about her sister, which I respect.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He gave me the licence and has not let me forget it.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She holds her meetings at my tables and pays for the ale; that is enough.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We have known each other since before the walls were mended; she heals, I pour.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: the captain
relations.note: My son serves him; he keeps the road clear and drinks little, which I note.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings the stone and the complaints; both are worth hearing.

memories.gist: I bought the Bell and Bush with my wedding money and a loan, and I have never regretted it.
In the Lean Year the inn fed half the square on watered ale and Petra's pies and asked nothing.
Aldric Marrow signed my licence over an ale and said I would remember it; I have.
Sister Elspeth sat with me the night my brother died and said the Hearth keeps us all.
The night the Guild and the Reeve's men shouted across my common room, I poured until they went home.

stances.why: Whoever has eaten at my hearth is under my roof's peace, and that is the whole of my trade.
The man who talks at the Bell and Bush pays for his own trouble.
Carters who pay the due drink less and stay away; but I will not say so to the Reeve's face.
I owe Aldric a favour and will pay it when he asks, not before.

sheet.secret: I have quietly put aside a purse for the day the licence is refused, though I would never say so to Aldric.

sheet.narrative: I have run the Bell and Bush kitchen since before the walls were mended, and I know every hand that has stirred my pots. Agnes is the best of them, and the girls know better than to burn a pie. My pies are what the town comes for, and I keep the store counted and the flour dry. Baldwin hears the arguments; I hear the kitchen, and the kitchen hears more.
values: the inn's name for good food
goals: keep the inn's store ahead of a hard winter
teach the serving girls to bake as well as I do
see Agnes stay on, whatever her sister does

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He hears everything and says nothing; I hear the kitchen and say plenty.

relations.name: Gareth Wade
relations.label: son
relations.note: He eats standing at my table and never tells me what is wrong with him.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She works beside me and never once asked for her sister's name to be spoken here.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She sends the sick to my kitchen door and I send them back with broth.

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Her barley broth is good; we trade recipes and complaints about the guards.

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: baker
relations.note: His bread fills my tables when the pies run short, and his son moons about my serving girls.

relations.name: Godiva Stanhope
relations.label: girl
relations.note: She wants work at the inn and has quick hands; I could use her.

relations.name: Edith Stanhope
relations.label: pie-seller
relations.note: She sells her pies at the gate and I sell mine in the inn; we are civil, and we both count the other's crusts.

relations.name: Godfrey Baker
relations.label: baker's son
relations.note: He brings the night batch round at dawn and lingers by my serving girls; a good baker, if he would keep his eyes on the loaves.

relations.name: Mildgyth Grey
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She cooks for the guards' mess and knows what a kitchen costs; we share the price of flour and the gossip of the gate.

memories.gist: I learned to bake from my mother in a kitchen smaller than this one, and her pies were never as good as mine.
In the Lean Year I stretched the flour with ground roots and no one at the tables complained.
The night the Guild held its meeting, I fed forty and the store still held.
Gareth came home drunk and sick and I sat up with him and said nothing to his father.

stances.why: A winter with an empty store is a winter with an empty room.
My mother fed every guest first, and the Hearth says the same.
She is the best cook I have had, and the town's talk is not her doing.
It is Baldwin's licence and the Reeve's due; I keep to the kitchen.

sheet.secret: I have been putting by a jar of marks under the flour bin against the day the inn cannot pay its way.

sheet.narrative: I stand the gate with a spear and count carters' loads for Tobin Marrow, and every evening I come back to my father's common room and drink what I did not earn. I would rather keep the inn than the gate, but he has never offered it and I have never asked. There is a carter in Kettlebridge I owe marks I do not have, and he will come up the stone road again. A man can only carry so much and then he drinks.
values: a quiet life behind the bar
goals: find the marks to settle with the Kettlebridge carter before he comes again
get his father to let him keep the inn
drink less than he did last week

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: father
relations.note: He would rather hear the town argue than hear me ask for the inn.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows when I have been drinking and never says it aloud.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He keeps a clean watch and a cold eye; I would not want to be short with him.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: fellow guard
relations.note: We stand the gate and he takes the due without flinching; I could learn that.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: He drinks at my father's table and grumbles at the outlaws; good company.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He comes through the gate with his stone and his complaints, and I count him through.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She has seen me drunk and said nothing, which I count as kindness.

memories.gist: I stood the gate the day the Coldwell folk were declared outlaws and watched them walk back into the woods.
My father taught me to pull ale before he taught me to hold a spear, and I remember which I liked better.
I lost at dice to a Kettlebridge carter at the Bell and Bush and borrowed to pay him; I have not paid it back.
The night of the broken match the whole square talked of it, and I poured for men who cursed the Cranes.

stances.why: A guard who is slack on the gate is a guard Tobin Marrow will not keep.
I have poured at that bar since I could reach it, and he has never said a word about handing it on.
The Kettlebridge carter's marks sit on me every time I stand the south gate.
When the common room is loud and the watch is done, the cup is the only thing that asks nothing.

sheet.secret: I owe a Kettlebridge carter marks I cannot pay, and I have been taking a little from the due at the gate to make it up.

sheet.narrative: I am the town mason of Brackenford, and I have kept these walls standing for twenty years with too little stone and too much argument. The Reeve's wall account is owed to me and I owe Silas Pike for the last load, and I am caught between a man who has marks and a man who has none, being the second. Every load that comes up the stone road pays the gate-due before it ever reaches my yard, and I curse Kettlebridge for the price and the gate for the rest. I build what I am paid to build: walls, chapel buttresses, the odd chimney, and I will not be shamed for wanting to be paid for it.
values: the town's walls before any man's pride
a fair price for good stone
my son's future in the trade
goals: get the Reeve to settle the wall account so I can pay Silas Pike
find stone that does not cost half a year's wages
see Stephen master the trade and build better than I have

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She has patched me up more times than I can count and never once nagged about the money.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: son and apprentice
relations.note: He has the eye for it, and grander notions than mine, which is as it should be.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He wants his marks and he is right to want them; I just cannot make them appear.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He owes me for the wall and pays me last, if at all. Old men forget what is not in their ledger.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman who cuts first and asks after. His stones cost me dear and his carelessness cost the giants their cairn.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She wants the gate-due gone, and so do I. That is enough to drink with her.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: I mend her chapel roof and she does not quibble over the price, which is more than the Reeve.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A builder like me, in timber because stone is dear. We share the same complaint and the same ale.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good lad with a cart; I have borrowed it and returned it sound.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due off my stone before I have even seen it. It is not his fault and I mind him anyway.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: friend's son
relations.note: Wilfred's boy, and a steady hand with timber; he talks of learning stonework from the Kettlebridge masons, and I cannot say I blame him, though it stings to hear it.

memories.gist: When the Lean Year came I worked for half pay and took grain instead, and still counted myself lucky to be working.
I built the chapel buttress with the sisters watching, and Sister Elspeth said a blessing over the stone, which I did not laugh at.
The last load Silas brought up the stone road was good stone and I set it in the south wall; the marks for it are still owed and Silas has asked twice.
I heard the tale of the cairn cutting and thought: a quarryman who does not know a cairn when he sees one is no quarryman. I would not have Ezra Holt in my yard.
Stephen laid his first full course of stone true and plumb, and I told him so plainly, which I do not often do.

stances.why: A wall holds because someone was paid to set every stone of it.
It is a tax on every stone and timber that comes to my yard, and it goes to the guards, not the walls.
I will buy from Kettlebridge when it is the only stone to be had, whatever I think of them.
If Stephen learns to set a stone true he will never want for work, whatever the Reeve does.
The sisters heal and keep the fire; the town is better with them, and their roof is mine to keep sound.

sheet.narrative: I am Joan Hobson, midwife of Brackenford, and I have brought half the town into the world and closed the eyes of a fair few besides. I work with the chapel sisters and with Hilda Smith when the bone-setting is needed, and I have never turned away a woman in labour, whatever her household or her husband's quarrels. My Reginald frets over the Reeve's account and Silas Pike's marks, and I let him fret, for fretting is his way of working. I have delivered Wenna Marrow's child's way into the world before, so to speak, and I will be there when her time comes, and I do not care what the town says of her.
values: a live mother and a live child
goals: see Wenna Marrow safely delivered of her first
keep the peace between Reginald and Silas Pike before it comes to blows
train another pair of hands to the midwife's work before I am too old

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a sore pocket; I would have him sleep more and curse less.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, who builds walls and dreams of better ones. He has his father's hands and my patience, mostly.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: friend and fellow healer
relations.note: She keeps the fire and the calendar and never asks who the mother is before she helps.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: Good with salves and herbs; I would have her at more births, for her hands are steady.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: expectant mother
relations.note: A weaver's daughter carrying the Reeve's grandchild; the town talks, and I pay no heed to talk.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: She sets bones and I deliver babes; between us we keep the guards on their feet.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He is old and he is hard, and I have seen what his ledger does to households. I am civil to him.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor of my husband
relations.note: He is owed and he is pressing; I understand a man wanting his marks, but I will not have shouting at my door.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A kind woman at the inn, and her sister's trouble is not hers to answer for.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I have heard her side and I have heard the Tolleys'; I would not choose between them at my table.

memories.gist: I delivered Wenna Marrow's mother's last child and now I am to deliver Wenna's first; the wheel turns and I am glad to be on it.
In the Lean Year I lost a mother and could not save her, and I sat with Sister Elspeth afterwards and neither of us said a word.
Reginald came home from the wall account with his jaw set and no marks, and I put his supper down and said nothing, for there was nothing to say.
Silas Pike stood in my yard asking for his money and Reginald had none to give, and I offered him tea and he took it, which shamed us both.
Stephen set his first full course true and came home grinning like a boy half his age, and I thought: he will do.

stances.why: A birth is a birth; the mother's household is her husband's business, not mine.
What is said in a birthing room stays there, or no one would ever call me again.
Reginald must air his grievances or they curdle; I let him talk and then I feed him.
They said worse of me once and it passed; Wenna's child will be born and the talk will pass too.
The sisters and I do the same work under different roofs; the common fire is the town's heart.

sheet.secret: I have known for a month that Wenna Marrow's child is coming early and the birth may go hard, and I have told no one, not even Reginald, for fear the town would make it a judgement on her.

sheet.narrative: I am twenty and I am my father's apprentice, and I have set more stones in the town wall than I can count, and I want to set better ones. A wall is a fine thing, but a wall is a thing that keeps people out; I want to build a thing that keeps people in: a hall, a tower, a house with a stone face that will stand when the wall has fallen. My father says stone is dear and the Reeve does not pay, and both are true, and I mean to build anyway. Cedric Tanner and I talk of it over ale, and Osbert Smith wants to learn the Kettlebridge masons' work as much as I do.
values: a fair day's pay for a fair day's work
goals: build one thing grander than a wall
learn the Kettlebridge masons' stonework if I can get near it
earn enough to set up as a mason in my own right

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: father and master
relations.note: He knows stone better than any man in Brackenford, and he will not hear of building anything but walls.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She has never once told me to be smaller than I am.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He wants to build in stone too, and between us we might just do it.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He wants the Kettlebridge stonework as badly as I do; we talk of going south together and never quite do.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor of my father
relations.note: He presses my father for marks and I cannot pay him either, and it galls me.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He has the town's marks and will not spend them on stone; I do not know what he is saving them for.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival's trade
relations.note: My father hates him; I would still learn from a Kettlebridge quarryman if he would teach me, whatever the cairn.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: fellow builder
relations.note: He builds in timber because stone is dear, same as my father — but he grumbles about the Kettlebridge price loud enough that folk listen, and I like him for it.

memories.gist: My father gave me my own trowel when I was fourteen and said nothing, and I have kept it clean ever since.
I laid my first full course of stone true and plumb, and my father told me so plainly, which he does not often do.
Cedric and I stood in the square and looked at the chapel and said we would build something better one day, and we meant it.
Silas Pike came to the yard for his marks and my father had none, and I stood there with my trowel in my hand and said nothing, and I have not forgotten it.
I saw the Kettlebridge stonework on the cart once, cut clean and true, and I thought: I could do that, if someone would show me.

stances.why: A wall keeps people out; I want to build something worth keeping people in.
A mason who will not learn from a rival is a mason who has stopped learning.
My father has done the Reeve's work and gone unpaid, and I will not spend my life that way.
The gate-due and the Kettlebridge price make stone a rich man's trade, and I am not a rich man.
He has forgotten more about stone than I know, even when he will not hear of a new thing.

sheet.narrative: I make bows and arrows in a shed by the north gate, and the guards and hunters come to me because there is no one else on this island who does it half so well. I was raised in Brackenford and I have never trusted Kettlebridge — their carpenters undercut us all and their masters look down their noses at honest work. Enid minds the stall and I mind the shed, and between us we keep the roof on. I want Robin to have a trade better than mine, though I would not say so to his face.
goals: keep the guards' custom
see Robin a fair shot and a better tradesman than me
pay off what we owe the Guild stall rent

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She sells what I make and never lets a bad bow leave the stall.

relations.name: Robin Fletcher
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick hands and a good eye; I want more for him than a shed.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The captain buys my arrows for the guards and pays on time.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She takes our stall rent and talks sense about the gate-due.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: customer
relations.note: A hunter who knows what a straight arrow is worth.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We both curse the Kettlebridge price for what we cannot get here.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings Kettlebridge goods through the gate and calls our due robbery.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: The boy plays with Robin and knows every guard at the gate.

memories.gist: My father taught me to tiller a bow at the bench by the north gate, and I have had that shed ever since.
In the Lean Year the guards' pay came late, but they still needed arrows, so I let the account run and they paid in the end.
A Kettlebridge carpenter sold the Guild a set of stall frames at half what I would charge, and Osric Abbot bought them.
Robin shot his first hare with the small bow I made him, and I was prouder than I let on.
The Reeve's gate-due is paid on the yew staves I bring in from outside, and I grudge every mark of it.

stances.why: I pay it on every stave and every load, and it eats the profit I make.
Their carpenters undercut us and their masters think we are peasants.
It is the one thing I do better than anyone, and I will not sell a bad one.
He has the hands for it; I want him to have a trade with a future.
Lose the stall and Enid loses her trade and her gossip both.

sheet.narrative: I mind the stall in the square, selling bows and arrows and odds and ends, and I hear more of the town's business there than Baldwin Wade does at his inn. Aldous is the maker and I am the seller, and we rub along. I worry about Robin — he is a fair shot already and too fond of the woods and the guards' talk. I keep on the right side of Mercy Abbot because the Guild's stall rent is what keeps us, and I would not say a word against the gate-due in front of the Reeve's people.
goals: keep the stall's custom through winter
see Robin apprenticed well
stay in Mercy Abbot's good graces

relations.name: Aldous Fletcher
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good maker, and stubborn as a gatepost about the Kettlebridge folk.

relations.name: Robin Fletcher
relations.label: son
relations.note: Too quick to run off to the woods; I want him safe and settled.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She holds our stall rent and she is fair about it.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A bright girl at the next stall; she will make a good Guild woman.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A lively boy; he and Robin are thick as thieves.

relations.name: Sigrun Beornson
relations.label: rival stallholder
relations.note: She sells hides and venison two stalls along and drives a hard bargain.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: The inn cook; she hears everything and tells me most of it.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: Proud and sore about her daughter, but her cloth is good.

memories.gist: I took over the stall from my mother with three bows and a basket of bowstrings, and I have held it every market day since.
In the Lean Year I sold my own pewter jug to buy grain, and told no one but Aldous.
Mercy Abbot let us keep the stall through a hard winter on half rent, and I have not forgotten it.
Robin brought home a hare he shot himself and I cooked it that night, and he talked of nothing else for a week.
The talk about Wenna Marrow in the square turned my stomach, and I said so to Aldith Weaver's face.

stances.why: The stall is our living and Mercy Abbot holds the rent.
What I hear at the stall sells as well as what I sell.
Say the wrong thing before the Reeve's people and the stall suffers.
He is quick and brave and I fear the woods and the wolves more than he does.
Aldous will not sell a bad one and I will not sell it cheap.

sheet.narrative: I help Da in the shed, holding the stave while he works it and sweeping up the shavings, and when he lets me I shoot my small bow at the butt behind the shed. Bram Fenner and I play at the gate and the guards know our names. I want to be as good a shot as the hunters one day, and I am not afraid of the woods — only a bit, at night.
goals: shoot straighter than Bram
see a real wolf track with Beorn's boy
make a bow of my own

relations.name: Aldous Fletcher
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me hold the stave and says my hands are quick.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She smells of the stall and always has something in her pocket for me.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the gate and he knows all the guards' names.

relations.name: Ulf Beornson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He sets snares with his da and knows the woods better than me.

memories.gist: Da made me a small bow and I shot a hare with it, and Ma cooked it that night.
Bram and I got chased off the gate steps by a guard, and we laughed all the way home.
I watched the hunters bring a wolf's pelt through the north gate and I have wanted to see one alive ever since.

sheet.narrative: I farm the Carter fields south of the wall, and I keep a cart. The cart earns as much as the field some years, carrying goods up to the gate for the Guild and for anyone who pays. I pay the gate-due on my own loads like any carter, and it rankles, but the guards keep the wolves off the road and I'd not have it said I dodged. Godric Rowan's strip is next to mine and we've shared a plough-team since we were lads.
goals: get Alfred settled with a cart of his own
pay off the new cart-wheel before winter
see the gate-due lowered if it can be done without losing the guards

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the hens and the garden and never once let the household go short.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: son
relations.note: Drives better than I did at his age; I want him on the road with a cart that's his.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My little one; she has the hens eating from her hand.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We share a plough and a grumble; his strip borders mine.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She hires my cart and pays on time; I'd not cross her.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: Takes the due off me at the south gate and counts every basket.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: fellow carter
relations.note: A Kettlebridge man, but he knows the road and his loads come through honest.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: neighbour farmer
relations.note: Good grain, fair prices; we've helped each other at harvest.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: blight took the berries and I carted the town store's grain out to the farms, glad of the work and shamed to take pay for it.
The day I bought the cart off an old carter at Kettlebridge and drove it home empty, proud as a lord.
Alfred drove the cart alone to the gate for the first time and brought back every mark.
Paying the raised gate-due on a load of my own grain and hearing Wat Fenner say it was the Reeve's word.
Edith was born in the front room with Joan Hobson attending and Cecily gripping my hand fit to break it.

stances.why: A carter who dodges the due loses his name on the road.
Wolves are real on the town road; I've seen what's left of a sheep.
It eats a load's profit and the Guild says it drives trade off.
The fields and the cart are for the children, not the other way round.

sheet.narrative: I keep the hens and the vegetable plot, and I sell eggs at the Guild stall in the square most market days. Herbert's cart takes him up and down the road, and I mind the house and the children while he's gone. I've no patience for town quarrels; eggs are eggs and folk must eat.
goals: keep enough eggs back to set a second clutch
see Edith learn to read a little with the chapel sisters
put by a few marks against a bad winter

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as the wall; I'd have no other on the cart.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: son
relations.note: Growing tall and full of the road; I'd keep him closer if I could.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My shadow; she knows every hen by name.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: Her stall rents are fair and she's never shorted me for an egg.

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: We mind each other's goods at the square and share the gossip.

relations.name: Mildgyth Grey
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We've cooked for the guards' mess together when the pot was short.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Quiet these days, and the town's talk about her daughter was cruel.

memories.gist: Selling my first eggs at the Guild stall and Mercy Abbot counting them out herself.
The Lean Year, when we ate our own hens and I cried over the last one.
Edith was born and Joan Hobson put her in my arms and said she'd be a worker.
A fox got into the henhouse and Edith sat up all night with the survivors.

stances.why: My mother kept us through worse on less.
The square's charter says anyone in peace; I sell to whoever comes with marks.
They stopped a carter on the road and I'll not have Herbert treated so.
Everything I put by is for Alfred and Edith.

sheet.narrative: I drive the cart for my father and I want to be a carter on the stone road, like Silas Pike, with my own cart and my own loads. I've watched him come through the south gate with stone from Kettlebridge and I know the road's a hard one, but it's the life I want. For now I help with the ploughing and take the eggs to the square when Mother can't.
goals: save enough marks for a cart of my own
learn the stone road as far as Kettlebridge
prove to Father I can handle a load alone

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the reins and the road; I want to make him proud.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She packs my bread and tells me to mind the wolves.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: sister
relations.note: I let her ride on the cart when Mother isn't looking.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter I admire
relations.note: He's been robbed twice and still drives the stone road; that's a carter.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He counts our load like we're thieves and takes the due off Father.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We race along the wall and he knows every guard's name.

memories.gist: The first time Father let me take the reins through the south gate and back.
Watching Silas Pike's cart come in loaded with Kettlebridge stone and thinking, that's the trade for me.
The Lean Year, when the cart sat idle and Father sold a plough to buy grain.
Edith fell in the ditch by the south field and I carried her home dripping.

stances.why: Silas Pike says if a load's late once, it's late forever in folk's minds.
I'll not plough another man's strip all my life.
Wolves and outlaws both, but a carter's pay is a carter's pay.
Their carters know stone and loads better than anyone here.

sheet.narrative: I help Mother with the hens and carry the eggs to the square in a basket. I like the hens best, even when they peck. When Alfred drives the cart I run after it to the gate until Mother calls me back.
goals: get the brown hen to let me stroke her
ride on the cart all the way to the gate

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me hold the eggs if I'm careful.

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lifts me up onto the cart.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He lets me ride when Mother isn't looking.

memories.gist: The brown hen laid an egg in my lap and I wasn't even frightened.
Alfred carried me home from the ditch and I got a honey cake.

sheet.narrative: I have baked Brackenford's bread for thirty years, and I am up before the crows each morning to do it. The bakehouse is the Reeve's, leased to me, and I owe him for that lease and know it every time I see him. My bread feeds the market and the gate guards, and I keep my head down between the Guild and the Reeve, because both of them can make my life hard. I am a plain man with a hot oven and a good wife's head for figures.
values: a fair loaf for a fair mark
feed the guards who keep the road
goals: keep the bakehouse lease and pay the Reeve what is owed
get good grain at a steady price from Osbert Ashby
hand the bakehouse to Godfrey when the time comes
sheet.mood: steady, a little worn, watchful of the Reeve

relations.name: Amice Baker
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the books and I keep the oven; I would be lost without her sums.

relations.name: Godfrey Baker
relations.label: son
relations.note: He bakes the night batch well enough, and he is impatient to have it all.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: The bakehouse is his and I owe him for the lease; I pay on time and say little.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: grain seller
relations.note: His grain is sound and he does not squeeze me, unlike some.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: customer
relations.note: His guards eat my bread; he pays, and I do not ask about the due.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: The Guild sets the market terms and I bake to them; she has never cheated me.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn takes bread from me and pays promptly; a good man to deal with.

memories.gist: The morning the Lean Year blight reached us, I had to halve the loaves and the guards grumbled to my face.
Aldric Marrow signed the bakehouse lease over to me at the guildhall and I have paid him every quarter since.
Godfrey pulled his first tray of loaves out of the oven by himself at fourteen, and I was prouder than I let on.
The night the wolves came down to the south gate, I kept the oven hot till dawn and the guards ate standing.
Osbert Ashby let me have a load of grain on trust one hard winter and I paid him back with the first batch.

stances.why: The bakehouse is his lease; a man who pays late loses his oven.
They keep the road clear, and they are my steadiest customers.
Guild and Reeve both buy my bread; I cannot afford to lose either.
My name is on every loaf that leaves this bakehouse.

sheet.secret: I have shorted the guards' loaves a little these lean quarters to keep the market loaves full weight, and I hope nobody weighs them.

sheet.narrative: I run the bakehouse beside Osgood and keep every mark of it in my head, because the books would only get wet or lost. I know what grain cost last winter and what it will cost next, and I know to the loaf how much the guards are owed. I am the one who remembers the lease and the quarter-days, and I am the one who tells Osgood when we can afford a thing. I have a sharp eye and I do not care to be cheated.
values: keep the accounts honest and tight
goals: keep the bakehouse solvent through winter
see Godfrey settled with a trade and a wife
never be short of grain in the store

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He bakes and I count; we have never needed to say which of us keeps us fed.

relations.name: Godfrey Baker
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants the bakehouse and he will have it, but not before he can keep the accounts.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: He holds the lease over us and he knows it; I watch the quarter-days like a hawk.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: grain seller
relations.note: A fair price and a full measure, most times.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: The Guild's terms favour the town and I work to them, but she has a head for trade.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn buys our bread and Petra pays without a fuss.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She has a good head and a kind hand; we talk of children and prices.

memories.gist: I found the store short a sack after the Lean Year and traced it to a rat hole, and I have kept the grain in sealed crocks since.
The quarter-day I paid the Reeve's man the lease in full with marks I had counted three times.
Godfrey brought home the innkeeper's daughter's name and I began to reckon what a wedding would cost.
Osgood and I baked through the night of the surge storm to feed the folk who came in from the road.
I taught Godfrey his letters at the bakehouse table so he could write a bill of sale.

stances.why: A bakehouse lives or dies on a few marks a quarter.
The town will not feed us if the oven goes cold.
The Reeve would let the bakehouse to another tomorrow.
Grain is the whole cost of a loaf and it moves with the weather.

sheet.secret: I have been putting by a few marks in a crock behind the flour bins for Godfrey's wedding, without telling Osgood, because he would spend it on a new oven door.

sheet.narrative: I bake the night batch so the town wakes to warm bread, and I am the one who slides the trays in while the house sleeps. I want this bakehouse for my own, and I am courting the innkeeper's daughter, though I have not yet found the words for her father. My father thinks I am not ready to keep the accounts; my mother thinks I am not ready to keep a wife. I mean to prove them both wrong.
values: one day the bakehouse is mine
goals: win the innkeeper's daughter and her father's leave
take over the bakehouse from my father
prove I can keep the books as well as the oven

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the oven, but he will not let me near the books.

relations.name: Amice Baker
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She says I am not ready; I mean to show her I am.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: His daughter is the one, and he watches me over his ale like a hawk.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: innkeeper's wife
relations.note: She has been kinder to me than her husband, and she knows her pies.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: customer
relations.note: His guards eat my night batch, and he has never once complained of it.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: grain seller
relations.note: I hope to deal with him myself one day, when the bakehouse is mine.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We drink together and talk of building something better than what we were given.

memories.gist: The first night I baked the whole batch alone, and not one loaf burned.
I saw the innkeeper's daughter laughing behind the counter at the Bell and Bush and have thought of little else since.
My father found a scorched tray and made me bake the night batch twice over to learn it.
The morning the guards came off the road after the wolves, I had hot bread waiting and Tobin clapped me on the shoulder.
Stephen Hobson and I sat on the wall and swore we would build in stone one day, whatever the Kettlebridge price.

stances.why: It is my father's now, and I will not have it handed to me; I will earn it.
She is the one I want, and I will find the words for her father.
A baker who cannot count his marks is a baker who loses his oven.
They are the steadiest custom in the town and they remember a good loaf.

sheet.secret: I have already asked the innkeeper's daughter to walk out with me, and she said yes, and neither of our parents knows it yet.

sheet.narrative: I have woven cloth at this loom for thirty years, and I will not have it said my daughter brought shame on the square. Tobin Marrow broke his promise to Hester Crane and married my Wenna, and now the town counts the cost of it against her — as if a weaver's daughter were a debt to be entered in the ledger. I sell my cloth at the Guild stall and I sell none of it to the Marrows, and I say so where anyone can hear me. Leofwine keeps his peace; one of us must.
values: keeping my own counsel where it costs nothing
goals: see Wenna held in respect in the square again
keep my loom busy and my cloth selling at the Guild stall
never let the Reeve's family forget how they used my girl
sheet.mood: proud, sore, and quicker to speak than she means to be

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She wears the town's talk for my sake and his, and I would take it off her if I could.

relations.name: Leofwine Weaver
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He says nothing and thinks much; I do the speaking for both of us.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: He broke his promise and my daughter pays the price of it in the square.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: His family took my girl into their house and let the town talk.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She gives my cloth a stall and a fair price, and she is no friend of the Reeve either.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: stallwright
relations.note: A good hand with a bench; he mends what the market breaks.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: stall girl
relations.note: Young, but she counts the terms straight.

relations.name: Elfgifu Rowan
relations.label: market neighbour
relations.note: Her cider and my cloth sit at the same stall, and she does not gossip about Wenna.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: stallholder
relations.note: We mind each other's goods when one of us must step away.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: She has never once said a word against my girl.

memories.gist: Wenna's wedding to Tobin, and the faces in the square that day — half of them counting what it cost the town.
The Lean Year, when the berry blight came and I wove nettle and old rags into cloth because no one could buy new.
Tobin Marrow breaking the match with Hester Crane a month before the wedding, and the whole square knowing it before I did.
Leofwine bringing home the first loom he built with his own hands, and my first bolt off it.
Telling the Guild stall I would sell no cloth to the Marrow household, and Linnet Abbot writing it in her book without a word.

stances.why: Tobin broke his promise and my daughter wears the shame of it; I will not sell him so much as a rag.
A woman's name is her trade, and the square will not buy from a house it gossips about.
Mercy Abbot's stall gives a fair price and does not ask whose daughter I am.
Cloth is what I have, and idle hands invite talk.
One of us must hold the house calm, and it will not be me.

sheet.secret: I think Tobin Marrow ruined my daughter's name, and I would see him pay for it in the square if I could do it without hurting Wenna.

sheet.narrative: I make looms and mend what the market breaks, and I keep my opinions where they belong — in my own head. My Aldith speaks for the house and I let her; she has the words and the right of it, mostly. Osric Abbot pays me steady for the stalls and benches, and a quiet man with steady work has little to complain of. I would like my daughter's name to be easy in the square again, and I would like my bench to stay busy while it happens.
values: a fair price for good timber
not saying more than I need
goals: keep the market stalls and benches sound for Osric Abbot
build a loom good enough to sell to another weaver
see Wenna easy in the town again without a quarrel in the square

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She speaks and I mend; it has worked these thirty years.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is happy with her Tobin, whatever the square says, and I will not be the one to sour it.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: son-in-law
relations.note: He is my daughter's husband and I will be civil to him, and no more than civil.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: employer
relations.note: He pays on the day and does not hurry a good joint.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She keeps the market in order, and order is worth paying for.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: trade acquaintance
relations.note: Thornby fish comes through his hands; we have spoken twice and been civil twice.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: fellow craftsman
relations.note: He wants to build in stone; I wish him timber and a fair wind.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: A good man with a wall and a grudge against the Kettlebridge price, which I share quietly.

memories.gist: Building my first loom in the shed behind the house, and Aldith's first bolt off it.
The Lean Year, mending the same market benches three times because no one could buy new timber.
Wenna coming home to tell us she would marry Tobin Marrow, and Aldith's face when she heard it.
Osric Abbot paying me for the guildhall benches and saying I was the only man in Brackenford who did not argue the price.
Hearing in the square that Tobin had broken the match with Hester Crane, and saying nothing at all.

stances.why: A carpenter who argues in the square loses the custom of half of it.
She has the words and the right of it, and I would only make it worse.
He is my daughter's husband and the father of the child she carries; a quarrel would fall on her.
I will not sell a bench that will not hold a man's weight.
The Reeve's licence keeps the market standing, and my bench in it.

sheet.secret: I think Tobin Marrow did wrong by Hester Crane, and I think he will do wrong by Wenna in some smaller way, and I have never said so to anyone.

sheet.narrative: I am a potter, and a good one, though you would not know it to watch my purse. Every jug and pot I sell at the square began as clay that came up the stone road from Kettlebridge, and the gate-due takes a mark off every load before Wat Fenner waves it through. I have stood at that gate and argued till my throat was raw, and it changes nothing. Mercy Abbot says the due should go, and I say so too, loudly, at the Guild meetings in the Bell and Bush.
values: a fair price for honest work
the market should be open to all
clay in the hand is better than marks in the ledger
goals: see the gate-due dropped so my clay comes cheaper
sell enough this season to put by for winter
keep Anselm's hands busy and out of the kiln
get Mercy Abbot seated as Reeve

relations.name: Alice Potter
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She has the better eye for a glaze and the cooler head when I am ranting.

relations.name: Anselm Potter
relations.label: son
relations.note: Breaks as many as he makes, but his hands are quick.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Brings my clay up the road and grumbles at the same due I do.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: patron
relations.note: She wants the due gone and trade back with Kettlebridge. So do I.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: Old man, and that due is his doing. He does not hear a potter.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: Takes my mark at the gate and is civil enough about it. It is still my mark.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: neighbour stall
relations.note: We mind each other's stalls when one of us must step away.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Grumbles at the due as much as I do over a cup.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: no grain to spare, and the pots went cheap to buy bread.
Standing at the south gate with a cart of clay, counting out a mark for the due and watching Wat Fenner drop it in the box.
The night Anselm was born, Joan Hobson's hands and Alice white as the clay.
Mercy Abbot at the Guild meeting saying the gate-due drives trade away, and me banging the bench in agreement.
A run of good jugs that sold out by noon, and Alice's glaze on them shining like wet slate.

stances.why: It eats my profit on every load of clay I must buy.
The square is for anyone who comes in peace; that is what the Charter says.
The Guild has done more for my trade than the Reeve ever has.
Their clay is in half my pots. I cannot hate the hand that feeds my wheel.

sheet.narrative: I keep the house and I keep the stall, and I keep Edwin from shouting at the gate guards more than once a week. My hands know a glaze better than his do; a little ash, a little lead, and the pot comes out of the kiln the colour of a storm cloud. I do not say much at the Guild meetings. I listen, and I count what we have left, and I make it stretch.
values: a quiet house and a full pot
do not borrow what you cannot repay
goals: get through winter with the store full
teach Anselm the wheel before he breaks every jug in the shed
see Edwin less angry about the due

relations.name: Edwin Potter
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good potter and a poor arguer. I let him talk and then I do it my way.

relations.name: Anselm Potter
relations.label: son
relations.note: All clay and elbows. I would not trade him for a shed of perfect jugs.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She is right about the due, but she talks more than she listens.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: market neighbour
relations.note: We share a stall wall and a good deal of gossip.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She brought Anselm into the world and I have not forgotten it.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: Her salves are good for a burn from the kiln.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: measuring out the last of the flour and telling Edwin it would be enough, and making it enough.
The first good glaze I made, the one like storm cloud, coming out of the kiln and Edwin going quiet for once.
Anselm at four, both fists in the clay, laughing, and me deciding not to scold him.
Sitting with Joan Hobson through a long night while the town slept, and her telling me to breathe.

stances.why: Marks are scarce and winter is long; a household lives on what it saves.
Edwin's anger at the due is real, but shouting at guards has never moved a mark.
He will not learn clay by being kept from it.
The Guild rents our stall; a civil word keeps it.

sheet.narrative: The clay is cold and squishy and smells like the river bottom. I make a pot and it falls over and I make another one and it falls over and Mama says that is how it goes. When Father is at the square I play in the shed, and sometimes I get the wheel to spin for a long time before it stops.
goals: make a pot that stands up by itself
see the kiln fire up close when Father lets me

relations.name: Edwin Potter
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me help when he is not shouting about the gate.

relations.name: Alice Potter
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She shows me how to push my thumbs in and not break the sides.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He knows all the guards' names. I know all the pots.

memories.gist: The day Father let me put my hands on the wheel and the clay went round and round and got taller.
Dropping a jug on the flagstones and watching it break, and Mama saying never mind, we will make another.

sheet.narrative: I have put up half the barns and a good share of the houses in this town, and every one of them in timber, because Kettlebridge will not sell us stone at a price a man can pay. I remember what they charged us the year the chapel roof was mended, and I have not forgotten it. I build for the Market Guild and for anyone else with the marks, and I build it square and true. My son Osbert works beside me, though his eye is on the stonework, and I cannot say I blame him.
goals: keep the building work coming in through the Guild
see Osbert settled in a trade with a future
get good stone at a fair price one day
sheet.mood: steady, a little sour about stone

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She mends bones and I mend roofs; between us the town keeps standing.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good hands, but he wants the stone trade and that means Kettlebridge, and I have my doubts.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A mason who curses the same price I do; we understand each other.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: patron
relations.note: The Guild pays on time, and she wants the gate-due gone, which would help my trade.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: stone seller
relations.note: He brings the stone and names the price, and I pay it through my teeth.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the due that makes every load dearer, and the walls are his to keep.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend's son
relations.note: A decent lad, and a good match for my Osbert's company.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman; they say he cut into the giants' cairn and brought trouble on the trade.

memories.gist: The year the chapel roof was mended, Kettlebridge named a price for stone that took my breath, and I built the whole thing in timber instead.
I built the Guild's new barn in a fortnight with Osbert and two hired hands, and Mercy Abbot paid the full price without a word.
During the Lean Year I took grain from the town store like everyone else and mended the store's roof for nothing, because it fed us.
A beam fell on a hired hand at the Rowan steading and Hilda set his arm while I held him; he was back at work by harvest.
Osbert came home talking of the Kettlebridge masons and their stonework, and I told him stone is dear and timber is honest, and he did not answer.

stances.why: Stone comes dear from Kettlebridge and timber comes from our own woods.
A builder is only as good as the hands he keeps, and I have held a bad wage in my time.
I have paid them and I know what they ask.
Mercy Abbot has never made me wait for my marks.
My father taught me that, and a crooked wall falls and takes a name with it.

sheet.narrative: I set bones and clean wounds, and the gate guards come to my door when they have been at the outlaws or each other. I learned what I know from my mother and from the chapel sisters, and Sister Alys still sends for me when a hurt is beyond her salves. Wilfred builds and I mend, and the house is quiet enough. I worry about Osbert going among the Kettlebridge masons, but a mother keeps her worries to herself.
goals: keep the guards and the town in one piece
see Osbert safe and settled
keep peace between the chapel and the old healers

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a long grudge; I let him have it and mend what he breaks.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants the stone trade; I want him to come home with all his fingers.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: She has the salves and I have the hands; we work well together.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: elder sister
relations.note: She keeps the common fire and the calendar, and she does not turn anyone from the door.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: Between us we have brought most of this town into the world.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: His guards come to me hurt, and he sends them; I will not say more.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: patient
relations.note: A big man with a short temper; I have stitched him twice and told him to keep his fists down.

relations.name: Alwin Wren
relations.label: old healer
relations.note: He knows the old charms and I know the bones; the sisters listen to us both.

memories.gist: I set a guard's arm at the gatehouse after the outlaws threw a stone at him, and he swore at me the whole time and thanked me after.
The Lean Year brought fevers to the town and I went from house to house with Sister Alys until we had no more salve and made more.
Osbert cut his hand to the bone on an adze and I sewed it and told him a builder needs his hands, and he laughed at me.
Wilfred came home from the chapel roof job in a fury over the stone price, and I let him talk it out and poured him cider.
I helped Joan Hobson with a birthing that went hard, and the child lived, and we sat down in the kitchen after and said nothing for a while.

stances.why: A hurt is a hurt, and the Hearth's peace is not mine to break.
What I hear at a sickbed is not mine to carry to the square.
They keep the road clear of wolves and worse, and they come to me bleeding for it.
Wilfred's quarrels are his; my son is mine.
Alwin Wren's charms and my mother's herbs have mended what the sisters' salves could not.

sheet.narrative: I have built with my father since I was a boy, and I am a good hand with timber, but timber is not what I want to build with. Stone lasts, and the Kettlebridge masons know how to cut and lay it, and I would learn from them if I could get among them. Stephen Hobson feels the same, and we talk about it over a pot. My father says stone is dear; I say a man should learn the trade that lasts.
goals: learn stonework from the Kettlebridge masons
build something grander than a barn
earn enough to keep a household of his own

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me everything I know and he will not hear of the stone trade.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She mends what I break and does not scold overmuch.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We both want more than a wall or a barn, and we talk of going to Kettlebridge.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: master mason
relations.note: He knows stonework, and he curses the Kettlebridge price; I would rather learn than curse.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He has been to Kettlebridge and back a hundred times; I have thought of asking him to carry a word for me.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman; they say he cut the cairn, but he knows the stone.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She pays for good work and she wants trade with Kettlebridge; that is where I would go.

memories.gist: My father and I raised the frame of the Guild's barn in a day, and I looked at it and thought it would be gone in fifty years while a stone barn would stand.
I watched the Kettlebridge masons unload dressed stone at the square and lay it true, and I stayed until they were done.
Stephen Hobson and I sat up late with a pot of ale and swore we would learn stonework, and the next morning I went back to the adze.
I cut my hand to the bone and my mother sewed it, and I told her a builder needs his hands and she laughed.
My father came home from the chapel roof cursing the stone price, and I said nothing, because I would have paid it to learn.

stances.why: Timber rots and stone stands, and the masons who lay it will always have work.
My father would keep me from Kettlebridge, but a trade is a trade.
I want to be known for what I build, not for whose son I am.
Stephen and I have talked of it long enough; a man should not go alone.
My father's temper is short on the stone question, and I have to live under his roof.

sheet.narrative: I am Benedict Cooper, and the barrels that carry this town's ale and berries are mine. My father was a cooper before me and I have kept the shed by the west wall these thirty years. Aethelred Tanner's leather bindings go on my barrels and he never lets me forget the debt. The stone road brings Kettlebridge hoops and their prices, and I pay the gate-due on every load like a fool.
values: a fair price for a fair barrel
goals: clear what I owe Aethelred Tanner
keep Baldwin Wade's custom at the Bell and Bush
see Martin made a master with his own mark

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She minds the stall and I mind the shed; between us the household stands.

relations.name: Martin Cooper
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick with a plane, but he wants the master's mark before he has earned it.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The Bell and Bush takes my barrels and pays on time; a good man to keep.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for bindings and he counts every strap twice.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: The Guild stall sells my wares; she wants the gate-due gone and I would not weep.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good hand with a bench; we talk wood and grumble at the due together.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: fellow tradesman
relations.note: Builds in timber like me, because stone costs the earth.

memories.gist: My father put the first plane in my hand and said a barrel that leaks is a lie.
The Lean Year: berries rotted in the fields and the barrels stood empty in my shed.
The day I took Martin on as apprentice and wrote his name in the book.
A Kettlebridge carter raised his hoop prices at the gate and I paid, because the ale must go out.
Juliana and I set up the stall in the square the spring after we wed.

stances.why: My name is on every cask; a leak is my shame.
Aethelred's bindings keep my barrels sound; I will not be a man who does not pay.
Every hoop and stave I bring in pays the due, and the price goes on my barrels.
I was years at the bench before my father let me sign a cask.

sheet.narrative: I am Juliana Cooper and I mind the wooden-ware stall in the square: barrels, buckets, noggins, whatever Benedict and Martin turn out. I know what a thing is worth and I do not let a buyer talk me down twice. The stall pays the Guild its rent and the household eats because of it. I keep the house and the store and I count what comes in.
goals: sell off the small wares before winter
see Martin married to a decent trade
keep a little by against a bad year

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Slow to anger and slow to change; I do the talking at the stall.

relations.name: Martin Cooper
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants to be a master at seventeen; he has not yet learned what a bad cask costs.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She takes the stall rent and sets the market terms; she is fair enough.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: fellow stallholder
relations.note: We watch each other's goods when one must step away.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn buys our buckets and noggins; she counts the inn's store close.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He holds Benedict's debt over us and I do not care for his manner.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She sells eggs by my stall and we share the morning's gossip.

memories.gist: The first morning I spread our wares on the square and sold every bucket before noon.
The Lean Year: the square was thin and I sold a bucket for half what it was worth to feed the house.
Martin's first barrel came off the bench crooked and I sold it cheap to a farmer and said nothing.
A Kettlebridge carter sneered at my prices and I sent him off with nothing.

stances.why: The stall feeds us; a bad bargain is a hungry week.
I pay the stall rent and keep the market terms, whatever the guards do at the gate.
People buy from a household that pays its way.
Martin has skill but he has not yet earned the master's word.

sheet.narrative: I am Martin Cooper, seventeen, and I am apprenticed to my father at the cooper's bench. I can raise a barrel from staves and set a hoop true, and I am better at it than he was at my age, whatever he says. I want my own mark and my own shed, and I will not spend my life under his eye. The gate-due and the Kettlebridge price make everything dear, and I am sick of hearing of it.
values: my own name on a cask
not being spoken for by my father
goals: finish my indenture and be made a master
earn enough to set up my own bench
take a wife when I have a trade to keep her

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is a good cooper but he will not hear that I am ready.

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She sells my work at the stall and tells me true what it fetched.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn's barrels come through my hands; he pays in coin and a word.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: His leather binds our barrels and he holds it over the house.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He makes cart frames and wants to build in stone; we talk of a trade of our own.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A mason's son who wants to build grander than a wall; good company at the inn.

memories.gist: The day my father let me set the hoops on a cask for the Bell and Bush and it held.
The Lean Year: no berries, no barrels, and I sat in the shed with nothing to do.
A carter told me my hoops were as good as any Kettlebridge work, and I have not forgotten it.
I watched Stephen Hobson's father lay a wall and thought I would rather build in wood and be my own master.

stances.why: I will not be a journeyman under my father's eye forever.
A cask that holds and is done by nightfall is a cask that sells.
Every stave I bring in costs more because of it, and my father just pays.
A man with no shed of his own has no business courting.

sheet.narrative: I have ground Brackenford's grain for thirty years, and the mill is as much mine as the lease is the Reeve's. The town counts every sack that goes in and every sack that comes out, and when the flour weighs light they look at me. I take my toll, no more, and if the millstones eat a handful in the grinding that is the stone's business, not mine.
values: a quiet life at the wheel
goals: keep the mill lease with the Reeve without being called to account
quiet the Guild's questions about the toll before they reach the square
see Hugh settled at the mill and the lease passed to him
sheet.mood: guarded, a little sour, sleeping badly

relations.name: Ethel Miller
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows what I take and has never once said it aloud.

relations.name: Hugh Miller
relations.label: son
relations.note: Eager for the mill, and too quick to say what he thinks in front of the Guild.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: He holds my lease and has not called me in, and that quiet worries me more than a summons would.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: questioner
relations.note: She counts flour at the stall and finds me short every time. She wants my mill in the Guild's hands.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: grain seller
relations.note: Good grain, and he does not weigh it twice.

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: customer
relations.note: He buys my flour and grumbles at the price, like every baker.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: scribe
relations.note: She writes the toll rolls neat, and I do not like how neat they are.

memories.gist: My father set me at the hopper at twelve and said the wheel would feed me if I fed it true.
The Lean Year: I ground the town store's grain day and night and never shorted a sack, and still they whispered about the toll.
I signed the mill lease with the Reeve in the guildhall, and he told me the town would be watching the measure.
Last market, Mercy Abbot stood at the mill gate and asked Ethel how many cakes a sack of flour makes. Ethel answered sweetly and we both knew what it meant.
Hugh took the wheel alone through a whole night's grinding and the flour came out fine. I was proud and said nothing.

stances.why: The miller's toll is the miller's wage; no man works the stones for nothing.
Once you say you were short, every sack you ever ground is doubted.
Aldric holds my lease and my quiet; better his ear than the Guild's ledger.
He says what he thinks to anyone who asks, and the Guild is always asking.

sheet.secret: For two years, when the stones run fine and the sacks are weighed light, I have kept a little more flour back than the toll allows, and sold it quietly through Ethel's cakes. Not much. Enough that the Guild's count is right and mine is not.

sheet.narrative: I was a baker's daughter before I was a miller's wife, and I have sold cakes at that gate for thirty years. The whole town passes my table, and most of them stop. I hear what they say about Godwin's measure, and I smile and take their marks and say nothing. A cake is a small thing to buy a silence with, but it is what I have.
values: a warm table at the gate
goals: keep the Guild's questions away from Godwin
keep the cakes selling and the household fed
see Hugh married and the mill safe in the family
sheet.mood: watchful, warm to customers, tired underneath

relations.name: Godwin Miller
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He grinds and I sell, and neither of us says the rest out loud.

relations.name: Hugh Miller
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, and too loud for his own good at the Guild stall.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: questioner
relations.note: She buys a cake and asks after the flour, and I know a question when I hear one.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: Old and slow, but he has not turned on us, and I count that.

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We trade cakes for broth and gossip, and she never carries tales.

relations.name: Pernel Pip
relations.label: scribe
