Reed brought home his first full creel at eight years old, grinning, and I pretended not to be proud and failed.

stances.why: My family has fished the upper pools for generations; the Fenwicks have no claim above the alder bend.
Hauling the old forest's fallen wood up the giants' track will foul the streams and the weirs, and the hollow needs its water more than the shelf needs roofs.
The Kettlebridge works foul the streams east of the forest, and I will say so to anyone who will hear.
The Old Green holds, and Pipwort keeps its memory; I'll argue my side but abide her ruling.
Alder Rush takes my smoked fish at a fair price, and a man who trades fair is worth keeping.

sheet.narrative: I came to this house as a bride and planted the berry rows myself, and I have watched the old forest shrink a little each year since. Osier frets about his pools and Sorrel Fenwick's weirs, and I let him fret; my worry is the axe and the smoke and the wolves coming closer to the clearing. Vetch Quill and I talk of it over the hives. The hollow must eat, but the forest is what feeds it, and I will not see it cut to the stumps.
values: the household fed and provisioned for winter
good relations with neighbours and the Eldest
goals: keep the berry rows and the garden yielding through the winter
persuade the hollow not to let the forest be cut close
see Reed settled with a trade and a strip of his own one day
keep the peace between Osier and the Fenwicks if she can

relations.name: Osier Willow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He frets at the water and I fret at the wood, and somehow the house holds.

relations.name: Reed Willow
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy. He wants the sea, and I want him to want the hollow, but I'll not hold him back.

relations.name: Vetch Quill
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk of the forest over her hives, and she sees it the same as I do.

relations.name: Sorrel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Osier's quarrel with her is not mine; she lost a husband and fishes to eat.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Takes our fish and our berries; a fair man with the hollow's store.

relations.name: Pipwort Bramblecap
relations.label: the Eldest
relations.note: She remembers when the forest was whole. I trust her to weigh the timber rightly.

relations.name: Yarrow Underbank
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He will not fell a living tree, and that is the right of it.

relations.name: Clover Mossfoot
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We argue about the seed rows, but she works hard and her flax is good.

memories.gist: The first spring in this house, planting the berry canes by the stream while Osier set weir stakes, and thinking the hollow was the whole world and enough.
Walking the forest edge with Vetch and finding the stumps where the Ferncross men had been, and the two of us resolving to speak at the common table.
Reed at eight, coming home with his first creel and a cut on his hand he was too proud to mention.
The winter the wolves came down to the berry rows and we kept the fire high all night and heard them in the dark beyond the garden.
The morning the smoke from Kettlebridge lay over the garden and the bees would not leave the hives, and I knew the forest was not as far from the works as we liked to think.

stances.why: The old forest feeds the hollow; if it is cut close there is no garden, no berries, no hollow.
The fallen wood is the hollow's own; the giants can wait until our own frames and gates are mended.
Neighbours you quarrel with are neighbours you cannot borrow from in a hard winter.
I have seen a thin winter and I will not see another if I can help it.
He is his father's son in the water and mine in the garden; whatever he chooses, he should choose it himself.

sheet.narrative: I help my father with the weirs and I know the streams nearly as well as he does, though he would say not yet. Reed Fenwick and I fish together sometimes, and it is awkward, because our mothers and fathers do not agree about the water. I want to see the sea at Lanternquay one day — the real sea, not the streams — and I think about it more than I should when there are traps to set.
goals: learn every pool and trap from his father
keep his friendship with Reed Fenwick despite the quarrel
see Lanternquay and the sea one day

relations.name: Osier Willow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows the streams better than anyone, and I want to know them like he does.

relations.name: Rush Willow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries about the wolves and the wood, but she lets me go to the water.

relations.name: Reed Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We fish together and I've told him his mother's weirs spread too far, and he took it better than his mother would.

relations.name: Sorrel Fenwick
relations.label: friend's mother
relations.note: She is sharp with my father, but she has been kind enough to me.

memories.gist: My father walking me the stream and showing me where the fish lie, and letting me set a trap myself for the first time.
Fishing the alder bend with Reed Fenwick and catching nothing, and laughing about it until our fathers called us home.
The night the wolves came down and my mother kept the fire high; I lay awake listening and was more excited than afraid.
A pedlar telling us of Lanternquay and the tide lanterns and the boats, and me thinking about it for days after.

stances.why: My father says so, and I have seen how the Fenwick weirs block the run.
The quarrel is between our parents, not between us, and I will not lose a friend to it.
There is a whole sea beyond the streams, and I mean to see it before I am old.

sheet.narrative: I keep the hollow's stall at the east road crossing, and every pack that goes out of Fernhollow or comes in by that road passes through my hands. Fibre and salves mostly, and a word with Nell Sedge's Reedmoor folk when they come. I owe Alder Rush for a load of fibre and I mean to pay it, but the pack that was opened at the crossing has set everyone counting their goods twice. Clover Mossfoot and I have grown close over the trade — she is Thistle's wife, and I have told no one, not even my own Clover, what that has come to mean to me.
goals: settle the opened pack at the crossing without the hollow splitting over it
pay Alder Rush what I owe for the fibre
keep the crossing stall trusted by both the hollow and Reedmoor
decide what to do about Clover Mossfoot before the talk gets louder

relations.name: Clover Hazel
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She builds the crates I pack and keeps me steady; I have not told her about Clover Mossfoot and it sits on me.

relations.name: Sorrel Hazel
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Four years old and already sorting berries at the stall; I want the crossing to be a good place for her to grow up in.

relations.name: Clover Mossfoot
relations.label: confidante
relations.note: Thistle's wife, and the one I talk to about the fibre trade and everything else; I don't know whether to step back or not.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trading partner
relations.note: He blames a woodcutter for the opened pack and wants us all to stand with him; I did not see it happen and won't swear to what I didn't see.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Holds my note for a load of fibre; he has been patient but he counts.

relations.name: Bracken Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Builds with fallen wood like my Clover; we talk tools and he keeps his opinions to himself.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Reedmoor's headwoman buys fibre and salves through me; she pays in fish and in straight talk.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Lakemead folk are good customers and good company; I would not see them squeezed by the Elmwick quarrel.

relations.name: Pipwort Bramblecap
relations.label: Eldest
relations.note: She keeps the hollow's memory and I keep its stall; I would not want her to hear the talk about me before I have sorted it.

memories.gist: My first season at the crossing stall, when Alder Rush trusted me with a load of fibre on a promise and I sold every pack before dark.
The night Clover Mossfoot stayed late at the stall helping me sort salves, and we talked until the crossing was dark and neither of us wanted to go home.
Sorrel was born in the room above the stall and my Clover cut the cord; the whole hollow fed us for a week.
Finding the Reedmoor pack slit open at the crossing, half the fibre gone, and Thistle Mossfoot saying it was the woodcutter he quarrelled with.
The woodcutter drinking at the crossing that night; I saw him there and no more than that, whatever Thistle says.

stances.why: A stall lives on its word; Alder's fibre note comes before anything I want for myself.
I saw the woodcutter at the crossing but not the pack opened, and I will not swear beyond that to satisfy Thistle.
If the hollow stops using the crossing, Reedmoor and the Lakemead trade goes with it and my family eats poorer.
The hollow is beginning to talk about me and Clover Mossfoot, and my daughter is four and hears everything.
I know her marriage is strained and I am unsure whether to step back; I have told no one, not even my wife.

sheet.secret: I have grown far too close to Clover Mossfoot, Thistle's wife, and have told no one — not my own Clover, not the Eldest. I am unsure whether to step back, and the not-knowing is worse than the guilt.

sheet.narrative: I build the hollow's shelves and crates from fallen wood — never a living tree, not for anyone. My wife Tansy keeps the stall at the east road crossing and I keep it standing and stocked, and our Sorrel runs the garden paths between us. Since the Reedmoor pack was found opened, the crossing has been all suspicion and counting, and I would sooner be at the woodpile than in the middle of it. Tansy has been quiet these weeks, and I have not asked her why.
goals: keep the crossing stall's crates and shelves sound through the quarrel
see the hollow's traders agree on the crossing again
build Sorrel a proper little bench and garden frame of her own
find out what is weighing on Tansy without pushing her

relations.name: Tansy Hazel
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She carries the stall and the talk that comes with it; she has been quiet lately and I have not pressed her.

relations.name: Sorrel Hazel
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Four years old and already knows which end of a mallet to hold; I am making her a bench of her own.

relations.name: Bracken Sedge
relations.label: fellow builder
relations.note: We trade tools and both refuse to fell a living tree; he is the one I would ask about a joint I cannot get right.

relations.name: Clover Mossfoot
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Tansy's close friend over the fibre trade; she has been kind to our Sorrel and I have no quarrel with her.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trading partner
relations.note: He carries our packs on the east road; since the opened pack he sees a thief behind every tree.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Holds Tansy's fibre note; he has not pressed us and I mean to keep it that way.

relations.name: Yarrow Underbank
relations.label: fellow woodworker
relations.note: Works fallen wood as I do; we argue about joints and agree about trees.

relations.name: Pipwort Bramblecap
relations.label: Eldest
relations.note: Keeps the hollow's memory; I would not have her think badly of my house.

memories.gist: The day Tansy and I set the crossing stall's first crates and shelves, and Alder Rush came by and said they would hold.
Sorrel's first steps, taken across the woodpile in the yard while I steadied her and Tansy laughed from the stall.
Refusing a woodcutter's offer of good oak from a felled living tree, and the cold look he gave me after.
Hearing the talk at the crossing after the Reedmoor pack was found opened, and knowing my Tansy was at the middle of it.
Tansy coming home late from the stall these past weeks and saying little, and me not asking.

stances.why: The old forest kept us before the hollow did; fallen wood is enough for any shelf or crate.
My family's living comes through that stall, and a hollow split over a slit pack serves nobody.
Thistle names a woodcutter he quarrelled with; I have seen no proof and will not add my voice to a grudge.
Tansy has enough talk around her at the crossing; she will not get more of it from me.
A bench and a garden frame of her own is a small thing I can give her while the hollow argues.

sheet.narrative: I am four. The garden is my favourite place, and the stall is my second favourite, because there are always berries to sort and people to watch. Mama Tansy lets me put the little packets in the crate and Mama Clover lifts me up to see over the top. I do not like the big dark caves up in the hills; I stay in the garden.
goals: sort the berries all by myself
see over the top of the stall crate

relations.name: Tansy Hazel
relations.label: mama
relations.note: Keeps the stall and lets me sort the berries.

relations.name: Clover Hazel
relations.label: mama
relations.note: Lifts me up high and makes things out of wood for me.

relations.name: Tamarisk Bramblecap
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: We gather berries together and she is not afraid of the caves either.

memories.gist: Sorting berries at the stall and putting the little packets in the crate all by myself.
Mama Clover lifting me up to see over the top of the stall crate, and everyone laughing.

towns.name: Kettlebridge
towns.character: a hill town of brick and iron on terraces above a river; works and foundries, a clock tower in the square
towns.ledger: Kettlebridge Works Council. Apprentices are bound by indenture until their term. Stone is sold at the Council's price. Runaway apprentices are to be returned to their masters.

sheet.narrative: I keep the foundry's books, and I know to the crate how short we are on the Lanternquay order. My father is proud and will not admit it, so I write to Mercy Abbot without telling him how far the letters go. Two years ago Tobin Marrow shamed me before both towns, and I have not forgotten; but I was relieved when he broke it, and that is mine to keep.
goals: Meet the Lanternquay stone order without breaking the works
Settle Lanternquay's debt before another load goes down
Reopen northern trade with Brackenford through Mercy Abbot
Keep the foundry books straight and her own counsel

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: father
relations.note: I keep his books and his secrets, but I cannot tell him how far my letters go.

relations.name: Prudence Crane
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She feeds the Council and hears everything; I can be quiet with her.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: former betrothed
relations.note: He shamed me before both towns; I will not forget, though I was glad of it.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: correspondent
relations.note: She wants the gate-due gone and trade back; I write to her without my father knowing how far.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: He wrote the seawall indenture; I copied it and know the clause is ambiguous.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She carries our stone south and wants the debt settled; we are polite.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: She has not paid for the last load and calls our price a drowning man's price.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: His fear keeps the ridge closed and the order short; I wish he would answer for it.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: workman
relations.note: He works cheap and well; my father uses him, and I count his hours in the book.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: would-be apprentice
relations.note: She wants to learn the foundry books from me; she is quick and I am inclined to teach her.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings our stone north and pays the gate-due. He hates it and I do not blame him.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: council master
relations.note: He says little at the Council table and means all of it. He grumbles at the gate-due as I do, and he has never once asked me to soften a figure in the book.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: quarry tally-keeper
relations.note: Her tally is the cleanest of any crew's, and she says to my face that her husband was careless on the ridge. I would rather have her honesty than his excuses.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He builds the seawall crates and complains about Dele's wages in the same breath. He is owed for brick and he is owed nothing for the grudge.

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: terrace cook
relations.note: She feeds the terrace's children for a mark a bowl and says the works' kitchen could pay more. She is not wrong, and I write the figures that prove it.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper's daughter
relations.note: She has a good eye for a cracked pot and a better one for people. She stays friendly with Bisi though her father will not, and I notice such things.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: ironware trader
relations.note: She trades our foundry's seconds and never tries to hide a flaw in them. Her stall fee is owed and she will get it; I keep the book straight.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: works cook
relations.note: She wants Silas off the road and I want the stone moving. We have argued it over the kitchen table and neither of us has won.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: the other woman
relations.note: The town blames her and my mother blames her, but she did not break the promise. I cannot look at her without seeing the broken match, and that is my burden, not hers.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: He fishes his uncle's drowned boat and resents our stone price. His mother owes us for the last load; he will hear the tally from me sooner or later.

memories.gist: Tobin broke our match a month before the wedding and married Wenna; I stood in the foundry yard while the town talked.
I was relieved when it ended; I did not want to leave the works for Brackenford.
I copied the seawall indenture into the foundry book and saw the clause could be read two ways.
I began writing to Mercy Abbot about reopening the northern trade, without telling my father how far it goes.
My mother set the Council's table after a sitting and I heard the masters argue the tithe and the stone price.

stances.why: The numbers are the only thing in the works that cannot be argued with.
They owe us for the last load, and we cannot carry them forever.
The ridge is closed and the order is short; Brackenford is the way to cover it.
My father would rather buy time than break his word, and I will not shame him.
Tobin shamed me before both towns; I will not forget, even if I was glad.

sheet.secret: I was relieved when Tobin broke the match; I did not want to leave the works.

sheet.narrative: I am foundry master and chair of the Works Council, and I built this works with my hands and my word. Aldric Marrow's son insulted my house when he broke his promise to Hester, and Kettlebridge remembers: stone goes south now as much as north. The cairn cutting closed the ridge, and I will not beg a giant's pardon, but the Lanternquay order must be met.
goals: Meet the Lanternquay seawall order and keep the works' name
Reopen the ridge quarry without begging the giants
Get Pell back and make an example of him
Keep the gate-due fought at every turn

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She keeps my books and knows the works better than any clerk; I am proud of her.

relations.name: Prudence Crane
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps my house and my table, and the Council eats from her hand.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: rival
relations.note: His son insulted my house, and he keeps the gate-due that robs every carter.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: betrayer
relations.note: He broke his promise to my daughter and shamed my house before both towns.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: council second
relations.note: Slow to speak and slower to forgive; he sits with me and I count on him.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: He holds the contracts and reads the seawall clause against me; I want it read again.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: He led the cutting and now will not climb; his fear costs the works, and he must answer.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He has been robbed twice and still carries our stone; I trust him on the road.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: hired hand
relations.note: He works cheap and does not complain; the quay folk are useful.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He builds the seawall crates and resents the cheap hands; I keep him working.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: She has not paid for the last load and calls our price a drowning man's price.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: runaway apprentice
relations.note: He ran from his indenture; I hold it and want him back to answer for it.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: foreman
relations.note: He worked the cutting beside Ezra and has not gone back up. He is steadier than Ezra, and I need him.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She carries our stone south and reads the clause her way. She will have her marks when the stone is cut.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: quarry tally
relations.note: She keeps the quarry tally straight and tells me her husband was careless. I would hear that from her before I hear it from anyone.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: quarry hand
relations.note: Silas's boy works the floor and wants his father's place. Ambition is no bad thing in a quarryman.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She sets the quarrymen's bones and says the cutting was wrong. I do not want a healer's sermons, but she is good at what she does.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: works cook
relations.note: She feeds the works and wants her husband off the road. A sensible woman with a sensible worry.

relations.name: Tobiah Marsh
relations.label: crate-maker
relations.note: He makes the crates for Silas's loads and grumbles at the Brackenford due. A careful man with a saw, and I pay him for it.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: the weaver's daughter
relations.note: She is the reason my daughter was shamed. I have nothing to say to her and less to say of her.

memories.gist: Tobin Marrow broke his promise to Hester a month before the wedding; I stood in the Council yard and heard the town talk.
The quarrymen cut into a giants' cairn on the ridge, and Hollbrenna closed the shelf to us; I will not beg her pardon.
I promised Lanternquay a great quantity of seawall stone at Hester's price, and the works cannot cut it fast enough.
Pell ran from the foundry before his indenture ended; I offered marks for word of him.
Silas Pike was robbed twice on the stone road and still brought the load through; I remember that.

stances.why: A contract is a man's word, and mine is the works.
Hollbrenna closed the shelf; I will not go to her on my knees.
He ran from his indenture, and if one boy runs the rest will follow.
Brackenford's due robs every carter and drives trade away.
Aldric's son insulted my house, and Kettlebridge remembers.

sheet.narrative: I keep the foundry house and its table, and the Council's masters eat here after every sitting. I hear what they say and I keep it. The Marrows owe my house an apology, and I have not had it; until I do, they will not sit at my table.
goals: Keep the foundry house and its table as it should be
See the Marrows apologise for the broken match
Keep the Council's masters fed and their talk in the house
sheet.mood: warm to her own, cold to the Marrows

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He built this works with his hands, and I keep his house and his table.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She keeps the books and her own counsel; I am proud of her.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: His son insulted my house, and he has never come to apologise.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: betrayer
relations.note: He broke his promise to my daughter and shamed us before both towns.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: council master
relations.note: He eats at my table and speaks slowly; I keep his plate warm.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: He winds the clock and writes the contracts; he is careful at my table.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: workman
relations.note: He works cheap for my husband; I have no quarrel with him.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He builds the crates and grumbles about the cheap hands; I feed him all the same.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: She has not paid for the stone, and I hear it at my table.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: works cook
relations.note: She feeds the works and I feed the masters. We understand each other's work.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: She keeps an ironware stall in the square and trades with our foundry. She is sharp and I like her.

memories.gist: Tobin Marrow broke his promise to Hester a month before the wedding; I set the table that night for a house that had been shamed.
I fed the Council's masters after the sitting where they argued the gate-due and the stone price.
Hester told me she was glad the match broke; I have kept that to myself.
I heard at my own table that Lanternquay had not paid for the last load.

stances.why: The Council eats here, and a house is judged by its table.
The Marrows shamed my house and have never come to say sorry.
A fed master speaks freely, and I hear what is said.
Hester and Josiah are my house, and I will not see them shamed again.

sheet.narrative: I am old master of the brickworks and second voice on the Works Council. I speak slowly and forgive more slowly. Josiah is my chair and my friend, but I think the tithe should be forgiven this winter, though I will not fight him over a farmer. The gate-due at Brackenford is a robbery, and I have said so.
goals: Keep the brickworks and the kiln yard in good order
See the gate-due at Brackenford dropped
Hold the Council together behind Josiah

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: council chair
relations.note: He chairs the Council and I sit second; he is a hard man but a straight one.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books and knows them; I respect that.

relations.name: Prudence Crane
relations.label: hostess
relations.note: She feeds the Council after every sitting, and I am glad of it.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: He writes the contracts and winds the clock; a careful man.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He rents my kiln yard and led the cutting; I keep my peace with him.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: farmer
relations.note: He is behind on his tithe, and I think it should be forgiven this winter.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He builds the seawall crates; he owes Josiah for brick and I hear of it.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He has been robbed twice and still carries; a good man on the road.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the gate-due that robs every carter, and I have no love for it.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: works hand
relations.note: He came up from the quay and works cheap. The builders resent him, but the man has to eat.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: quarry foreman
relations.note: He worked the cutting beside Ezra and has not gone back up the ridge since. A foreman who will not go where he sends his men is no foreman; still, he has not lied about it, and I am slow to condemn a man for fear.

relations.name: Verity Ashcombe
relations.label: farmer's wife
relations.note: She knows which strips will fail and keeps the seed store against it. If the Council had her sense, we would count Hedley's greens and be done. I will not fight Josiah over a farmer, but she is the one I would listen to.

memories.gist: I sat second on the Council when Josiah sent stone south to Lanternquay as much as north to Brackenford.
The quarrymen cut into a giants' cairn on the ridge; I said little, but I remember the silence in the Council yard.
I argued at the sitting that Hedley Ashcombe's tithe should be forgiven this winter, and Josiah would not hear it.
I buried an old foundry hand who had worked beside me; the Crane men carried him.

stances.why: The winter is hard and the store is short; a farmer cannot pay in grain he does not have.
Brackenford's due robs every carter and sours the road.
The works stand on the Council, and the Council stands on Josiah.
The brickworks and the kiln yard are my life's work.

sheet.narrative: I cook for the works' kitchen, up before the clock strikes five to get the porridge on for a hundred hands. It's honest work, but I'd trade every mark of it for Silas off that stone road. Twice they've taken his load, and the Council won't pay for a guard. He says the works need the berries; I say the works can find another carter.
goals: Get Silas off the stone road and onto the fish road with Juno
Keep the works' kitchen running and the hands fed
Put by enough marks to see the children through winter
sheet.mood: worried, stretched thin, quietly angry at the Council

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He's a good man and a stubborn one; I'd have him home every night if I could.

relations.name: Elias Pike
relations.label: son
relations.note: Rides the cart's tail and thinks he's a man already; I want him off that road too.

relations.name: Tamsin Pike
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Keeps the scraps for the dogs and chatters at my elbow; she's the light of the kitchen.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He pays my wages and won't pay for a guard on the road; I keep my tongue civil.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: A decent woman on the fish road; I'd trust her to keep Silas safe if he'd go with her.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: scribe
relations.note: Writes the Council's contracts; I've asked him plain what a carter's due is, and he tells me straight.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: I buy ironware from her stall; she talks too much, but she's fair.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Brings greens and roots to my kitchen; I wish he'd bring more of them.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: His crew's stone is what fills the cart, and his carelessness on the ridge is why the giants are angry; I have no patience for him.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: foundry daughter
relations.note: She keeps the books and is fair about the kitchen's account, which is more than her father is about the road.

memories.gist: The night Silas came home with the cart empty and a cut on his arm, and I couldn't stop shaking.
Cooking my first works' supper alone when the old cook took ill; a hundred hands and not a complaint.
Tamsin born in the little room off the kitchen yard, with the bells ringing for the noon shift.
Elias riding the cart's tail for the first time, proud as a lord, and me watching from the gate.
Arguing with Silas at the kitchen table about the fish road, and him saying the stone road is his trade.

stances.why: A husband who comes home is worth more than a carter's wages.
If the works need the berries, the works should keep the road safe.
They robbed my Silas twice and I'll not forgive it.
A cook is judged by her pot, and I'll not be shamed.

sheet.narrative: I've carted stone on the stone road for fifteen years and never lost a load till the Coldwell folk took to the woods. Now I pay the gate-due at Brackenford and still get robbed on the road, and the Council won't put a guard on me. I've asked Wat Fenner for an escort on the next run and I mean to hold him to it. Ruth wants me on the fish road with Juno; she may be right, but the stone road is my trade.
values: a fair day's work for a fair day's pay
not being made a fool of
goals: Get an escort of guards for the next cart run
Make Reginald Hobson pay for the last load of stone
Keep the works' trade and my good name

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She's the best cook in Kettlebridge and the best sense in the house; I know she's right and I can't say it.

relations.name: Elias Pike
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good lad on the cart's tail; I'll not have him robbed like his father.

relations.name: Tamsin Pike
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My little one; she keeps the dogs fed and me smiling.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: Takes my due at the south gate; I've asked him for an escort and I mean to hold him to it.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I know her by sight and I fear her people; she's the reason I carry a knife now.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: She buys my stone at Brackenford market and pays fair; I'd rather deal with her than the gate.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Owes me for the last load and says he can't pay till the Reeve settles; I'll not be put off again.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: His gate-due eats my profit and he keeps it; I'll pay it and hate it.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He gives me the loads and won't pay for a guard; I'll not beg him twice.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: A good sort on the fish road; Ruth would have me go with her, but that's not my trade.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: His crew loads my cart; a hard man, but he knows stone.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: contract writer
relations.note: He writes the Council's contracts and my load tallies both; a man who keeps the clock keeps a sharp eye on what comes through the gate.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: quay trader
relations.note: He buys iron and sells rope and tar, and he calls the gate-due robbery like any sensible man; we have shared a jug when I have been down the fish road.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She brought both my children into the world and she is the one person in that house I would not press for a debt.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: deserter
relations.note: A quay guard who ran and now keeps company with Marta's people; if there is a man on the road who knows how a cart is taken, it is him.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: robber
relations.note: He has had his share off my cart twice, and I hear he wants more men for the next one; I will not go past Coldwell without Wat Fenner and another guard beside him.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: mason's son
relations.note: A decent lad learning his father's trade; I would sooner deal with him over a load than with his father, who cannot find the marks to pay me.

memories.gist: The first robbery: men out of the trees by Coldwell and my load gone, and me shaking on the cart seat.
The second robbery, and them laughing as they took the berries; I swore I'd not be taken so easy again.
Hearing from a Coldwell man on the road that a foundry boy had joined them; I fear he'll be made to rob me a third time.
The day I first drove the cart alone to Brackenford, and the gate guard took my due and waved me through.
Elias riding the cart's tail and learning the ruts and tolls beside me.

stances.why: Twice robbed is enough; I'll not go out alone again.
It's robbery at the gate after robbery on the road.
They know the ambush places and they've taken my load twice.
I've carted it fifteen years; I'll not be run off it by outlaws or my wife's worry.
I carried the stone and paid the due on it; he owes me.

sheet.narrative: I ride the cart's tail and I'm learning the road's ruts and tolls. Father says I'll drive the cart alone one day, but since the robberies he keeps looking back at me. I want to be a carter like him, and I want to see the outlaws caught.
goals: Learn to drive the cart alone
See the Coldwell outlaws caught
Make my father proud

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's the best carter on the road and he's teaching me.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She wants Father off the road, but she always has a hot supper for us.

relations.name: Tamsin Pike
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Little pest, but she's all right.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: Takes the due at the gate; Father says he might guard us on the road.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She goes up and down the fish road and never seems afraid; I watch how she does it.

memories.gist: Riding the cart's tail for the first time, holding on tight and watching the ruts go by.
Hearing the men talk of the robbery and seeing Father's cut arm.
Helping load stone at the quarry and getting a nod from the foreman.

stances.why: A carter's son should know every rut and toll.
They hurt my father and I want them stopped.
That's what it means to be a man on the road.

sheet.narrative: I keep the kitchen scraps for the works' dogs and I play in the yard. Mother is always cooking and Father is always on the road. I like the dogs best, and I don't like it when Father is late.
goals: Feed the dogs every day
See Father come home safe

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She smells of the kitchen and she always has a bit of bread for me.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: father
relations.note: He brings me back a sweet from Brackenford when he can.

relations.name: Elias Pike
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He's bossy but he plays with me sometimes.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: He lets me watch the clock wound if I stand still, and he does not mind my questions.

memories.gist: Feeding the works' dogs scraps from the kitchen and them licking my fingers.
Waiting at the yard gate for Father's cart to come back and running to meet it.

sheet.narrative: I am a quarrier, and a good one; I can read a seam of stone the way other men read weather. Last year I led the crew up the ridge and we cut into stones that were not stones, and I swear by the Hearth I did not know what they were until the giants came down. Now the shelf is closed and Josiah Crane presses me to answer for it, and I will not climb that ridge again for any master's order. I owe Tavvik for meat and I pay when I can, and I do not sleep well when the wind comes off the mountains.
values: an honest day's work for an honest wage
goals: keep my place with Josiah Crane without climbing the ridge
pay off what I owe Tavvik before he comes asking
find stone enough to fill the Lanternquay order from somewhere else
hear no more talk of the cairn

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She says I was careless and she is not wrong, and I would rather she did not say it at the table.

relations.name: Bramwell Holt
relations.label: son
relations.note: He carries water up to the crew and hears too much of the men's talk.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He pays well and presses hard; he wants ridge stone and I will not get it for him.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: foreman
relations.note: He worked the cutting beside me and has not gone back up either; we do not speak of it.

relations.name: Tavvik
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: A giant who carries meat down the track; I owe him and I dread the day he collects.

relations.name: Orrum
relations.label: accuser
relations.note: Hollbrenna's son wants me to answer for the cairn, and I have no answer that would satisfy him.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: He rents my crew a kiln yard and has not turned us out over the cairn, which is more than some would.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A builder who thinks quarrymen are paid too much and work too slow.

relations.name: Hollbrenna
relations.label: the elder
relations.note: She forbade the shelf to all of us for what my crew cut into, and I cannot blame her, and I cannot undo it either.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She carries stone down the fish road and asks after the ridge; I tell her what I can and no more.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: friend's wife
relations.note: She begs Silas to take the fish road instead of the stone road, and I cannot say she is wrong to.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He owes me nothing and I owe him for a load of props; he has been robbed twice and still loads the cart, and I want that road kept open.

memories.gist: The morning we broke into the cairn: flat dressed stones in a ring, and then the giant standing on the ridge above us, saying nothing.
Hollbrenna's word coming down the track: the shelf closed to Kettlebridge, and no quarry crew to climb the ridge.
Josiah Crane in the quarry yard, asking how much ridge stone the Lanternquay order still needs, and not liking my answer.
Tavvik setting down a haunch of meat at the yard gate and saying he would be paid, slowly if need be.
Bramwell carrying the water up and standing too close while the men talked of the cairn.
Corin dressing a block in the yard, and telling me plain that I should have known better.

stances.why: I have said it a hundred times and it is true; no quarrier cuts a cairn on purpose.
Whatever Josiah offers, the giants are up there and I am not going to meet them.
A debt to a giant is not one to let sit; he has been patient and I would keep him so.
They have families on the terrace and I led them up the ridge once already.
Corin will say her piece and Bramwell is listening; better the yard hears it than the house.

sheet.secret: I have walked up the track alone at dusk to look at the broken cairn and left a flat stone on it, and I have told no one, not even Corin.

sheet.narrative: I am a mason, and I dress the stone my husband's crew raises; a block that is not square is a block that will not hold. I keep the quarry tally for Josiah Crane and I know to the load how much ridge stone the Lanternquay order still wants, and that is the trouble: Ezra will not climb and I cannot make him. He was careless up there and I tell him so at home, because someone must. I fear the giants will come down the track one day, and I keep the yard swept and the tally straight so that whatever comes, our house is in order.
goals: get the Lanternquay order filled from some other face
make Ezra face what he did without breaking him
keep Bramwell away from the ridge and the talk of it
keep Josiah Crane satisfied with the tally

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good quarrier and a stubborn man; he was careless on the ridge and he will not hear it twice.

relations.name: Bramwell Holt
relations.label: son
relations.note: He listens at the yard gate and comes home with the men's talk in his head.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He wants his stone and he is right to want it; I keep the tally so he cannot say we cheated him.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: foreman
relations.note: He was beside Ezra at the cutting and he will not speak of it either; two men keeping one silence.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She said plainly the cutting was wrong, and I respect her for it though it is my husband she speaks of.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: master's daughter
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books and asks after the tally; she is fair and she does not nag.

relations.name: Tavvik
relations.label: giant
relations.note: He brings meat down the track against the elder's word, and one day that will bring the elder down too.

relations.name: Gaudra
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: A giant of the shelf I have never met, and I would rather it stayed that way.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: foreman's son
relations.note: He works the quarry floor and thinks his father has gone soft about the ridge; I have heard him say the cairn was only stones, and I do not care for it.

memories.gist: The day the crew came down off the ridge with their tools on their shoulders and would not say what they had found.
Josiah Crane reading the tally aloud in the yard and asking where the ridge stone was.
Dressing a block in the yard while Ezra sat on the wall and would not look at the ridge.
Bramwell asking me what a cairn is, and me not knowing what to tell him.
Odile Vance saying at the well that the cutting was wrong and the giants had right on their side.

stances.why: If the masters cannot trust the count they will not trust the crew, and we live by the crew.
I will not pretend at my own table that he did right; someone in this house must say it.
They are patient, not forgiving, and the track runs to our town.
He is eleven and afraid of it already; he does not need the men's talk to make it worse.
The Lanternquay order must be met and there is stone in the lower faces that no giant ever laid.

sheet.secret: I have twice written the ridge loads in the tally as though they came from the lower face, because Josiah would not take 'none' for an answer.

sheet.narrative: I carry the water up to the crew in a bucket that is too big for me, and I like the quarry because there is always something happening. Since the cairn was cut the men go quiet when I come near, and my father does not go up the ridge any more. My mother says I am not to go up there either, and I do not want to: I saw the giant on the skyline once and I still dream of it.
values: keeping out of the men's way
goals: carry the water without spilling it
be allowed to hold the measuring rod
not to go up the ridge
sheet.mood: watchful, a little frightened, eager to be useful

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is the best quarrier in Kettlebridge and he does not go up the ridge any more.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She dresses the stone and keeps the tally, and she says the ridge is not for me.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: foreman
relations.note: He was at the cutting and he has not gone back up either; he is kind to me in the yard.

relations.name: Perry Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He climbs the clock tower steps and I climb the quarry spoil; we race.

relations.name: Nella Marsh
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She knows her letters and reads the crate marks to me.

memories.gist: Seeing a giant standing on the ridge above the quarry, still as a stone, while the men below said nothing.
Carrying the water up and the men stopping their talk when I came near.
My mother asking me what a cairn is and me not being able to answer.

stances.why: My mother said not to, and the giant is up there.
If I carry the water well they let me stay and listen.

sheet.narrative: I came up the fish road from Lanternquay after the Surge took our lower quay, and I have built with whatever stone and salvage Kettlebridge would sell me since. Josiah Crane pays me what he pays, and I take it, because my family eats. The works builders say I undercut them; I say I price what I can live on, and I keep my temper and my friends.
values: a fair day's work for a fair day's pay
goals: keep steady work enough to feed Ife and the children
save a little against a bad winter
see the seawall built at Lanternquay one day
stay on good terms with Mara Quell and the quay folk

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the stall and the children fed; I keep the work coming.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with numbers and quick with her tongue — she'll go further than the terrace.

relations.name: Tayo Oyelaran
relations.label: son
relations.note: Born on the quay and still jumps at the works' bells.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He pays me what he pays, and I take it. He's not a bad master, only a hard one.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: The Warden and I came up together in the old days; she still sends word down the road.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He says I undercut him. I say I price what I can live on. We pass in the yard and say nothing.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: master's daughter
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books and doesn't look down on the terrace. Bisi wants to learn from her.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A quay builder like me; we drink together when I'm down at Lanternquay.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Gideon's wife keeps the ironware stall; she's civil enough when the men aren't about.

memories.gist: The night the Surge took the lower quay: I carried Ife and the children up the steps with the water at our heels.
Walking the fish road north with everything we owned on my back, not knowing what Kettlebridge would offer.
The first day Josiah Crane put a trowel in my hand and said the wage, and I said yes because the children were hungry.
Gideon Fenwick saying in the Council yard that the terrace should be sent back to the quay, and me holding my tongue.
Drinking with Ostrander Vane on the quay steps the last time I was down, talking about the seawall we'll never get stone for.

stances.why: A man who won't work is a man who won't eat; I take what work is offered and do it well.
The works men want me to shout so they can say the terrace is trouble. I won't give them that.
Ife and the children eat because I swallow my pride and take Crane's wage.
Mara Quell and the quay folk took me in when I was young; I don't forget a kindness.
Salvage won't hold another surge. The wall must be stone, whatever Crane charges for it.

sheet.secret: He sometimes wonders whether coming to Kettlebridge was a mistake, and whether the quay would take him back if the wall were ever built.

sheet.narrative: I keep the cook-stall on the poor terrace and feed the terrace's children for a mark a bowl, because somebody must. The works' kitchen pays less than it might and the builders' wives look at me as if I brought the flood with me. I charge the yard boys now, and I don't apologise for it.
values: a fair price for a fair bowl
the terrace looks after its own
goals: keep the stall turning enough to feed the family
see Bisi learn the foundry books and rise above the terrace
get Tayo past his fear of the bells and the smoke
see Dele treated as a builder, not a beggar

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He keeps his temper with the works men; I keep mine with the works' kitchen. We do it for the children.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She minds the stall and counts better than I do. She'll not stay on the terrace if I can help it.

relations.name: Tayo Oyelaran
relations.label: son
relations.note: Born on the quay and still frightened of the smoke and the bells. He clings to his sister.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He'd send us back to the quay if he could. I've heard what he says in the yard.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She keeps the ironware stall and is civil enough, but she's Gideon's wife first.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: works cook
relations.note: The works' kitchen could pay more and doesn't. Ruth knows it and says nothing.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: master's daughter
relations.note: She's fair with Bisi and doesn't look down on us. More than her father does.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: The Warden sent word when we came up; she's never forgotten Dele or me.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour's daughter
relations.note: She and Bisi are thick as thieves, and I'll not visit Gideon's words on his girl. But she's Fenwick's, and she'll hear her father's talk at her own table.

memories.gist: The Surge night: I held Tayo and Bisi on the high steps while Dele went back for the pots.
Opening the cook-stall on the terrace the first week, with one pot and no customers, and feeding the yard boys for nothing to get them coming back.
Hearing Gideon Fenwick say the terrace should be sent back to the quay, and deciding then to charge the yard boys for their bowls.
Bisi bringing home her first tally of the stall's marks, all correct, and me proud enough to cry.
The works' kitchen hiring a terrace girl for less than a mark a day, and me saying nothing because the girl needed the work.

stances.why: A bowl for a mark is a fair price, and no child on the terrace goes hungry if I can help it.
The yard boys can pay; the works' kitchen pays less than it might, so I make up the difference where I can.
We are not beggars and we are not the flood. The terrace works and pays its way.
She's quick with numbers; if Hester Crane will teach her the books, she'll not end her days over a cook-pot.
They pay the terrace cheap and then complain we take their work. I won't forget it.

sheet.secret: She has started putting by a few marks in a jar behind the flour, in case Dele's work dries up and they must go back to the quay.

sheet.narrative: I mind Mama's stall when she's out and I'm quicker with the tally than anyone on the terrace. I want to learn the foundry books from Hester Crane, and I will, if I can get the chance. Tayo follows me everywhere and I don't mind.
values: don't let them look down on the terrace
goals: learn the foundry books from Hester Crane
keep Mama's stall tally straight
look after Tayo
see the quay at Lanternquay one day

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: father
relations.note: He works hard and never shouts at the works men. I want to be like that.

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the stall and the family; she says I'll not end my days over a cook-pot.

relations.name: Tayo Oyelaran
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He follows me about the terrace and jumps at the bells. I look after him.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books and doesn't look down on us. I want to learn from her.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Her father says things about mine, but Lottie and I are friends anyway.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: father's rival
relations.note: He says my father steals work by taking low pay, but my father works for what he's given. I keep my tongue when he's near the stall, and Lottie and I don't talk about it.

memories.gist: The Surge night: I held Tayo on the high steps and watched the water take the lower quay.
Mama teaching me the stall's tally and letting me keep the marks in the box for the first time.
Hester Crane showing me the foundry ledger and saying I had a good hand for figures.
Hearing Gideon Fenwick say the terrace should be sent back to the quay, and deciding I'd prove him wrong.

stances.why: Mama's stall lives or dies on the tally, and I keep it straight.
If I can read the foundry books, I can rise above the terrace. Hester Crane will teach me if I'm patient.
Papa and Mama work for us; I mind the stall and Tayo.
The works folk think we're beggars. We're not. I won't let them say it in front of me.

sheet.secret: She has been practising her letters in secret on the back of the stall's tally sheets, so she can read the foundry books before she asks Hester Crane.

sheet.narrative: The smoke is loud and the bells are loud and I don't like them. I stay close to Bisi and Mama's stall, and I watch the yard boys carry things. The terrace is big and the sky is grey.
goals: stay near Bisi
not be frightened by the bells

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the stall and holds me when the bells ring.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: father
relations.note: He carries me on his shoulders when he comes home.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She lets me follow her about the terrace and tells me what the numbers mean.

memories.gist: The Surge night: water and shouting and Mama holding me tight on the high steps.
The first time the clock tower struck and I hid under the stall until Bisi found me.

sheet.narrative: I have worked stone since I was a lad, and I have been foreman on the ridge long enough to know a bad cut before the hammer falls. When Ezra picked that line across the cairn stones I told him the ground looked wrong, and he went ahead anyway; I will not take a crew back up there, not for Josiah Crane nor for the Council. My wife Odile says the giants are owed an answer, and I reckon she is right, but the answer is Ezra's to give, not mine. I keep the quarry floor below the ridge and my house by the clock tower, and I will not be shamed into climbing again.
values: an honest day's work for an honest day's pay
a foreman's word is his bond
goals: keep my crew off the ridge and my name clear of the cutting
see Ezra stand up and answer for the cairn
hold my foreman's place under Josiah Crane
get Corwin to look higher than a terrace farmer's daughter
sheet.mood: grim and set in his ways

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She says what I will not say aloud, and she is usually right about it.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good hand with stone, but he thinks a foreman's place is owed him and a farmer's girl is good enough.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: He chose the ridge and now he will not climb it. The answer is his to give, and he gives it to Josiah instead of the giants.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: quarryman's wife
relations.note: She keeps the tally straight and does not spare her husband at home. I can respect that.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He pays my wage and presses me to press Ezra. I will not be pressed up that ridge.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: council master
relations.note: Slow to speak and slower to forgive. He would not send a crew up there either.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A terrace farmer with opinions about quarrymen. His daughter is the one Corwin has set his heart on.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: He writes the contracts and winds the clock. A man who keeps things in order.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He builds the seawall crates and grumbles about the stone price like the rest of them.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: Works cheap and the yard mutters. He has not been up the ridge either, so he does not know what he is cheap about.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A hard worker on poor ground, and that counts for something. But a foreman's son can look higher than a terrace strip, and I have said it once too often already.

memories.gist: The morning Ezra chose the line across the ridge and I told him the ground looked wrong; he laughed and set the first drill.
The day the drill broke into the cairn stones and the whole crew went quiet, and I knew we had done something that could not be undone.
Josiah Crane in the Council yard telling me to take a crew back up and finish the ridge order, and me saying no to his face.
Odile setting a quarryman's arm by the clock tower while I held the man still, and her telling me afterwards that the cairn cutting was a sin.
Corwin at the supper table saying his father had gone soft about the ridge, and me leaving the table rather than strike him.
The Lean Year, when the works went short and the quarry crews took half wages and the terrace families queued at the works' kitchen.

stances.why: I told Ezra the ground was wrong and I will not take men up there to prove it again.
He chose the line. The giants are owed an answer, and it is not mine to give.
A foreman who loses men to his own pride is no foreman.
A foreman's son can do better than a terrace farmer's daughter, and I have said so once too often.
The masters sit in the yard and set the price; it is the crews that take the risk.

sheet.narrative: I keep the healer's room by the clock tower, and quarrymen come to me with broken fingers and crushed feet and I set them as best I can. I buy my herbs from a Tanglewood woman who walks the old forest paths, and she has taught me more than the works' doctors ever did. When they cut into the cairn I said in my own house and to anyone who asked that it was wrong, and I have not changed my mind; the giants keep their dead on the ridges and we had no business there. Silas will not go back up and I do not press him, though Josiah Crane presses him enough for both of us.
values: heal whoever comes to the door
the dead are not to be disturbed
a healer keeps her own counsel
herbs and patience over the works' doctors
goals: keep the quarry crews mending and the salves stocked through winter
see the cairn cutting answered for, and the giants' peace mended if it can be
keep Silas from being driven up the ridge by the Council
see Corwin settle with a girl who will not make him a stranger in his own house

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He carries the ridge on his shoulders and will not say so. I set his hands when the stone splits them.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has his father's stubbornness and none of his patience. I wish he would stop measuring himself against Silas.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: Careless is the kindest word I have for it. He should have known what the stones were.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: quarryman's wife
relations.note: She says at home what I say in my room, and it costs her. I send her salve for her hands.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He wants the ridge stone and does not care what was disturbed to get it.

relations.name: Odile Wrack
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: A Kettlebridge woman gone down to the quay. We trade herbs and complaints when she comes up.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: She sets bones on the quay and buys from the same Tanglewood woman. I would trust her with a bad break.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A decent man with a daughter who works hard. Silas is wrong about her.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: neighbour's daughter
relations.note: She came to me for a salve for her father's knees and stayed to talk of the poor strip. A good girl.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: Brings me herbs and news from the road. His back is bad and he will not rest it.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: Sells me ironware and works' seconds and never cheats the weight.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: Writes a clean hand and keeps the clock honest. I have him copy my salve lists.

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: herb-seller
relations.note: Her salves are honest and her roots are sound. She left the chapel and will not come back through the gate, and I cannot say I blame her.

memories.gist: The week the crews came down from the ridge with their hands shaking, and I set three broken fingers in one evening and heard the same story each time.
Telling Silas at our own table that the cairn cutting was a sin, and him not arguing, only sitting with his cup.
The Tanglewood woman showing me how to draw the fever out of a quarryman's cut with a poultice of old forest leaves.
Corwin bringing Rosalind Ashcombe to the door for a salve and watching her like a lad at a fair, and me pretending not to notice.
The Lean Year, when half the terrace came to my room with coughs and no marks to pay, and I took what they could give and no more.

stances.why: The giants keep their dead on the ridges and we had no business there. I have said so and will say so again.
A healer who asks a man's quarrel before she sets his bone is no healer.
He told Ezra the ground was wrong and was not heard. I will not be the one who drives him back up.
Hollbrenna closed the shelf for a reason, and someone should go and speak to her plainly.
Silas has said his piece once too often. The boy will marry where he will, and Rosalind is no bad choice.

sheet.narrative: I work the quarry floor under Ezra Holt and I am not ashamed of it, but I mean to have my father's foreman's place and I do not see why wanting it should be a sin. My father will not go back up the ridge and the crews mutter about it; I think a foreman who will not climb is no foreman, cairn or no cairn. Rosalind Ashcombe is the best thing in my life and her father looks at me like I am the tithe collector come round, and my own father looks at her like she is beneath us, and neither of them has asked me what I want.
values: a man makes his own place
the crew respects a foreman who climbs
hard work and a fair wage
goals: take my father's foreman's place on the ridge
marry Rosalind Ashcombe with both fathers' blessing, or without them
get the ridge crews working again so the Lanternquay order is met
prove to Silas that I am not a boy to be told who to court

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: father
relations.note: He thinks I am soft for wanting the ridge worked and soft for wanting Rosalind. I am neither.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She does not lecture me. She asks questions and then sets my hands when the stone splits them.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: She wants to try a new crop on the poor strip and I would dig the whole terrace for her.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: crew boss
relations.note: He chose the ridge and he will not climb it, and the crews pay for it. A foreman should climb.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: her father
relations.note: He looks at me like the tithe collector. I have never taken a thing from his strips.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: He wants the ridge stone and the crews up there. He does not care that my father will not go.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Quick with numbers and quick with her tongue. She minds her mother's stall and wants the foundry books.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: crew wife
relations.note: She keeps the tally and does not spare Ezra at home. I like her for it.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She minds her father's stall and has a good eye for a cracked pot, and she does not care whose father says what.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: Hauls our stone north and hates the gate-due. He knows the road better than the Council does.

memories.gist: My first day on the quarry floor under Ezra, and my father watching from the lip of the cut without a word.
The crews coming down from the ridge after the cairn was cut, and the talk of it in the yard, and my father saying he would not go back up.
Rosalind Ashcombe laughing at something I said at the square stall, and me walking her back to the terrace steps and not wanting to go home.
Supper at our table when my father said a foreman's son could do better than a farmer's daughter, and my mother set down her spoon and said nothing.
The clock striking noon over the square while I counted the loads on the quarry cart and thought that one day the tally would be mine to keep.

stances.why: A foreman who will not go up the ridge is no foreman, whatever the crews mutter about the cairn.
Josiah needs the ridge stone for the Lanternquay order, and the works cannot eat pride.
Neither her father nor mine has asked me what I want, and I want her.
He will not climb and he will not say why beyond the cairn. The crews notice.
Bisi and Lottie and Rosalind are worth more than the masters' opinions of them.

sheet.narrative: I have built half the seawall crates on the fish road, and I have yet to be paid for the last load of brick I took from Josiah Crane. That is not the worst of it. The worst is Dele Oyelaran, who came up from the drowned quay and now takes works contracts at half the rate, and the Council lets him. I have said in the Council yard that the terrace should be sent back to the quay, and I meant it. A man cannot keep a family on what Dele leaves of the trade.
goals: get Dele barred from works contracts
collect what Josiah Crane owes him for the brick
keep the crate work coming in
see Lottie settled and Perry apprenticed well

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the stall and the marks, and she wishes I would hold my tongue. I wish she would see what Dele is doing to us.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Sharp as a nail, that one. She will make a trader yet.

relations.name: Perry Fenwick
relations.label: son
relations.note: Always up the clock tower. I was the same at his age, but he needs a trade in his hands.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He undercuts honest Kettlebridge rates and the Council does nothing. He should go back to the quay.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He owes me for the last load of brick, and I owe him for the load before. It is a knot I cannot untie.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: foundry master's daughter
relations.note: She sets the seawall price and keeps the books. Fair enough, but she is her father's daughter.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: the rival's daughter
relations.note: Lottie is friendly with her. I would rather she was not, but I will not say so to the girl.

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: the rival's wife
relations.note: She feeds the terrace for a mark a bowl and undercuts the works' kitchen the same way her husband undercuts my yard. I have nothing against her pot, only the price.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: quay runner
relations.note: She comes up the fish road for stone and carries my crates down. She is polite enough, but she is quay through and through, and quay stone is what is keeping Kettlebridge work from the north.

relations.name: Tobiah Marsh
relations.label: crate hand
relations.note: A careful man with a saw, and he grumbles at the Brackenford due the same as I do. He works my yard when the crates are wanted and I would rather have ten of him than one Dele.

memories.gist: The day I took the last load of brick from Josiah Crane's yard, and he said the payment would come after the seawall order was filled. It has not come.
Standing in the Council yard and saying out loud that the terrace should be sent back to the quay. Ambrose Vell nodded. Josiah said nothing.
The morning I lost the Elmwick barn job to Dele's crew. The builder told me he could not refuse the price.
Mabel and I counting the marks in the locked box after the stall's best market day this year. Not enough for the brick debt.
Perry halfway up the clock tower steps again, and me hauling him down by the collar.

stances.why: He takes works contracts at half the rate and the Council lets him. That is not trade, it is theft from every builder in Kettlebridge.
They came up after the Surge and they have been undercutting us ever since. The quay should keep its own.
I delivered the load and I have not been paid. A debt is a debt, even between masters.
I build the crates for the fish road and I will not lift a finger to help Dele's crew with them. The quay can wait.
Whatever the Council says, Mabel and the children eat first.

sheet.narrative: I keep the ironware stall in the square and I know the price of a cracked pot better than most. Gideon is a good builder and a poor diplomat, and he has made an enemy of Dele Oyelaran in front of the whole Council yard. I still take Ife's marks over the stall, because marks are marks and the terrace has to eat. I wish my husband would hold his tongue, but I will not say so where the neighbours can hear.
values: a fair price and a fair word
not making enemies you cannot afford
goals: keep the stall's trade with the terrace and the foundry both
see Lottie learn the trade properly
keep Gideon out of trouble with the Council
pay off the stall fee she owes to no one, but keep the box full

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good builder with a short fuse. I wish he would let the Council yard go and come home to his supper.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has a better eye for a cracked pot than I had at her age. She will keep the stall one day.

relations.name: Perry Fenwick
relations.label: son
relations.note: Up the clock tower again. He will break his neck before he learns a trade.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: foundry master's daughter
relations.note: She buys ironware and pays on the day. I would trade with her all day if I could.

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She buys a pot and pays in marks, and her marks are as good as anyone's. I do not ask where they come from.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: Lottie's friend
relations.note: A quick girl. She minds her mother's stall and she is polite to me, which is more than her father is to Gideon.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: my husband's rival
relations.note: I have nothing against the man's trade, but he has made my Gideon bitter and that is hard to forgive.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: He writes the stall's contracts and he is fair about it. Perry would do worse than learn letters from him.

relations.name: Ottilie Ashcombe
relations.label: neighbour's daughter
relations.note: Verity's girl, always hanging about the stall with her eyes on the harbour. She counts the ironware as careful as Lottie does, and she has never yet dropped a pot.

memories.gist: The day Gideon came home from the Council yard with his jaw set and said he had called for the terrace to be sent back to the quay. I said nothing and put his supper down.
Ife Oyelaran buying a pot from the stall and paying in marks, and me taking them without a word. Gideon was in the yard and did not see.
Lottie spotting the crack in a pot before I did and pricing it down without being told. I was proud and I told her so.
Hester Crane coming to the stall for ironware and paying on the day, and saying the foundry would need more crates before the month was out.
Perry up the clock tower steps and me calling him down before the clock struck and he fell.

stances.why: Ife Oyelaran's marks spend the same as anyone's. I will not turn away a customer for my husband's quarrel.
Gideon has made an enemy of Dele in front of the whole yard, and enemies cost more than they are worth.
Whatever happens in the Council, the stall keeps the family fed and the box full.
She has the eye for it. A girl with a stall is a girl who will never go hungry.
Hester Crane pays on the day and needs ironware. That is a trade worth keeping sweet.

sheet.narrative: I mind the stall when Mother is cooking, and I know a cracked pot when I see one. Bisi Oyelaran is my friend and she is quick with numbers, and I do not care what Father says about her father. I want to keep the stall one day, and I want to see the quay at Lanternquay before I am old.
values: a good eye for a cracked pot
seeing the world beyond the square
goals: keep the stall's trade good
stay friends with Bisi despite the fathers
see Lanternquay and the tide lanterns
learn to price a whole stall's stock by eye

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She taught me the stall and the eye for a crack. I want to be as good as her one day.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is angry a lot, but he built the crates on the fish road and I am proud of that.

relations.name: Perry Fenwick
relations.label: brother
relations.note: Always up the clock tower. I tell him he will fall, and he tells me he will not.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Quick with numbers and quick with her tongue. Father does not like her, but he does not mind the stall's marks.

relations.name: Ife Oyelaran
relations.label: Bisi's mother
relations.note: She cooks at the terrace stall and she is kind to me when I buy a bowl.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: foundry master's daughter
relations.note: She comes to the stall and pays on the day. She has a quick eye for the books, like Bisi.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: He winds the clock and writes the contracts. He says a trader should know her letters.

memories.gist: Spotting the crack in a pot before Mother did and pricing it down without being told. She said I had the eye.
Bisi Oyelaran showing me how to add a column of marks in my head faster than I could count them on my fingers.
Father coming home from the Council yard with his jaw set and Mother putting his supper down without a word.
Perry halfway up the clock tower steps and me shouting at him to come down before the clock struck.
