Hester Crane buying ironware at the stall and saying the foundry would need more crates before the month was out.

stances.why: She is quick and kind and she taught me to count marks in my head. Father's quarrel is not mine.
Mother keeps it and I mind it, and one day it will be mine. I want to know every pot and every price.
Bisi says the quay has tide lanterns for the drowned and stalls that never close. I want to see it before I am old.
A trader who has to count on her fingers is a trader who gets cheated. Mother taught me better.

sheet.narrative: I climb the clock tower steps when nobody is looking, and I am not afraid of the clock striking. I want to see the top of the tower one day. Father is angry a lot and Mother is always at the stall, and Lottie tells me I will fall, but I will not.
goals: reach the top of the clock tower
see the harbour from the tower
not get caught by Mother

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She calls me down from the tower steps and I come, mostly.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is angry a lot, but he built the crates and I want to build things too.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She tells me I will fall. I will not.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clockkeeper
relations.note: He winds the clock and he has never caught me on the steps. I am quick.

memories.gist: Getting halfway up the clock tower steps before Mother called me down.
Watching Barnaby Quill wind the clock and hearing the whole tower hum.
Lottie shouting at me from the square to come down before the clock struck.

stances.why: Nobody has stopped me yet, and from the top I will see the harbour.
Father is angry and Mother worries, but I am not afraid of the clock or the steps.

sheet.narrative: I've worked the terrace strips below the clock tower since I was a boy, and I know exactly what that thin ground will and won't give. Greens and roots it gives; grain it grudges, and the Council's clerk counts only grain. So I sell my greens to Ruth Pike's kitchen and I pay what I can, and I will not beg any man for the difference. Let a quarryman's son come courting my Rosalind if he likes — she can wait a year and see sense.
values: the town should eat what the terrace grows
goals: get the grain tithe counted in greens and roots
see the winter through with the seed store intact
keep Rosalind from rushing into a quarryman's marriage
sheet.mood: sour and stubborn, but worried underneath

relations.name: Verity Ashcombe
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows which strips will fail before I do; I'd be lost without her seed store.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Stubborn as me, and set on that Vance boy and her new crop. She can wait a year.

relations.name: Ottilie Ashcombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Always chasing hens off the rows and talking of the harbour. Let her dream.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: Writes the Council's contracts and counts only grain. A fair man with a hard ledger.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: councillor
relations.note: Slow to speak and slower to forgive, but he has heard my case and not laughed at it.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Buys my greens for the works' kitchen and pays on time. A good woman with a hard husband.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her yard is next to my strips; we trade eggs and gossip over the fence.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: Proud for a man who works another man's stone. Wants my daughter and a foreman's place.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: rival
relations.note: Thinks my girl beneath his son. We'll see whose ground feeds the town this winter.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: the terrace strips gave next to nothing and we ate the seed store down to the last sack.
The Council's clerk came round with the tithe book and would not write down a single bunch of greens, only grain.
Rosalind told me she means to marry Corwin Vance, and I told her to wait a year and see if he's still standing.
The cairn cutting on the ridge: the quarrymen broke into the giants' stones and now the shelf has shut its gate on us.
Verity and I planted the poor strip together the spring we married, and it came up better than anyone said it would.

stances.why: the terrace grows greens and roots; the Council should take what the ground gives or take nothing
a man who begs for his tithe has already lost the argument
the Vances work other men's stone and talk as if they own the ridge
a year will show whether the boy is steady or only eager
Ruth Pike pays on time and the town must eat what we grow

sheet.narrative: I keep the terrace hens and the seed store, and I can tell you which strip will fail by the look of the soil in spring. Hedley frets at the tithe and the clerk's hard ledger, and I let him fret; I would trade eggs and roots against it tomorrow if the clerk would write them down. Rosalind is set on her new crop and her quarryman, and I say let the girl try — the poor ground will teach her what I cannot. Ottilie talks of nothing but the harbour, and I have not the heart to tell her I have never seen it either.
values: thrift and a full seed store
goals: trade eggs and roots against the grain tithe
keep the seed store through the winter
see Rosalind settled without a family quarrel
sheet.mood: steady and watchful, tired of the tithe talk

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Proud and stubborn, but he works that poor ground harder than any man could ask.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has my eye for the strips and her father's stubbornness. Let her try her crop.

relations.name: Ottilie Ashcombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Dreams of the harbour and the tide lanterns. I've never seen them either.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Trades eggs at her stall and hears the square's gossip before anyone.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: clerk
relations.note: If anyone can put eggs and roots in the tithe book, it's him, if he'll hear it.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Feeds the works' kitchen and knows what a fair price is.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: Eager and not unkind. He may do for Rosalind yet.

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: council master
relations.note: Old Vell is slow to hear anything new, and the tithe is his to rule on.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I rationed the seed store by the handful and the hens kept us alive when the strips gave nothing.
Rosalind came to me about Corwin Vance, and I told her a farmer's daughter can marry a quarryman if he's steady.
The Council's clerk counted only grain and would not write down a single basket of roots or eggs.
I taught Ottilie the names of the hens and which eggs to leave for setting.
The spring the poor strip came up green, Hedley laughed for the first time in months.

stances.why: eggs and roots are what the terrace gives; the clerk should write what is given
a household that eats its seed has nothing next spring
the poor ground will teach her more than my warnings can
Hedley's stubbornness is right in its heart but it will not fill the tithe book
Mabel hears everything and her stall takes our eggs without a word

sheet.narrative: I work the terrace strips with my father, and I have a mind to try a new crop on the poor ground — clover and roots to hold the soil, whatever the old men say. I am courting Corwin Vance, and both our fathers have opinions they were not asked for; mine says wait a year, and Corwin's says a farmer's daughter is beneath a foreman's son. I am tired of the grumbling on both sides. The ground is the only thing here that tells the truth.
values: trying what the old men won't
goals: prove a new crop on the poor strip
marry Corwin Vance without the fathers' quarrel
win a strip of her own to farm

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows the ground better than anyone, but he will not hear of a new crop or of Corwin.

relations.name: Verity Ashcombe
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She says let me try, and she means it. She has my back against Father.

relations.name: Ottilie Ashcombe
relations.label: sister
relations.note: All hens and harbour dreams. I'd take her to see the sea myself if I could.

relations.name: Corwin Vance
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: Steady on the quarry floor and gentler than his father. I mean to have him.

relations.name: Silas Vance
relations.label: his father
relations.note: Thinks me beneath his son. A foreman's pride is a thin thing to build a marriage on.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her stall hears everything; she trades fair and doesn't talk down to farmers.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk at the stall about the boys and the Council and the price of everything.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Buys our greens for the works' kitchen; she'd buy clover seed too if it grew.

relations.name: Bisi Oyelaran
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Quick with numbers, and she wants to learn the foundry books.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: his mother
relations.note: She set my mother's wrist straight last winter and never once spoke down to us. If Corwin takes after anyone, it's her.

memories.gist: I told Father I meant to marry Corwin Vance, and he told me to wait a year as if I were a child.
Corwin walked me along the clock tower steps and said his father would come round; I am not so sure.
The Lean Year, when the strips failed and Mother rationed the seed store by the handful.
I sowed a patch of clover on the poor strip without telling Father, and it came up thick as a mat.
Silas Vance looked me up and down at the square and said nothing, which was worse than saying it.

stances.why: the poor ground needs clover and roots, not another year of the same failing grain
he is steady and kind, and his father's pride is not his
both of them have opinions they were never asked for
I have worked other people's rows long enough
the soil says what will grow, and no clerk or foreman can argue with it

sheet.narrative: I drive the hens off the seed rows and help Mother with the eggs, and when the work is done I climb the clock tower steps and look south as far as I can see. They say Lanternquay is all neon and boats and tide lanterns lit for the drowned, and I have never been past the square. Rosalind says she will take me one day. I keep a gull's feather in my pocket for luck.
values: the harbour and the wide world
goals: see Lanternquay and the tide lanterns
keep the hens out of the seed rows
grow tall enough to climb the clock tower alone

relations.name: Verity Ashcombe
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She teaches me the hens and the eggs and never laughs at my harbour talk.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: father
relations.note: Grumbles about the tithe, but he lets me climb the tower steps when the work's done.

relations.name: Rosalind Ashcombe
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She says she'll take me to Lanternquay one day. I believe her.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She minds her mother's stall and knows the price of everything in the square.

relations.name: Perry Fenwick
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: He climbs the clock tower steps too, and we race to the top.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: mother's friend
relations.note: She has an ironware stall and sometimes gives me a sweet.

memories.gist: Rosalind told me about Lanternquay and the tide lanterns, and I have wanted to see them ever since.
I chased the hens off the seed rows for a whole morning and Mother gave me a cake for it.
The clock struck while I was on the tower steps and I near fell down the stair with fright.

stances.why: the harbour and the tide lanterns are the only thing worth dreaming of past the square
the hens and eggs are my work and Mother trusts me with them

sheet.narrative: I have kept Kettlebridge's clock and its contracts for thirty years, and I have never yet seen a clause that needed a second meaning. The tower runs slow in cold weather and I wind it at dawn and dusk; the Council's ledgers run slower, and I keep those too. I wrote the seawall indenture myself, and the clause about late stone is plain, and I will not have it argued into something else by Josiah Crane or by a Lanternquay runner. I lodge Juno Reyes when she is in town, and I am civil to her, but a sealed contract is a sealed contract.
values: the town's order and its clock
goals: keep the clock and the Council's contracts exactly as written
see Pell's indenture honoured, though he will not hand the boy to a beating
settle the seawall clause without changing a word of it
keep his lodging and his ledgers in good order
sheet.mood: even, watchful, a little weary of being pressed

relations.name: Ambrose Vell
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: Slow to speak and slower to forgive, like me; we have sat through many Council sittings and seldom disagreed.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: master
relations.note: Chair of the Council and my employer in a sense; he presses me on the seawall clause and I will not be pressed.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: colleague
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books well; she has not said which way she reads the clause, and I wish she would.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: lodger
relations.note: A decent runner, and she pays for her bed; but she argues the clause favours the works, and she is wrong.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: runaway apprentice
relations.note: I wrote his indenture and I want it honoured; I have heard where he is and I have not told Josiah, because the boy was beaten.

relations.name: Hedley Ashcombe
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: A good farmer behind on his tithe; I am sorry for him, but the ledger counts grain, not greens.

relations.name: Verity Ashcombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She keeps the seed store and knows her strips; she will not thank me for the tithe, and I do not blame her.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: A steady man on the road; he pays the Brackenford due and hates it, and I write the tallies that say what he carried.

relations.name: Ostrander Sallow
relations.label: correspondent
relations.note: The quay's letter-keeper; we write to each other about the seawall and the drowned, and he is careful with his words.

relations.name: Nella Marsh
relations.label: pupil
relations.note: A bright child learning her letters; I teach her at the tower foot and she is quicker than most of the Council.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: He says he did not know what the stones were on the ridge. I write what men say; I do not always believe it.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Sets bones by the clock tower and speaks her mind about the cutting. She is right, and it is not my office to say so.

memories.gist: The first time I wound the clock alone, the rope burning through my hands, and old master Tolliver watching from the stair.
Writing the seawall indenture by lamplight, and thinking the late-stone clause plain as a pike staff.
Josiah coming to the tower to argue the clause, and me holding the sealed copy and saying it would not be changed.
Pell's indenture, written in my own hand, and the boy's mark at the bottom; and later hearing from a carter that the boy had run.
Juno Reyes sleeping in my back room after a wet road, and arguing with me over supper that the clause favours the works.
Ambrose Vell and me sitting late after a Council meeting, saying nothing, which is the best kind of company.

stances.why: The clock does not renegotiate the hour, and neither does a sealed indenture.
I wrote it; it says what it says, and I will not have it read otherwise by either side.
The Council's ledger counts grain, and a clerk who falsifies an account is no clerk.
His indenture binds him, but the boy was beaten, and I will not be the one to put him back in that yard.
The town sets its day by my tower, and a slow clock is a lie told to everyone at once.

sheet.secret: He has heard Pell is at Coldwell with the outlaws and has not told Josiah, because the boy was beaten in the foundry yard.

sheet.narrative: I make crates, props and shutter-boards for the works, and I make them square. A saw cuts true or it cuts twice, and I've no patience for the second cut. The gate-due at Brackenford is robbery on my timber, and I say so at the yard when Gideon's not counting. I keep my words short and my marks counted, and I'd rather be at the bench than anywhere.
goals: Get the gate-due off his timber
Keep steady work from Gideon Fenwick's yard
Put by enough marks to see the children fed through winter

relations.name: Sabina Marsh
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the marks and I keep the saw; between us the house stands.

relations.name: Nella Marsh
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with numbers like her mother. I'd have her learn a trade that pays.

relations.name: Ewan Marsh
relations.label: son
relations.note: Underfoot in the sawyard, but he'll learn to keep clear of the blade.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: master
relations.note: He gives me work and I give him crates. He's not a bad sort, but he watches the yard close.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: My crates ride his cart north. He hates the gate-due as much as I do.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: scribe
relations.note: Writes the contracts that bind us all. He knows his letters and I know my saw.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: She sells my crates at the square and takes her cut. Fair enough.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: council master
relations.note: Chair of the Works Council. He sets the prices and we live with them.

relations.name: Corin Holt
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Keeps the quarry tally. Her man cut the cairn and she says so at home.

memories.gist: The day the gate-due was raised, Silas came back from Brackenford cursing and we all stood in the yard and cursed with him.
Teaching Nella to count the crates in the sawyard when she was six; she had it right before I did.
The Lean Year, when the works ran short and Gideon laid off two hands; I kept my bench but took less pay.
The night Ewan was born, and the clock struck while Sabina was in labour and he's feared the sound since.
The cairn cutting on the ridge; I said to the yard that a man should know what stones he's cutting into.

stances.why: It's a tax on my own work crossing a gate I didn't build.
A saw cuts true or it cuts twice, and I won't have my name on a crooked crate.
Marks in the box and bread on the table before any quarrel with the Council.
Talk is cheap and the yard is full of it; I'd rather be at the bench.

sheet.narrative: I buy and sell worked iron and clay at the square, and I keep the household's marks in a locked box because Tobiah would lend them to any carter with a hard story. I know what a thing is worth and what a person will pay, and I don't confuse the two. The stall fee to Mabel Fenwick is owed and I'll pay it, but not before I've counted what's left.
goals: Pay off the stall fee to Mabel Fenwick
Build up the locked box against a hard winter
See Nella learn her letters well enough to keep books

relations.name: Tobiah Marsh
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a saw and no head for marks. I keep the box locked for both our sakes.

relations.name: Nella Marsh
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with numbers and proud of her letters. She'll go further than the stall.

relations.name: Ewan Marsh
relations.label: son
relations.note: Still afraid of the clock. He'll grow out of it when he's taller than the bell.

relations.name: Mabel Fenwick
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: I owe her a stall fee and she knows it. She's fair but she remembers.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: scribe
relations.note: He teaches Nella her letters and writes the Council's contracts. A useful man to know.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: foundry books
relations.note: She keeps the foundry books and knows a fair price. I'd trade with her before her father.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He carries Tobiah's crates north and brings clay back. He pays on time, mostly.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: Minds her mother's stall and has a good eye for a cracked pot. Nella could learn from her.

memories.gist: The day I bought the locked box from a pedlar and put the first marks in it; Tobiah laughed and said I'd guard it like a dragon.
The Surge two winters ago, when the quay families came up to the poor terrace; I sold iron cheap to a woman with three children and didn't tell Tobiah.
Nella reading her first letter from the psalter Barnaby lent her, and getting it right.
The Lean Year, when the works kitchen cut the bowls to half and I counted every mark twice.
The day the Council raised the gate-due at Brackenford; Tobiah came home and wouldn't speak, and I put an extra mark in the box.

stances.why: A mark spent is a mark gone; I'll know what's left before I part with any.
Every load Tobiah's crates ride on pays it, and the price comes out of our box.
Nella knowing her letters is worth more than a stall fee; it's a way out of the yard.
Mabel's fee will be paid, but on my counting, not hers.

sheet.narrative: I count the crates in the yard and I know my letters, which is more than most girls my age. Barnaby Quill teaches me from the psalter and says I'm quick. I want to keep books like Hester Crane one day, and I don't see why I shouldn't.
goals: Learn more letters from Barnaby Quill
Count every crate in the yard without a mistake

relations.name: Sabina Marsh
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the marks and says I'll go further than the stall. I mean to.

relations.name: Tobiah Marsh
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me to count crates. He says a saw cuts true or it cuts twice.

relations.name: Ewan Marsh
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He's afraid of the clock and follows me about. I don't mind.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He lends me the psalter and says I'm quick. I want to learn all of it.

relations.name: Lottie Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She has a good eye for a cracked pot and doesn't mind that I know my letters.

memories.gist: The first time I read a whole line from the psalter without stopping, and Barnaby said I'd do.
Counting the crates in the yard with Father and getting the same number he did.
Ewan crying when the clock struck and me holding his hand till he stopped.

stances.why: Barnaby says a girl who can write is worth two who can't, and I believe him.
Father says a saw cuts true or it cuts twice, and the same goes for counting crates.
Ewan needs me and Mother needs the marks counted. I'll not let them down.

sheet.narrative: The clock is loud and it makes me jump. I like the sawdust and the smell of the wood, and I follow Nella about the yard. When the bell goes I put my hands over my ears.
goals: Not be afraid of the clock

relations.name: Tobiah Marsh
relations.label: father
relations.note: He smells of sawdust and lifts me over the woodpile.

relations.name: Sabina Marsh
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She holds me when the clock goes.

relations.name: Nella Marsh
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She holds my hand and I follow her about.

memories.gist: The clock striking and me crying, and Nella holding my hand.
Sitting in the sawdust while Father worked, and the smell of the wood.

towns.name: Lanternquay
towns.character: a dense harbour town of concrete blocks, neon and street stalls, busy at all hours
towns.ledger: Lanternquay. The quay is for whoever works it. Lanterns for the drowned are lit at dusk; do not put them out.

sheet.narrative: I am the Harbour Warden of Lanternquay, and I have been since before the surge, and I will be after it. My brother drowned when the lower quay went, and I keep his boat-hook on the wall behind my chair. Kettlebridge sold us stone at a drowning man's price, and I have not paid the last tally, and I will not until I see a wall. I light the tide lanterns when I can face the dead, and some nights I cannot, and Ilse Ostrander tells the whole quay so.
values: my own hand on the marks
goals: get stone for a seawall without paying Kettlebridge's price
hold the quay together through the winter
keep my brother's name out of other people's mouths

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: son
relations.note: He fishes his uncle's ground in his uncle's boat and does not know I see the ghost in it.

relations.name: Dory Quell
relations.label: niece
relations.note: My brother's girl, and I will not lose another of that blood to the water.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: stone-seller
relations.note: He named a price for our wall that only a man who never drowned could name.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: She holds the tally and writes me courteous letters about marks I do not have.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She carries my word up the fish road and comes back with the truth of what Kettlebridge says.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: He went to Kettlebridge for work after the surge; he writes, and I miss his plain sense at the table.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: lantern-keeper
relations.note: She lights them beside me and counts the nights I do not come.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: builder
relations.note: He patches the lower quay with salvage and means well, but every beam is a mark not spent on stone.

relations.name: Ostrander Sallow
relations.label: scribe
relations.note: He keeps the drowned list and my letters, and never once asked me why I was late to the lanterns.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She set my brother's hand once and told me plainly the lower quay should wait for the wall; I did not want to hear it and she was right.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: lantern-watcher
relations.note: She says the tide lanterns are lit too late and says it to everyone but me; I know the hour I come down to the steps.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She wants her stall rebuilt in stone and asks me when the wall will start; I have no answer that is not a debt.

memories.gist: The night the surge came, I stood on the upper quay with a rope in my hands and watched my brother's roof go under.
Kettlebridge sent a little stone, at full price, and Josiah Crane's letter named the sum as though it were a kindness.
Dele Oyelaran shared a boat with me the summer before the surge, and after it he packed for Kettlebridge and I did not stop him.
Dory asked me why the lanterns are lit and I told her for the drowned, and she has been afraid of them since.
Hester Crane's tally came down the fish road in Juno's pack and I read it twice and put it in the strongbox unopened.
Wick brought the boat home patched with a plank from the lower quay, and I said nothing, and he knew I had seen it.

stances.why: A price like that is a knife at the throat, and I will not hand over the quay's marks for a promise.
My brother's name is on the drowned list and the list does not shorten.
The strongbox is the quay's only sure thing, and I count it myself.
They sent a little stone at full price and thought it charity.
I carry that duty alone, and some nights I cannot face it, and that is between me and the drowned.

sheet.secret: She has not paid the stone tally and cannot; the strongbox holds less than the quay believes, and she has begun to wonder whether she will ever light the lanterns without her brother's face in them.

sheet.narrative: I fish the harbour mouth from my uncle's boat, the one they pulled him out of, and I have patched it three times with timber off the lower quay. Cormorant says the ground is his; my uncle fished it before Cormorant had a keel. My mother sits with the strongbox and will not pay Kettlebridge, and the wall does not get built, and I have counted what is in the box and it is not enough.
goals: hold the harbour mouth against Ostrander Cormorant
see the seawall begun before another winter
keep the boat afloat and the nets whole

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She carries the quay and the dead both, and will not let me carry any of it with her.

relations.name: Dory Quell
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: My uncle's girl; I taught her the gulls' names and she will not go near the lanterns.

relations.name: Ostrander Cormorant
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He says the harbour mouth is his and has cut my nets twice to prove it.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: rival's son
relations.note: A decent hand on a boat, which makes it worse that his father is a thief of ground.

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: fishing partner
relations.note: She fishes the dawn tide with me and does not ask about the strongbox.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Her tally sits in my mother's box like a stone in a boot.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: stone-seller
relations.note: He sells us stone at a price that keeps the lower quay in splinters.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She brings the tally down the fish road and has the grace to look away when she hands it over.

memories.gist: They pulled my uncle out of the harbour mouth and I took his boat home alone that night.
Cormorant's crew cut my nets on the good ground and I found them at dawn, and he laughed on the quay.
I patched the boat with a plank off the lower quay and my mother saw it and said nothing at all.
Dory asked me to name the gulls with her and I did, all of them, and she laughed for the first time since the surge.
I opened the strongbox when my mother was at the lanterns and counted the marks twice, and it is not enough for a wall.

stances.why: He fished it before Cormorant had a boat, and I will not be pushed off it.
My mother says it, and I half believe it, but the lower quay is falling in the water now.
Nobody else will tell me the truth of what the quay has, and I have a right to know.
Every winter the stone costs more and the quay gets less.
My mother misses them and the quay talks, and I will not have it said to me.

sheet.secret: He has been counting the marks in his mother's strongbox, and he knows the quay cannot pay Kettlebridge and cannot build the wall, and he has not told her he knows.

sheet.narrative: I live in the Warden's house with my aunt Mara, and I know every gull on the quay by name. My father drowned when the water came, and I do not remember his face well, only his hands. Wick lets me help with the nets, and I stay away from the tide lanterns because they are for the drowned and I do not want to be called.
goals: name every gull on the quay
help Wick with the boat
not go near the lanterns

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She keeps me and feeds me and goes quiet on lantern nights.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He taught me the gulls and lets me hold the net while he mends it.

relations.name: Dory Gull
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play under the stalls and neither of us likes the dark water.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: lantern-keeper
relations.note: She and my aunt light the lanterns and she looks at me sadly when she does.

memories.gist: The water came up over the lower quay and my aunt held me on the steps while the roofs went under.
Wick sat me on the boat and made me name the gulls one by one until I got them all.
I went too near the tide lanterns once and my aunt pulled me back and would not say why.

stances.why: They are for the drowned and my father is one of them.
Wick taught me that knowing a thing's name makes it less frightening.
Wick lets me and it means I am not too small.

sheet.narrative: I run the fish road because the quay needs stone and I know how to carry a load. The works promised us a price and a seawall, and now they say the stone is late and the tally is unpaid. I keep my mouth shut about who I see on the road, but I don't forget.
goals: see the seawall built before winter
get the stone price honoured
keep the fish road open

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: employer
relations.note: She speaks for the quay and I run for her; she lost her brother in the Surge.

relations.name: Hester Crane
relations.label: stone-seller
relations.note: She set the price and holds the tally; she's sharp but fair on the road.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We grew up together; I heard he's alive but I don't speak of it.

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She fishes the dawn tide and worries about me on the road.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: He patches the lower quay and wants proper stone; we want the same thing.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: contract-holder
relations.note: He says the wording is plain, but plain to whom?

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: fellow carter
relations.note: I offered him a place on the fish road; the stone road is a fool's road now.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He fishes the harbour mouth and resents the stone price as much as I do.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: Her son Kai was my friend; she still hopes he'll come back.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: foundry master
relations.note: He promised the quay stone and cannot cut it fast enough; that is his problem to answer for.

relations.name: Ostrander Sallow
relations.label: lodging
relations.note: Keeps my letters and a bed between roads; he writes the tide lantern list and I am on it twice.

relations.name: Rennick Vane
relations.label: road guard
relations.note: Walks the fish road with me and does not believe Kai ran for cowardice. Neither do I.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: He cut the cairn and closed the ridge, and now the works cannot cut the stone the quay paid for. I have no patience for a man who says he did not know.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: crate-builder
relations.note: Builds the crates my stone rides in and curses the price of every load. He wants the wall built, same as me, but he counts the marks louder than the risk.

relations.name: Ruth Pike
relations.label: carter's wife
relations.note: She begs Silas off the stone road and I do not blame her. If he takes my offer, she will have one less night of waiting, and I will have one more pair of hands.

memories.gist: The night of the Surge, I helped pull people from the lower quay and heard the tide lanterns ring.
My first run on the fish road, carrying cooked fish to Kettlebridge and bringing back a crate of stone.
Hester Crane showed me the tally and said no more stone until the marks are paid.
I heard from a Coldwell carrier that Pell is alive and with the outlaws, and that Kai is there too.
Silas Pike told me he was robbed again on the stone road; I told him to take the fish road.

stances.why: The next surge will take more than the lower quay if we don't build.
The works agreed to the risk; the clause favours them, not us, and they should pay.
He's my friend and the quay guard would hang him; I won't be the one to speak.
The stone road is a fool's road now, and I told Silas so.

sheet.secret: I know Kai Ostrander is alive and with the Coldwell outlaws, and I have said nothing.

sheet.narrative: I fish the dawn tide and smoke what I catch for Ilse's stall. The harbour mouth is our living, and I've seen both Wick and Ostrander cut nets over it. I want a quiet life and a full smoker, and I'll not take sides in a feud that costs us the catch.
goals: keep the smoker full
see the harbour mouth feud settled
support Ostrander's building work

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She runs the fish road and I worry every time she goes.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He builds and patches and wants the quay proper; I want him safe.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: fishing partner
relations.note: We fish the dawn tide together, but his feud with Cormorant is bad for us all.

relations.name: Ostrander Cormorant
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He claims the best ground and won't back down; nets have been cut.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: stall-owner
relations.note: I smoke for her stall; she's fair and her knees are bad.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay, but she and Ostrander clash over the lower quay.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: mother-in-law
relations.note: She heals and disapproves of building before the wall; she's usually right.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He fishes with his father and wants his own boat; the feud is not his fault.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: Knows the price of everything on the quay and pays for fish on time.

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: night cook
relations.note: Feeds the night crews and buys my smoked catch when the dawn boats come in late.

memories.gist: The dawn after the Surge, I found the lower quay gone and my uncle's boat smashed against the steps.
I watched Wick Quell and Ostrander Cormorant shout over the harbour mouth while their nets tangled.
Ostrander patched the lower quay with salvage and I held the lamp for him till the small hours.
I smoked a whole catch for Ilse's stall and she paid me in marks and a bowl of noodles.

stances.why: The harbour mouth is our living, and cut nets mean an empty smoker.
The lower quay will be taken again if the wall isn't built.
Juno and Ostrander are my life; I'll not see them hurt by pride.
The tally is real, and no stone comes without marks.

sheet.narrative: I build and patch on the quay because the lower quay is my living and my home. Mara Quell says wait for the seawall, but the town is rotting while she argues about stone. I've patched with salvage and I'll build in stone when I can get it, and I'll not be laughed at by Sootwood or cheated by Kettlebridge.
goals: rebuild the lower quay in stone
get proper stone at a fair price
see the seawall started

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She fishes and smokes and keeps me steady; I build for her.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She says no building until the seawall is paid, but the quay can't wait.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She thinks I'm rash, but she patches me up when I fall.

relations.name: Marrow Wrack
relations.label: fellow builder
relations.note: He knows stone better than most and the Kettlebridge builders cheated him.

relations.name: Dele Oyelaran
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We drink when he's down from Kettlebridge; he works cheap and they resent him.

relations.name: Gideon Fenwick
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He's grasping and says Marrow cheated him; I say he cheated Marrow.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: sawyer
relations.note: He says the seawall will never be built; I want an apology before I buy his timber.

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: charcoal-burner
relations.note: She laughs at the drowned quay; Sootwood should keep its talk to itself.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She wants to rebuild her stall in stone; she understands.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She runs the stone down and knows the tally; we want the same wall.

relations.name: Odile Wrack
relations.label: healer
relations.note: Sets the builders' bones after a fall and grudge Kettlebridge for the cold welcome; she is right to.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: stone-seller
relations.note: Sells the quay stone at a drowning man's price and calls it market terms.

relations.name: Rennick Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He walks the fish road with the runners and keeps the peace at the stalls; a steady guard, and he does not believe Kai ran for cowardice, which is more sense than most on this quay.

memories.gist: The morning after the Surge, I stood on the lower quay and saw nothing but water where the houses had been.
I patched the lower quay with salvage timber and Mara Quell told me I was wasting my time.
Gideon Fenwick accused Marrow Wrack of cheating him over a load of brick, and I told him he was a liar.
Orvin Hollis said at the stalls that the seawall would never be built and the stone price was a swindle.
Dele Oyelaran and I drank to the quay's future and cursed the Kettlebridge price.

stances.why: The lower quay is rotting and the next surge will take the rest.
Kettlebridge charges a drowning man's price; the ridge is ours if we can get it.
Sootwood laughed at the drowned quay; I'll not buy their timber until they say sorry.
He's a good builder and Kettlebridge cheated him; I'll not see him shamed.

sheet.narrative: I have kept a noodle stall on this quay for thirty years, and I know every face that comes to it at dawn and every one that doesn't come back. When the Surge took the lower quay it took my neighbours, and then last year it took my son Kai in a different way — he walked off his guard post and never came home, and the quay calls him deserter. A letter came to me not long since, in a hand I know, and I have not shown it to a soul. I light the tide lanterns with Mara Quell as I always have, but I light mine at dusk, whatever she does, because the drowned don't wait on grief.
values: the drowned are owed their light
feed people before you judge them
goals: keep Kai's secret and keep him alive
see the tide lanterns lit at dusk every night
keep the stall earning through the winter
hear word of Kai again without the Warden hearing it first

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is alive, and every day I say nothing is a day I keep him so.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She grieves her brother, I know it — but the lanterns are not hers to be late with.

relations.name: Wick Brine
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He saw the letter and said nothing. That silence is worth more than marks to me.

relations.name: Ostrander Sallow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He keeps the lantern list and writes my letters; if anyone could read a thing without telling it, it is him.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She thinks the lanterns are lit too late, and she is right, and I will not say why I side with her.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trade neighbour
relations.note: She knows the price of every bowl on this quay and never yet cheated me.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: young friend
relations.note: A good girl at the stall; she asks after Kai and I give her the same answer I give everyone.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She tends my knees and asks no questions about the ones I don't answer.

relations.name: Rennick Vane
relations.label: guard
relations.note: He walks the fish road and says Kai did not desert for cowardice. I could kiss him for it and I daren't.

relations.name: Dory Quell
relations.label: child
relations.note: The Warden's niece, afraid of the lanterns; she eats my noodles and I keep my mouth shut about her aunt.

memories.gist: Kai at twelve, hauling a pot of broth off the stall fire and burning his hand, laughing about it before he cried.
The night of the Surge: the lower quay going under, lanterns bobbing out on the black water, and the Warden's brother not coming back.
The morning Kai's guard cloak was found folded on the tide steps with no note in it, and the quay began to call him deserter.
Wick Brine coming to the stall with a folded paper and not meeting my eye, and me reading it twice before I could breathe.
Mara Quell and me standing at the lantern posts at full dark with the wicks still cold, and her saying nothing when I asked her why.
Feeding the night crews through a winter storm, bowls handed over the counter faster than I could fill them, and every face asking after Kai.

stances.why: The drowned do not care how the Warden grieves; a light lit late is a light that failed someone.
If the Warden learns he lives at Coldwell she must act, and I will not hand my son to a rope.
A bowl of noodles costs me little and buys a person's patience; it is how I have kept my stall and my peace.
They named my boy deserter without asking me a thing, so I owe their questions nothing.
I lost neighbours to the Surge; the wall matters more than a new stall front, whatever the rebuilders say.

sheet.secret: Kai sent word that he is alive and living with the outlaws at Coldwell; Ilse has told no one, and knows Wick Brine saw the letter and has kept quiet.

sheet.narrative: I have set bones and eased coughs in this room behind the fish market for thirty years, and I know the quay's aches better than the Warden does. My son Ostrander is right that the lower quay cannot wait for a seawall that may never be paid for — I have seen what the tide does — but I will not say so where Mara Quell can hear me. I keep my mouth shut and my door open, and I mend what the sea and the stone leave broken.
values: the quay's people before its plans
a healer owes no quarrel to a patient
patched things must be kept until better comes
silence is safer than a Warden's anger
goals: keep her healer's room and her good name on the quay
see Ostrander's patched lower quay hold through the winter without open quarrel with Mara Quell
keep Ilse Ostrander's knees tended and her stall fed
buy enough salves from the Tanglewood woman before the winter coughs come
sheet.mood: watchful and tired, with a warm word for anyone who comes in hurt

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is right about the lower quay, and I will not say it aloud to the Warden.

relations.name: Rennick Vane
relations.label: son
relations.note: Steady on the road; I sleep easier when he walks it.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay and I owe her my respect, but she will not hear the builders' side.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: patient
relations.note: Her knees ache worse each winter; I strap them and take no mark for it.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: Rennick walks her road; a brave girl carrying fish and stone both.

relations.name: Mira Sallow
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: We share herbs and complaints; she frets at the terrace cough as I do.

relations.name: Odile Wrack
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: Good hands with a broken bone; her family came down hard and I say nothing of it.

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: salve-seller
relations.note: Her salves are honest and her prices are not; I buy from her anyway.

relations.name: Wick Brine
relations.label: guard
relations.note: He walks the night road; I keep a light in the window for him and Rennick.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She cooks at the fish market and wants her stall rebuilt in stone; I say mend the wall first, but her fried bread has fed my boys often enough.

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: good-daughter
relations.note: She fishes the dawn tide with my Ostrander and smokes the catch for Ilse's stall; a hard worker, and I set her shoulder after a fall last spring.

memories.gist: The Surge came in the night and took the lower quay; I spent until dawn setting bones in the fish market with seawater to my knees.
Ostrander dragged salvage timber up from the shore and patched the lower quay himself; I bound his hands after and told him to be careful of the Warden.
Rennick came back from the fish road with a cut from a wolf and would not sit still for the stitching.
I strapped Ilse Ostrander's knees through a bad winter and she fed me noodles for a month after, which I did not refuse.
I bought salves from the Tanglewood woman at the fish market and asked her what she put in them; she would not say, and they worked.

stances.why: A healer's room has no quarrel in it; I have stitched guards and smugglers alike.
Patched shelter is better than none, whatever the Warden's plan says.
Mara Quell speaks for the quay, and my room stands on her goodwill.
The coughs come every year and the Tanglewood woman's salves are the only thing that eases them.

sheet.secret: I have told Ostrander plainly that I think the Warden is wrong to hold the lower quay back, and that if it comes to a quarrel at the stalls I will stand with my son.

sheet.narrative: I walk the fish road with the runners and keep the peace at the stalls, and I have seen enough of the road to know what a man does when he is afraid. Kai Ostrander did not run from cowardice — I have carried the same fear myself on the night watch — and I will not have him called a deserter in my hearing. My mother thinks I am too ready to say what I think; my brother thinks I am too slow to say it. Both of them are wrong, and both of them are family.
values: the road is kept by those who walk it
a man's fear is not the same as his shame
the stalls settle their own quarrels before the guard does
family is family, whatever the Warden says
goals: keep the fish road clear and the runners safe between the quay and Kettlebridge
see the truth of Kai Ostrander's desertion known, or at least not spat on
keep his post under Mara Quell without being made her instrument against his brother
earn enough marks to keep his own room near his mother's
sheet.mood: steady and a little stubborn, slow to speak and slower to be moved

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She mends what the road breaks; I bring her the cuts and say nothing of the rest.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is right about the lower quay and wrong to say it so loud.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She pays me and I serve her; she is not always right about the builders.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: I walk her road and she does not slow for me, which I respect.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: old friend of the quay
relations.note: I knew him before the Surge; a man does not turn coward in one night.

relations.name: Wick Brine
relations.label: fellow guard
relations.note: He knows the smugglers' paths and I know the wolves'; between us the road is kept.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her son is gone and she still sets a bowl out for the night crews; I eat there.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She wants her stall in stone; I keep the peace while she argues for it.

memories.gist: The Surge took the lower quay in the night; I pulled two men out of the water and lost a third I could not reach.
Kai Ostrander and I stood the night watch together before the Surge, and he was the calmest man on the quay when the wind got up.
I walked Juno Reyes up the fish road through a pack of wolves and we came through with the fish and the stone both.
My mother bound a gash on my arm from a road wolf and told me I was a fool to walk it alone; I walked it again the next night.
I broke up a quarrel at the morning stalls between two fishers over a net, and both of them cursed me for it equally, which I took as fair.

stances.why: I stood the watch with him; fear does not make a coward of a man who does his duty.
The runners carry the quay's living up and down that road, and the wolves do not wait.
She pays my wage, but she is not always right, and I will not be her hand against my brother.
A guard who steps in too early makes two quarrels where there was one.

sheet.secret: I have told no one but my mother that I think Kai Ostrander ran because he was ordered to do something he would not do, and that if he came back to the quay I would hear him out before I raised a spear.

sheet.narrative: I keep the rope, tar and nail stall on the quay, and every fisher from the harbour mouth to the outer shoals owes me something or buys from me sooner or later. I came up hauling lines and I know what a boat needs before her owner does. The marks come slow in winter and the Kettlebridge nails come dear, but I pay my debts and I expect mine paid. Lately I have had to say so louder than I like.
values: keep the stall stocked before the purse
the quay looks after its own
goals: get the rope and tar money out of Wick Gull and Orvin Hollis
clear what I owe Josiah Crane for the iron nails before the next load
see Sella settled with a man who can keep her
keep the stall's name good with every fisher on the quay

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows the price of everything and I would be lost at the stall without her.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick and willing, but she has her eye on the fish road and I want her settled here.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He sells me iron nails and I owe him for the last load; he never lets a mark rest.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: A loud man with a good tongue and an empty purse; two tides now he has owed me for rope and tar.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: A good woodcutter and I like him, but a season of rope and tar is a season of marks.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent lad, but a crewman with a net to buy is not yet a household.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His cart brings the stone and takes my marks; the gate-due at Brackenford is robbery on both of us.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay and I pay her stall fee; she has enough on her plate with the seawall.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her noodle stall is two along from mine and she buys my lamp oil by the barrel.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: Orvin's good for the rope money and she's the one who'd see it paid; she keeps the Sootwood plots and trades roots at the stalls, so we talk plain enough.

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: Nia cooks the night crews and pays what she can, but she's not the one who took the rope, and I'll not shame her at the stalls for her husband's slack.

memories.gist: The night the surge came I hauled my tar barrels up the steps two at a time and still lost half of them to the water.
I bought my first load of iron nails from Josiah Crane on credit and paid it back inside a season; he has trusted my word since, but he still counts it.
Wick Gull took rope and tar off me before the last good catch and swore he would pay when the boats came in; the boats came in and he did not.
Sella was minding the stall alone when a deep-water man tried to talk her down on a coil of line; she held the price and he paid it.
I stood at the tide lanterns the night they read the list of the drowned, and my own name could have been on it if the surge had come an hour later.

stances.why: I have carried too many men's rope through a lean winter to let a debt slide.
Every load of nails I buy comes through Brackenford's gate and the due is added to my price.
The stall feeds us, but Sella's future is worth more than a season of marks.
The surge taught me that no stall stands alone when the water comes.
If the lower quay goes again, my stall goes with it.

sheet.narrative: I keep the pie and eel stall beside Bramwell's, and I know the price of every fish and every coil of rope on this quay. The marks live in my apron and I can tell you to the penny what we have and what we owe. Bramwell frets over the debts owed to us; I fret over my girl, who looks at a crewman the way I once looked at a man with a stall. I feed half the quay and hear the other half.
values: feed people well and they will come back
a household's marks are its own business
let the girl choose, but see she is kept
goals: get the stall's marks back from the debts owed to us
see Sella courted by someone who can keep her, without breaking her heart
keep the pie and eel stall the best on the quay
put by enough for the winter when the boats lie up

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a heavy purse-hand; I keep the marks because he would lend them all away.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: I see how she looks at Ostrander Mackerel, and I remember looking so myself.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A quiet, decent boy; he buys a pie and eats it slow, and he is kind to Sella.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We swap eels for noodles and gossip, and she has fed my family on credit more than once.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: He eats well enough at Nia's stall to pay something on the rope.

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A hard worker at the night stall; I would not have her man's debts laid at her door.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She set my wrist when I fell on the steps and charged me a pie for it.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She brings the Kettlebridge news and my girl admires her; I would see Sella on that road only with a good man beside her.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His timber comes down and my eels go up. A season of rope isn't worth a quarrel with him.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He sells salt and dried goods two stalls over and undercuts my eels with his cart. A fair trader, mind, but I count my marks twice when he's in the market.

relations.name: Dory Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her smoke shed's behind the market and her fish comes out sweet. We keep to our own stalls and that suits us both.

relations.name: Lyss Fenner
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her soup and bread at the tide steps catches the early boats before they reach my pies. We send each other what's left at the end of the morning.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She sells me lamp oil and dried fish for my stall, and she's right that the tide lanterns go up too late. I tell her so when the watch comes round.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her roots and eggs come down from Sootwood to my stall, and I send charcoal money back up the wood road with her man. A steady woman, though I wish she'd not talk so loud of the seawall never being built where my Sella can hear it.

memories.gist: The surge took the lower quay and the stall of a woman I had traded with for years; I fed the survivors from my own pot that night.
Sella was small and stood on a crate to reach the counter, and she sold a whole tray of pies before I came back from the fish market.
Bramwell came courting with a coil of good line under his arm instead of flowers, and I knew then he was the man for me.
I counted the marks in my apron after a good market day and found we were short; Bramwell had lent them to a fisher who never came back to pay.
Ostrander Mackerel bought two pies and gave one to Sella, and I pretended not to see it.

stances.why: On this quay a woman who cannot count her marks is cheated by noon.
The stall has fed half the quay on credit and they remember it when the boats are in.
I would not have my daughter married off by her father's measure of a man's purse.
What a household has is its own business, and I mean to keep ours.
I have cooked for the men who patch the lower quay with salvage, and salvage will not hold another surge.

sheet.narrative: I mind my father's stall when my mother is cooking, and I can tell a good coil of line from a bad one by the feel of it. I like the quiet of the stall and the noise of the quay both, and I want to see the fish road before I settle to anything. Ostrander Mackerel buys a pie most days and eats it slow, and my father watches him do it.
values: hold the price and never be cheated
the road is out there and I mean to see it
family first, but a girl has her own eyes
goals: learn the fish road and see Kettlebridge with my own eyes
keep the stall's name good while my mother cooks
make my own mind up about Ostrander Mackerel

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He measures every man by his marks, and I wish he would measure Ostrander by something else.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She sees more than she says, and she has not spoken against Ostrander yet.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He is quiet and kind and he does not talk over me like the deep-water men do.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She has walked the fish road and comes back with the Kettlebridge news; I would go with her tomorrow.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He fishes with his father and wants a boat of his own, and he is good company at the stalls.

relations.name: Tam Harrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He runs errands for my father and knows every bit of gossip on the night market.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor's family
relations.note: Father says his name loudly now. I serve him his eel and say nothing.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her stall's by ours and she always asks after Mother. She's kind and she knows everything.

relations.name: Sable Harrow
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: She keeps the oil and salt stall by the night market and counts every mark twice. Mother says she's sharp; I think she's just had to be.

memories.gist: I held the stall alone during a squall and sold a whole coil of line to a deep-water man at my father's price.
The night of the tide lanterns I stood with my mother and watched the names of the drowned read out, and I was glad ours were not among them.
Ostrander Mackerel brought me a pie he had bought from my own mother's stall, and we laughed about it on the steps.
Juno Reyes came back up the fish road with stone dust on her boots and told me what Kettlebridge's clock tower looks like, and I have wanted to see it since.

stances.why: I have heard the road described all my life and I mean to walk it myself.
My father taught me that a stall that haggles is a stall that starves.
My father measures Ostrander by his purse, and I think that is the wrong measure.
I want the road, but I would not leave my mother with the stall and the debts.

sheet.narrative: I fish the deep water past the harbour mouth, where the big shoals run. My boat is sound and I keep her so; the sea does not forgive a slack rope or a patched sail. I have a temper, they say, and perhaps I do, but I do not suffer fools or liberties. Wick Quell sets his nets too close to mine and thinks the Warden's name gives him the harbour, and I will not back down from that.
values: not being taken for a fool
goals: hold my fishing ground against Wick Quell
keep my boat and gear in good repair
see Wick settled with a boat of his own when he is ready

relations.name: Tamsin Cormorant
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the house and the marks, and she knows when to leave me be.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: son
relations.note: He crews for me and learns the water; he will have his own boat when he has earned it.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He sets his nets too close and thinks the Warden's name gives him the harbour.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: She pays a fair price for a good catch and does not quibble.

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She fishes the dawn tide with Quell's son; I keep my distance.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay, but her family take liberties on the water.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: crew
relations.note: He crews on my boat and works hard; he will have his own net one day.

memories.gist: The Surge took the lower quay and the houses on it; my boat rode it out because I had doubled the mooring lines that morning.
Wick Quell's net fouled mine at the harbour mouth and we shouted across the water; since then there has been no peace between us.
I taught Wick to gut a fish before he could read; he was quick and not squeamish.
I bought my boat with marks saved over seven years and a loan from Perrin Tallow that I paid back to the last mark.
I found my nets cut one morning and knew whose hand it was, though I could not prove it.

stances.why: The sea is not the Warden's to give out, and no family owns the harbour mouth.
A fisherman with a bad boat is a dead fisherman; everything else waits.
If I give ground to Quell now, he will take the next ground and the next.
I borrowed for my boat and paid it back; a man who does not pay is no better than a thief.
Stone from Kettlebridge comes dear, and the lower quay has been patched before; I would rather see the money in boats.

sheet.secret: I cut Wick Quell's net the second time, not the first, and I would do it again.

sheet.narrative: I sell fresh fish at the morning stalls and keep the household's marks in a box under the floor. My man is quiet until he is not, and my son is learning the water beside him. I have no love for Kettlebridge: they sell us stone at a price that would make a saint swear, and the lower quay still lies in rubble. I trade with Ilse Ostrander for noodles and gossip, and I keep my head down when the men talk of nets and ground.
values: a good name at the stalls
goals: keep the household's marks safe through the winter
see Wick crew on his own boat before I am old
get a fair price for fish and not be undercut

relations.name: Ostrander Cormorant
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is quiet and then he is not; I know which mood means trouble.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is a good boy and a quick hand; I want him settled before the sea takes him.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We trade fish for noodles and news, and she does not cheat me.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trader
relations.note: She knows the price of everything and pays on the nail.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He is his mother's son and thinks the harbour belongs to him.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay but her family take liberties.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good girl; she and Wick are friendly and I do not mind it.

memories.gist: The Surge took the lower quay and the houses on it; we watched from the upper steps and counted the boats that did not come back.
I sold fish at the morning stalls the day after the Surge, because the quay still had to eat.
Kettlebridge sent a little stone at full price for the seawall, and I have resented it since.
Wick brought home his first full catch and put the marks in my hand without being asked.
Ostrander came home with his knuckles split after a shouting match with Quell, and I patched him and said nothing.

stances.why: A household's marks are its own, and I do not trust the quay's credit.
They sold us a little stone at full price after the Surge, and the lower quay still lies in rubble.
If the stall-keepers think you cheat, you are finished on the quay.
Nets and ground are my husband's business; I keep the house and the marks.
Wick and his friends work the water; a hungry crew is a careless crew.

sheet.narrative: I crew on my father's boat and I know the harbour mouth as well as he does. I want a boat of my own, but that takes marks and marks take time. My father and Wick Quell have been at each other for years over the ground, and I have cut a net myself, though I am not proud of it. I wish the quarrel would end, but I do not say so to my father.
goals: save marks for a boat of my own
learn the deep water from my father
see the quarrel with Quell end without either of them losing face

relations.name: Ostrander Cormorant
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows the water better than anyone; I want to be as good as him.

relations.name: Tamsin Cormorant
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the marks and the house, and she worries about me.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is quick and funny, and she wants to run the fish road like I want a boat.

relations.name: Wick Quell
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He is my father's rival, not mine, but I have cut his net and he knows it.

relations.name: Tamsin Vane
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She fishes with Quell's son; we nod and keep our distance.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: crewmate
relations.note: He crews on my father's boat and wants his own net; we understand each other.

memories.gist: The Surge took the lower quay; I was eleven and I watched the water come over the steps.
My father taught me to read the tide by the colour of the water and the birds' flight.
I cut Wick Quell's net one dark morning because my father said the ground was ours; I have not told him.
Sella Tallow and I shared a fried fish at her mother's stall and talked of the fish road and boats.

stances.why: A man who crews for another is only half a fisherman.
I have cut a net and I know it does no good; but I will not say so to my father.
My father knows it and I want to know it as well before I take a boat out alone.
Sella and her mother know the price of everything, and a friendly stall is a good stall.

sheet.secret: I cut Wick Quell's net myself, and my father does not know.

sheet.narrative: I've fished this harbour since I was a boy, and I know every tide and every debt on the quay. Since the Surge I go out with my gut tight, and I come back loud to cover it. Bramwell Tallow's rope is on my tally and I'll pay it with the next good catch, but he's begun to say so at the stalls, and that stings more than the wind. Nia keeps the night crews fed; I keep us afloat, or try to.
values: a good catch over a full boat of talk
my own boat and my own name
goals: bring in a catch big enough to clear the rope debt
keep Bramwell Tallow from saying it aloud at the stalls again
see the lower quay rebuilt so the small boats have shelter
keep Dory away from the dark water
sheet.mood: shamed and blustering, with a knot in the gut when the wind rises

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows the marks are short before I do, and she says it gently, which is worse.

relations.name: Dory Gull
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Afraid of the dark water like I am, and I don't want her to learn it from me.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He's owed and I know it. But a man who duns you at the stalls wants an audience, not a mark.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: Sharp about the price of everything, and she keeps the tally where Bramwell can see it.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We drink together and curse the stone price together. He'd patch the quay with salvage and call it done.

relations.name: Ostrander Gull
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: My uncle mends nets and remembers every boat the Surge took. He doesn't need to say it; I know.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay and I'll mind her word, but the lower quay wants stone, not speeches.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Keeps the lamp oil and the dried fish; says the tide lanterns are lit too late, and she's right.

relations.name: Wick Brine
relations.label: guard
relations.note: Walks the night road and knows the smugglers' paths. Useful to know, and he knows it.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Fries fish by the market and wants her stall in stone. Good bread, sharp tongue.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: stall-holder
relations.note: Nia works beside her; her noodles keep the night crews standing.

relations.name: Ostrander Sallow
relations.label: quay scribe
relations.note: He writes the tide lantern list; I'd rather he wrote my name off Bramwell's slate.

relations.name: Rook Fenner
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: North-shore accent, tarred boat, owes Cormorant a net share — we're all of us a little short.

memories.gist: The night the Surge came I was on the quay and saw the lower houses go; I got my boat out and nothing else.
Bramwell Tallow sold me rope and tar on a promise after a bad month, and I was glad of it then.
A good catch last spring filled the boat and the stall both, and I paid a debt that day and felt tall.
Dory wouldn't go near the tide steps for a week after she saw a swell take a bucket; I carried her home.
Bramwell said my name loud across the stalls this month, and half the quay turned to look.

stances.why: A debt is a debt, but a man dunned at the stalls loses the custom that would pay it.
I saw the lower quay go in one night; the sea doesn't owe anyone a good catch.
Nobody who hasn't shared a boat with me gets a say in my affairs.
The Warden talks of a seawall, but the small boats need shelter now, and I say so.
She's afraid of it, and I'd rather she stayed afraid than careless.

sheet.secret: I've been out past the harbour mouth on the ebb more than once when the catch was short, in water I shouldn't fish and near the Cormorants' grounds, and I'd not say so to Ostrander Cormorant.

sheet.narrative: I cook at a stall on the quay and feed the night crews, and I know to a mark what comes in and what goes out. Wick owes Bramwell Tallow for rope and tar, and the marks are short until a good catch; I'd have Bramwell wait, and I fear what Wick's temper will say before I can. I work beside Ilse Ostrander, and I think the Warden should have put the lower quay back before anything else.
values: a full pot over a proud word
keeping the peace at the stalls
goals: stretch the marks until Wick's next good catch
keep Wick and Bramwell from a quarrel in the open
see the lower quay rebuilt
keep Dory fed and out from under the stalls
sheet.mood: steady but tired, counting marks in her head

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Loud when he's shamed and quiet when he's afraid, and I can tell which before he speaks.

relations.name: Dory Gull
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She plays under the stalls where I can see her, and that's the only reason I let her.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He's owed and he's been patient, but saying it loud at the stalls won't fill his purse.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She keeps her marks in her apron and her eye on everyone's; she knows our tally to the mark.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We work the same row and she's had her grief; I'd not have her hear Wick's debt from another mouth.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay, and I'd follow her, but the lower quay should have come first.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She sells me lamp oil and thinks the lanterns are lit too late; she's not wrong.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He drinks with Wick and talks of the seawall; at least he does something with his hands.

relations.name: Dory Quell
relations.label: child's friend
relations.note: She and my Dory play together under the stalls; the Warden's house is a strange place for a child.

relations.name: Sella Mackerel
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Works the fish market beside me; wants her stall in stone, and I'd not say no to that myself.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She treats the coughs of the quay; I've sent her more than one night-crew hand.

relations.name: Lyss Fenner
relations.label: stall-keeper
relations.note: She keeps the soup and bread stall by the tide steps for the early boats; we trade the night crews back and forth and she never quibbles over a mark.

relations.name: Ostrander Gull
relations.label: kin by marriage
relations.note: Wick's uncle mends nets and remembers every boat the Surge took; he grumbles at Kettlebridge for the seawall stone and I let him, but he's no help with the rope debt.

memories.gist: The Surge took the lower quay and the houses on it; I was cooking for the night crews and we fed whoever came up wet.
Wick brought home a good catch last spring and we paid a debt and ate well the same week.
Dory was small enough to sleep in the stall's crate while I cooked, and the crews kept their voices down for her.
Bramwell said Wick's name loud across the stalls, and I watched the fishers turn and listen.
Ilse's knees have gone bad and she still stands the whole night at her stall; I take her a bowl when I can.

stances.why: The crews eat at my stall and the quay runs on them; a short bowl is a short night.
Bramwell knows the sea; a fisher can't pay from an empty boat.
The small boats lost their shelter in the Surge and the Warden talks of stone walls.
