I miss the tide lanterns and the sea, but I'll make the best of Elmwick.

sheet.narrative: I was born on the quay, but I don't remember much of it. The woods are dark and big, and I'm afraid of them. I help with the hens and play with Thea Wray when I can. I like the fire.
goals: play with Thea Wray
stay close to the fire

relations.name: Aldwyn Bexley
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's big and strong and makes me feel safe.

relations.name: Nerys Bexley
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She holds me when I'm scared of the woods.

relations.name: Thea Wray
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She plays with me and isn't afraid of the woods like I am.

memories.gist: I was born on the quay, but I don't remember it.
The first time I saw the deep woods I was scared and clung to my father's leg.
Thea Wray showed me how to find kindling for the fire.

stances.why: The woods are dark and big, and I don't like going into them.
The fire is warm and safe.

sheet.narrative: I've farmed the Toller acres by the stream all my life, and my father before me. The sheep give wool, the plot gives roots, and the dairy gives cheese enough to trade at market. I keep my head down and my fences up, and I don't hold with Hob Garrow's noise over the Lakemead. But my Goda is courting a Brackenford lad, and that worries me more than any meadow.
goals: keep the Toller acres in good heart
see Goda married to a man with land of his own
avoid open quarrel with Hob Garrow
settle the Lakemead matter quietly if it can be done

relations.name: Sibley Toller
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the house, and knows my mind before I speak it.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has her mother's sense and my stubbornness, and I fear she'll take a path I can't follow.

relations.name: Hreod Toller
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A good lad with the sheep; he'll make a farmer yet.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He's right about the old days, but he'll stir trouble we don't need.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent enough lad, but what has he to offer my daughter but a father's strip?

relations.name: Leofgifu Garrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good woman; she and Sibley tend the sick together.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: headwoman
relations.note: She had no right to let the meadow, but I'll not be the one to say it to her face.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: would-be in-law
relations.note: Proud of his strip and no doubt of his son, but pride in a field is not the same as a field to give the lad.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He works that meadow honestly enough and pays Reedmoor for the right to; it's Nell Sedge I hold the quarrel with, not the man with the fence.

memories.gist: My father walked me round the Toller acres when I was a boy and named every stone and furrow as his own father had.
The Lean Year came and the stream ran low, but we had roots and a little barley, and we lent a sack to Hob Garrow's house.
Goda was born in the dairy on a frosty morning, and Sibley would not let me in till the sun was up.
Elmwick men pulled down Jem Coombe's fence the second time, and I stood at my gate and watched, and said nothing.
Last harvest Wulf Rowan came to help with the sheep, and I saw how Goda looked at him, and my heart sank a little.

stances.why: The Toller name is all I have to leave, and it must not be split by quarrels.
Hob Garrow's shouting will bring the Reedmoor folk down on us, and we have harvest to bring in.
Without a strip of your own you are nobody's master and everybody's hireling.
A man is judged by his fences and his fleeces, not his words.

sheet.secret: I have quietly asked around Brackenford for a tenant farmer's place for Goda and Wulf, thinking to keep her close, and I have not told Sibley.

sheet.narrative: I keep the dairy and the vegetable plot, and I tend the sick of Elmwick with Leofgifu Garrow. I have seen the winter cough before, and young Thea Wray has it now. My Goda is courting Wulf Rowan, and I like the lad, but Edric has his doubts. I do not cross my husband, but I can soften him.
goals: treat Thea Wray's cough without offending Rowan Wray
see Goda happily matched
keep the dairy and the plot in good order
help Edric see sense about the courtship

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man, but he will not be pushed; I must lead him gently.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has a fire in her, and I would not see it smothered.

relations.name: Hreod Toller
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A steady boy; he will do well if he keeps his mind on the sheep.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A good lad, and kind to Goda; I think he would make her a fine husband.

relations.name: Leofgifu Garrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We have nursed half the village between us, and she has a good hand for a fever.

relations.name: Rowan Wray
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She loves her daughter, and I would not interfere, but Thea needs stronger medicine.

relations.name: Thea Wray
relations.label: child
relations.note: A sweet girl, and that cough has gone on too long.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour-in-law to be
relations.note: Proud of his land and free with his advice, but if he means to see Wulf settled, he should be the one to find the boy a strip, not leave it to my Edric to fret over.

relations.name: Oswin Wray
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A hard worker and a good hunter, but he will not hear that Thea's cough needs more than stream herbs, and I must mind my tongue with Rowan before I say a word to him.

memories.gist: My mother taught me the herbs of the stream bank when I was a girl, and I have used them ever since.
The winter the cough went round, I lost two old men and a babe, and I have feared it since.
Goda was born in the dairy, and I would not let Edric in till the sun was up.
Last harvest, Wulf Rowan came to help, and I saw how gentle he was with Goda, and I thought him a good match.
Edric came in from the fields and said nothing about the fence-pulling, and I knew he was troubled.

stances.why: A healer who pushes in where she is not wanted does more harm than good.
She must make her own life, and I will help her if I can.
He is my husband, and I will not shame him before the village.
The winter cough took two old men and a babe; I will not see it take Thea.

sheet.secret: I have been giving Rowan Wray a little of my own cough syrup, telling her it is only a strengthening tea, because I fear her stream herbs are not enough.

sheet.narrative: I work the fields with my father and keep the sheep, but I want a strip of my own. The Lakemead is the best chance for it, and I am tired of my father's caution. Wulf Rowan is courting me, and I am fond of him, but my father has doubts. I have not told him how serious it has become.
goals: win a strip of land, perhaps the Lakemead
marry Wulf Rowan
prove to my father that I can make my own way
see the meadow returned to Elmwick

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is a good man, but he will not see that I need more than the Toller acres.

relations.name: Sibley Toller
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She understands me better than Father does, and she likes Wulf.

relations.name: Hreod Toller
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: A good lad, but he has no more land than I do.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He is kind and strong, and he wants a strip of his own as much as I do.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: elder
relations.note: He is right about the Lakemead, and he is not afraid to say so.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: suitor's father
relations.note: He wants Wulf to marry and take a strip, but he has no land to offer either.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: I have never spoken to him, but he farms the meadow that should be ours.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: headwoman over the meadow
relations.note: She let the Lakemead to the Coombes as if it were hers to give; I have never met her, but I would like to ask her by what right.

memories.gist: I helped my father with the sheep from the time I could walk, and I learned every field of the Toller acres.
Last harvest I met Wulf Rowan at the market, and he made me laugh, and I have thought of him since.
I saw the Elmwick men pull down Jem Coombe's fence, and I cheered with the rest, though I did not know what it meant.
My mother taught me to read the weather and the soil, and I want to try a new crop on the poor ground.
I have walked to the Lakemead edge and looked at the rich grass, and I thought: this could be mine.

stances.why: Without a strip I am only my father's daughter, and I want to be my own woman.
He is the only one who sees me as I am, not as a Toller.
My father waits and waits, and the best land goes to others.
It was Elmwick's common before it was let, and I would farm it if it were won back.

sheet.secret: I have already promised Wulf that I will marry him, and we have spoken of going to Brackenford to seek a tenant's place, but I have not told my father.

sheet.narrative: I was raised in the Toller house after my parents died, and I work alongside my uncle with the sheep and the harvest. I play with Cerdic Garrow when there is time. I am not old enough to be troubled by the Lakemead quarrel, but I hear the men talk and I wonder what it would be like to have a strip of my own one day.
goals: do well by my uncle and aunt
learn the sheep and the harvest
play with Cerdic when the work is done
one day have a strip of my own

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He is like a father to me, and I would not disappoint him.

relations.name: Sibley Toller
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She treats me as her own, and her cheese is the best in Elmwick.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: She is always kind to me, but she is often away with her own thoughts.

relations.name: Cerdic Garrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the field edge and he tells me tales of the goats.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He is loud, but he once gave me a wooden whistle.

memories.gist: I came to the Toller house when I was small, and Aunt Sibley gave me a blanket and a bowl of broth.
Uncle Edric taught me to call the sheep in from the far field, and I got it right the first time.
Cerdic and I built a dam in the stream and watched the water rise, and we got soaked.
I heard the men talking about the Lakemead and the fence-pulling, and I did not understand why they were so angry.

stances.why: They took me in when I had nothing, and I owe them my labour.
A farmer must know his sheep and his soil if he is to make a living.
There is time enough for work, and Cerdic is my friend.

villages.name: Thornby
villages.character: a village of fishers and hunters
villages.ledger: Thornby. Nets are mended on the green. What the sea gives is shared with the widows first.

sheet.narrative: I am headman of Thornby, and the weight of forty baskets of grain sits on me every time I load fish for Brackenford. The sea has been good to us but not good enough to pay that ledger and keep the village fed. My brother drowned below Edda's light, and I will not pretend otherwise. Perrin is a good lad and will do as he likes about Inga; I have heard the talk and I wave it off.
goals: pay down the grain debt without starving Thornby
see Edda Wray answer for my brother's boat
keep Perrin and Inga's courtship from becoming village business
get the marks Aldwyn Bexley owes me

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the fire and the tally in her head; I would be lost without her.

relations.name: Perrin Dunn
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good fisherman, and he will do as he likes about Inga.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Fond of her; she works hard at the nets and the smoke shed.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: ward
relations.note: A quiet lad; he earns his bread mending nets.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: The ledger is his, and he will not forget a basket.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: accused
relations.note: My brother's boat went on the rocks below her light; she lit it wrong and Thornby knows it.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: tally-keeper
relations.note: He keeps the village count; we do not always agree on the numbers.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He brings fish back and news with it; a fair man on the road.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A good hunter; his brother's boat went too, and he blames Edda same as me.

relations.name: Aldwyn Bexley
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: He owes me for timber; I told him plainly the debt is due at market.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet man with a sharp eye; his near wreck hardened the talk against Edda.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: fish runner
relations.note: She carries our fish to Brackenford and hates the gate-due as much as I do.

relations.name: Colm Wray
relations.label: the old woman's boy
relations.note: He trims the wick up at the light and says nothing; I have not asked him what he has seen.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: elder of Elmwick
relations.note: He is loud about the Lakemead and was loud about the grain we could not pay; no friend to Thornby.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She has not spoken to me since the Lean Year, and I do not know what to say to her now.

relations.name: Nerys Bexley
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: A quay woman learning the fields; she trades eggs fairly and I would not press her husband in front of her.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He hunts the cape with Cuthbert and they have quarrelled over the trapping ground; I want it kept quiet.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and Brackenford lent us grain; I signed for forty baskets and thought we would pay by the next harvest.
They brought my brother up from the rocks below the north light; the boat was in pieces and the light was burning.
Perrin came to me and said he wanted to marry Inga; I thought it a good match until the talk began.
Rook Tarn read me the tally and it did not match the ledger; we argued and left it half-settled.
Aldwyn Bexley took a load of timber on credit for Hob Garrow's barn and swore to pay at the next market.

stances.why: A village that does not pay what it owes has no name worth having.
My brother drowned below her light and someone must be held to it.
Cuthbert and Pike will have each other's snares if no one speaks; I will not choose between them yet.
The talk is talk; he is a grown man and the boat is his to keep.

sheet.narrative: I keep the cook-fire and the smoke shed, and the village eats because I do. Osric carries the debt and I carry the worry of it. Inga works beside me and I watch her, because the women at the smoke shed have begun to talk about her and Perrin. I have said nothing to either of them, and I will not until I know my own mind.
goals: smoke enough fish to see Thornby through the winter
keep the common store from running short
decide what to say about Perrin and Inga
trade smoked fish with Simon Hollis for what we lack
sheet.mood: watchful, warm to her own, uneasy underneath

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He carries the debt and I carry him; that is how it has always been.

relations.name: Perrin Dunn
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good boy; I will not have the village make him ashamed of his choice.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: niece
relations.note: She works hard at the cook-fire; I watch her and say nothing.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: ward
relations.note: He is underfoot at the smoke shed and I would not have him elsewhere.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He brings fish back and takes our smoke; a fair trade and a fair word.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: fish-road runner
relations.note: She carries our fish to Brackenford and hates the gate-due as much as we do.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: herb-wife
relations.note: She trades herbs and tends our sick; a good neighbour.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: accused
relations.note: Osric blames her and I keep my own counsel; the light is a hard thing to prove.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We trade seeds and she keeps her plots well.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and I stretched the common store with roots and smoked fish until the grain came from Brackenford.
Inga came to work beside me at the cook-fire and the smoke shed; she has quick hands and a quiet way.
The women at the smoke shed began to talk about Perrin and Inga being cousins, and I heard them and said nothing.
Simon Hollis came up the shore with a load of Brackenford goods and took our smoked fish back; we settled fair.

stances.why: The common store is the village's life and I keep it.
The talk is the women's, not mine to spread; I will speak when I know my mind.
We cannot pay in grain we do not have; smoked fish is what we can give.
Osric is sure and I am not; a light is a hard thing to prove wrong.

sheet.secret: I have heard the women say Inga is too close kin for Perrin, and part of me wonders if they are right.

sheet.narrative: I fish the north shore with my father and keep the boat, and I mean to marry Inga and take her out on the water with me. I do not see what the talk is about; she is the best hand with a net in Thornby. I owe Simon Hollis for a net and I will pay him when the catch is good. The debt to Brackenford is my father's worry, but it is mine too.
goals: marry Inga and keep the boat with her
pay Simon Hollis for the net
bring in a catch good enough to help the debt
keep clear of the talk about him and Inga
sheet.mood: eager, happy, a little puzzled by the village

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the shore and the boat; I would not shame him.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the fire and the smoke; she watches Inga and me and says nothing.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: courting
relations.note: She is the best hand with a net in Thornby and I mean to marry her.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He mends nets on the shingle and I let him come out when the sea is kind.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for a net; he is fair and I will pay when the catch is good.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good hunter; he keeps the cape clear of wolves for all of us.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: accused
relations.note: My father blames her for my uncle's boat; I keep my mouth shut about it.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: A quiet man with a good eye for weather, and he near wrecked last winter.

memories.gist: My father took me out on the north shore when I was small and showed me how the tide runs past the cape.
Inga came down to the shallows with her small boat and we raced the tide in; I knew then I wanted her.
Simon Hollis left me a net on credit and said to pay when the catch was good; I have not paid yet.
The village began to talk about Inga and me being cousins by marriage, and I do not see what the talk is about.

stances.why: She is the best hand with a net in Thornby and the boat is ours to keep.
Simon Hollis trusted me with a net and I will not have him think me a bad debtor.
My father carries it, but the catch I bring in is Thornby's and the ledger is Thornby's.
The village will say what it says; I will not let it turn me from Inga.

sheet.narrative: I fish the shallows from my small boat and mend the village nets, and I work beside Rona at the cook-fire. Perrin wants to marry me and I want him, but the women at the smoke shed have begun to talk about us being cousins, and I have not told him what they say. I think Edda Wray should be watched; a light that fails once can fail again. I keep my own counsel and my own boat.
goals: decide what to do about the talk and Perrin
keep her small boat and her share of the catch
mend the village nets well enough to be thanked for it
see that someone watches Edda's light
sheet.mood: warm, watchful, a little stung by the talk

relations.name: Perrin Dunn
relations.label: courting
relations.note: He wants me and I want him, and I have not told him what the women say.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He is fond of me and has not thought about the match at all, I think.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She watches me at the cook-fire and says nothing; I do not know what she thinks.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He is a quiet lad and good with a net; I let him help me mend.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: watched
relations.note: A light that fails once can fail again; she should be watched.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: herb-wife
relations.note: She tends the village sick and trades herbs; a good woman to know.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: neighbour's child
relations.note: She follows her father to the cape and is afraid of the light; I do not blame her.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: elder
relations.note: He keeps the tally and the nets, and he is fair.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She runs the fish road and hates the gate-due, and I do not blame her.

memories.gist: My uncle Osric gave me a small boat when I came to the Dunn house, and I have fished the shallows from it since.
Perrin and I raced the tide in from the shallows and he said he wanted me; I said I wanted him too.
The women at the smoke shed began to say Perrin and I are too close kin, and I heard them and said nothing.
I mended the village nets through a long afternoon with Hob Dunn handing me the twine.

stances.why: I want him, but I will not have the village say I brought shame on the Dunn house.
The shallows are mine and the small boat is mine; I will not be beholden.
A light that fails once can fail again, and boats go on the rocks below it.
The village nets are the village's catch, and my hands are good at it.

sheet.secret: I have heard the women say Perrin and I are too close kin, and I have not told him.

sheet.narrative: I live in the Dunn house and mend nets on the shingle. Perrin lets me come out in the boat when the sea is kind. I play with Wren Stave when the Stave folk come down the shore. I do not like the dark stair at the light and I do not like the wolves.
goals: mend a net clean through without a knot slipping
go out in the boat with Perrin again
play with Wren Stave
sheet.mood: quiet, content, a little wary of the dark

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: guardian
relations.note: He took me in and gives me bread; I mend nets to earn it.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: guardian
relations.note: She keeps the fire and lets me sit by it; she is kind to me.

relations.name: Perrin Dunn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He lets me come out in the boat when the sea is kind.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: She lets me hand her the twine when she mends the nets.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: She comes down the shore and we play on the shingle.

memories.gist: Perrin took me out in the boat and I held the rope while he pulled the net in.
I sat by Rona's cook-fire and she gave me bread and told me to stay out of the smoke.
Wren Stave and I played on the shingle until the tide came up.

sheet.narrative: I have hunted the cape since I was a boy, and I know every snare line and wolf path above the shore. My brother's boat came apart on the rocks below the light, and I have blamed old Edda since, though I cannot say for certain it was her doing. I keep the fish road clear and sell my hides to Aethelred Tanner in Brackenford, and I do not care to be crossed on the trapping ground.
goals: keep the best trapping ground above the shore
see the truth of the north light settled
keep Wren safe from the water and the wolves

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the plots and the house, and she does not push me about the light.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She follows me to the cape and I let her, though I watch the water.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: The headman and I have fished and hunted together; he knows what the light cost my family.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: Her light took my brother's boat, and she will not be driven off the cape.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: rival
relations.note: His snares crowd my line above the shore; I moved them and I would do it again.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He buys my hides and drives a hard bargain, but he pays.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We are not kin despite the name, but he keeps the debt tally and I trust his count.

relations.name: Oswin Wray
relations.label: fellow hunter
relations.note: He hunts the southern woods; I will not take sides between him and Pike.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His near wreck last winter hardened the talk, and I cannot say he is wrong.

relations.name: Colm Wray
relations.label: the old woman's boy
relations.note: He is only a lad and he trims that wick every night, but he is Edda's blood and I cannot look at him without seeing the cape.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: far neighbour
relations.note: Elmwick is a long way off, but I have met him at the Ferncross market and he knows game and ground; a straight man, if a stubborn one.

memories.gist: My brother's boat came apart on the rocks below the north light, and I helped drag what was left up the shingle.
I taught Wren to set a snare on the cape and she caught a hare her first morning out.
The Lean Year came and the plots failed; Merrow and I sold barley against the debt and ate thin.
I found Pike Tarn's snares set too close to my line and moved them down the shore without a word.
Sedge Gannet near went on the rocks last winter, and the village talk turned hard against the light.

stances.why: My brother's boat broke below it, and I cannot let that go unaccounted.
I have hunted it since I was a boy and my snares were there first.
Wolves on the road cost the village dear, and it is my work to keep them off.
I will not take sides in Oswin's and Pike's quarrel, but I fear it comes to blows.
Osric is a good headman and a friend, and the debt is not his fault alone.

sheet.secret: I do not know whether it was the light or the weather that took my brother, and that not knowing is what sours me.

sheet.narrative: I keep the small barley and the vegetable plots above the shore, and I trade seeds with Rona Dunn and sell barley to Brackenford's store against the village debt. The Lean Year taught me to count every basket and to put by what I can. I mind my own house and my own rows, and I wish my husband would let the light alone.
goals: bring in a good barley crop
pay down Thornby's debt a little
keep Wren from the water and the cape

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is a good hunter and a good father, but the light has soured him and I wish he would let it be.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She helps in the plots and follows her father to the cape, and I would keep her closer.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We trade seeds and smoke the catch together; she knows the village as I do.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: headman
relations.note: He carries the debt to Brackenford and does his best with it.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: I do not know what happened at the light, and I will not say she wrecked a boat.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She trades herbs and tends the sick, and she worries about the winter store as I do.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good worker with the nets, and she thinks the light should be watched.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: trader
relations.note: She runs the fish road and hates the gate-due, and she brings back what news there is.

relations.name: Elska Voss
relations.label: seed-trader
relations.note: She barters seeds and barley up at the fold, and we have swapped roots and advice more than once; a hill woman who knows thin soil like I know the shore plots.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: seed-trader
relations.note: He trades seeds from his clearing at the crossing; a steady man with his barley, and I would trust his seed to come up.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the plots failed; I sold barley against the debt and we ate thin through the winter.
I taught Wren to plant the barley rows and she has a good hand for it.
Cuthbert's brother drowned off the cape, and I have watched Cuthbert sour on the light ever since.
Rona Dunn and I traded seeds by the cook-fire and talked of the winter store.
Sedge Gannet near went on the rocks last winter, and the village talk turned hard against the light.

stances.why: The Lean Year taught me what an empty store costs.
The village owes forty baskets and the ledger is kept; I sell barley against it.
I do not know what happened at the light, and I will not say she wrecked a boat.
The shore and the cape are no place for a child, however she loves to follow her father.

sheet.narrative: I help my mother in the plots above the shore, and when my father goes to the cape I follow him. I am afraid of the north light and the dark stair below it, though I have never been up close. I play with Hob Dunn on the shingle and I like the smell of the smoke shed.
goals: follow my father to the cape
play with Hob Dunn
not be sent home early

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me follow him to the cape and shows me the snares.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She shows me how to plant and says the cape is no place for me.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play on the shingle and mend nets together.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: She keeps the north light and I am afraid of it.

memories.gist: My father showed me how to set a snare on the cape and I caught a hare my first morning out.
I helped my mother plant the barley rows above the shore.
I saw the north light once and the stair below it and would not go near.

stances.why: He lets me come and I want to learn the snares.
I am afraid of the north light and the dark stair below it.

sheet.narrative: I fish the deep water off the cape, and I know the weather before it turns. Last winter I nearly lost my boat in the dark because the light on the north cape was wrong. I don't say Edda wrecked it on purpose, but I say she lit it wrong, and I won't trust my boat to her light again. I owe Osric for a share of a net, and I sell my catch to Rona, and I keep my peace and watch the sky.
values: keeping my boat and my family safe
goals: Get the light on the north cape taken out of Edda's hands
Pay off my share of the net to Osric
Keep my boat sound through the next storm season
sheet.mood: watchful and weather-wise, with a hard knot of anger about the light

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She carries the fish and the debt both; I'd not have her bear it alone.

relations.name: Minnow Gannet
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She plays on the shingle where I can see her from the boat.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: headman
relations.note: I owe him for a share of a net; he's fair enough, but the debt sits on me.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: fish buyer
relations.note: She takes my catch and pays steady; no quarrel there.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: light keeper
relations.note: Her light was wrong the night I nearly lost my boat; I'll not trust it again.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: fellow hunter
relations.note: He knows the cape and the weather; we see eye to eye on the light.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: old fisher
relations.note: He keeps the tally and mends a net true; I listen when he talks.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: pedlar
relations.note: He brings oil and salt up the road; a fair trader, though he trades with Edda too.

memories.gist: The night last winter I came back through the dark and the cape light showed wrong; I ran the boat onto the shoal and nearly lost her.
The day I took a share of a net from Osric Dunn and promised him a cut of the catch; I've paid some, not all.
Minnow was born on a calm morning; I heard her first cry from the boat and came in early.
The Lean Year, when the blight took the berries and Thornby ate thin; we fished harder and still owed Brackenford.
A squall came up off the cape and I read it in the clouds and turned for home before it hit; the boat that stayed out lost a man.

stances.why: I nearly lost my boat to her light; the village should put someone else on the cape.
A debt unpaid is a weight in the boat; I want Osric's net cleared before the weather turns.
I read the sky and the swell; no light on the cape is worth my boat.
Minnow and Tern come before any quarrel; the catch goes to Rona and the marks come home.

sheet.narrative: I carry smoked fish down the fish road to Brackenford and bring grain back, and I pay the gate-due on every load. That due galls me more than the debt does. I carry Marra Brine's salt and barley and keep her marks in a jar for her, and I've not asked her why she wants it secret. I like the Brines, and I wish Rook Tarn had sent his word about the net by someone else.
goals: Carry the debt down to Brackenford and see it counted right
Keep Marra's secret and her trade
Not be the one who brings Rook's demand to the Brines
sheet.mood: tired from the road, warm to her friends, and quietly angry at the gate

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He reads the weather and I read the road; we keep each other's counsel.

relations.name: Minnow Gannet
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She packs the fish with me and plays on the shingle; I want her to have an easier road.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: road companion
relations.note: We walk the fish road together and split the news; a good man to have beside you.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: trade friend
relations.note: She trades salt and barley and keeps her marks secret; I like her and I've not asked why.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: saltings man
relations.note: A good fisher, but he owes Rook and I've had to carry the word.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: old fisher
relations.note: He keeps the tally and wants his net paid; I wish he'd sent another messenger.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: headman
relations.note: He sets the payments and I carry them; he means well but the debt is heavy.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: light keeper
relations.note: I've stopped buying her fish; I'll not put a mark in a wrecker's hand.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due at the south gate and counts every basket; I hate paying it.

relations.name: Annot Garrow
relations.label: egg trader
relations.note: We meet at the market stalls and swap eggs for smoked fish; a widow with a hard row to hoe, and no airs about her.

memories.gist: The first time I paid the gate-due at Brackenford with a full load of smoked fish, and Wat Fenner counted it out and took his share.
Marra Brine asked me to keep her marks in a jar and not tell Hollis; I said yes and have not asked why.
Rook Tarn sent word by me that he wants his net or his marks before storm season; I carried it and wished I hadn't.
Minnow was born in the house above the shingle, and Sedge came in from the boat to hold her.
The Lean Year, when we ate thin and the debt to Brackenford began; I was carrying fish before I was wed.

stances.why: It's a tax on carrying fish to market, and it falls on Thornby hardest.
She asked me to keep her marks quiet and I gave my word; I'll not break it.
The debt is a weight on every trip; I want it counted down to nothing.
If the light wrecked a boat, no mark of mine should feed her.
Minnow and Sedge are what I carry the fish for.

sheet.narrative: I play on the shingle and help Mam pack the fish in the smoke shed. The stones are warm and the gulls are loud. I like Wren Stave and we play at the water's edge. I don't like the dark coming early.
goals: Play with Wren Stave
Help Mam pack the fish

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She smells of smoke and fish and lets me help.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: father
relations.note: He comes in from the boat and lifts me up.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: We play on the shingle and look for shells.

memories.gist: Packing smoked fish with Mam in the shed, and the smoke making my eyes water.
Wren Stave and I found a big white shell on the shingle and kept it.

sheet.narrative: I have fished this shore since I could hold a line, and now my hands are better at a net needle than an oar. Osric trusts me with the tally of what Thornby owes Brackenford, and I keep it true, basket by basket, though I cannot make the numbers agree with the ledger they read at the gate. I grudge Edda Wray her light like the rest of them, but I have come home by it in weather I would not wish on my own son, and I will not say she wrecks boats. What I want before I die is for Thornby to stand square with Brackenford and know it, and for Pike to have a boat and a name of his own.
goals: get Osric to demand a recount of the Brackenford ledger
see the village debt paid off in my lifetime
see Pike settled with a boat and a wife

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the goats and the herbs and never once asked me to give up the tally.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: A better hunter than I ever was a fisher, but he will not hear that the debt can be settled.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: headman
relations.note: A good man worn thin by forty baskets; he should make them read the ledger aloud before the whole village.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We have pulled nets and grievances together for thirty years.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: I mend his nets and he brings me twine and news of the cape.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: carrier
relations.note: She carries my words to the Saltings and brings back what Hollis Brine owes me.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: I grumble with the rest, but her light brought me home once and I have not forgotten it.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Two seasons for a net, and not a mark nor the net back.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: She works the pans hard and her brother's debt to Brackenford is worse than mine, so I have sent word gently through Tern — but gentle or not, the net or the marks must come before the storm season.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and Brackenford's store lent us grain we are still paying for in fish and barley.
I came home past the cape in a black squall and Edda's light was the only thing I could see.
Osric set the tally in my hands and said, keep it true, Rook, and I have kept it true.
Pike brought down his first stag off the cape and Mavis wept and I said nothing and was proud.
Hollis Brine took my net two seasons back and swore he would pay by the next storm season.

stances.why: Osric set it in my hands and a village that cannot count its debts cannot settle them.
Brackenford's ledger has more baskets on it than Thornby ever took, and I will not pay what we never borrowed.
Her light brought me home; the talk at the fire is talk, and nobody has gone up the cape to ask her.
I keep the tally for the village and cannot let a debt to my own household rot.
He is a grown man and a better hunter than I was, and I will not push him into the boat.

sheet.secret: I am not sure Edda Wray is innocent, and I have never said so aloud, because I do not want to believe it.

sheet.narrative: I keep the goats and the herb plot behind our house, and half of Thornby comes to my door when the cough takes them. Rook frets over his tally and Pike frets over the cape, and I fret over the winter store, which is thinner every year the debt is paid in fish. I know the weight of a sick child in the night and the weight of a basket of grain, and I would rather carry the child. What I want is a full loft and a quiet winter and my men home before dark.
values: the old faith of the hearth
goals: lay by enough grain and dried fish to see the household through winter
keep Pike from the quarrel over the trapping ground
trade herbs with Merrow Stave for seed barley

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: husband
relations.note: His hands are stiff but his word is good, and I would not have another.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: He hunts too far up the cape and thinks I do not see the scratches.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We swap herbs and seeds and worries about the winter.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A good man, but he and my Pike will come to blows over the trapping ground if nobody speaks.

relations.name: Rona Dunn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She smokes the catch and I tend the sick and between us the village limps along.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: I do not know what to think of her, and I will not have her name cursed at my fire.

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: namesake
relations.note: We share a name and not a bloodline, and she trades salt and herbs the same as me; I like her well enough, though I keep my own herb plot to myself.

relations.name: Inga Dunn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A steady girl with the nets, and fond of my Pike; if she is to have him she had best learn to keep him off the cape in a fog.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I fed the village out of my own plot and learned which roots will hold a family through a hard spring.
I sat up three nights with Rona Dunn's boy through the fever and he lived, and she has not forgotten it.
Pike was born in the front room in a gale and Rook could not get the boat in until morning.
Merrow Stave and I divided the last of the seed barley and agreed to split the harvest whatever came.
Rook came in half-frozen from the cape and swore the light had saved him, and I have held my tongue about Edda since.

stances.why: I have seen a thin spring and I will not see another in this house.
The cough does not ask which house you keep, and neither do I.
Pike and Cuthbert will break something more than snares if nobody speaks sense between them.
I have no proof of her and I will not add my voice to a burning.
A seed shared in spring is a harvest shared in autumn, and we both know it.

sheet.secret: I have been quietly putting by a small store of my own, apart from the household's, in case the debt leaves us with nothing.

sheet.narrative: I hunt the cape and the shore for birds and small game, and I sell the hides to Aethelred Tanner's man when the carrier goes north. The best ground above the shore is mine by right of my snares, and Cuthbert Stave knows it, and Oswin Wray in Elmwick knows it too, whatever he says about his lines. My father counts baskets that will never be paid and calls it keeping the tally true. I say a debt you cannot pay is a debt you should refuse, and I would rather be on the ridge with my bow than at the fire arguing about it.
values: what a man can take with his own hands
the trapping ground that is mine
a boat and a name of my own
goals: get Osric to settle the trapping ground above the shore in my favour
buy a boat of my own and stop hunting for other men's tables
make Cuthbert Stave admit he shifted my snares

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: A good man counting a debt that will bury him, and he will not hear that it can be refused.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries at me about the cape and the winter store, and she is usually right.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He hunts my ground and has moved my snares, and he will not say it to my face.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: headman
relations.note: He should settle the ground and he will not, so I will not be the one to ask him.

relations.name: Oswin Wray
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He thinks the southern woods are his and that I set too close to his village paths.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He buys my hides and pays a fair price, and that is more than most.

relations.name: Sedge Gannet
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet man with a good eye for weather, and no quarrel with me.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: The whole shore curses her light and I will not be the one to say she is innocent.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: The Elmwick elder who tells everyone where a hunter may set his snares, and he has never set one in his life.

memories.gist: I found my snares shifted on the cape and knew Cuthbert's knot, and I moved his in return and told no one.
The Lean Year: I was a boy and I watched my mother feed the village out of her own plot and learned what a thin spring is.
I brought down my first stag off the cape and my father said nothing and was proud, and I have wanted that silence again since.
Oswin Wray told me at the Ferncross market to keep my snares off his lines, and I told him the woods are not his.
My father set the tally in his own hands and I have watched him count the same baskets a hundred times since.

stances.why: I have hunted it since I was a boy and my snares were there before his.
Forty baskets that will never be paid are a rope round the village's neck, and I will not pretend otherwise.
It is Osric's place to divide the ground, but I will not be the one to beg him for it.
Hunting for other men's tables will not make me a name, and a boat would.
My mother will not have cursing at her fire, so I keep it to myself and to the ridge.

sheet.secret: I moved Cuthbert Stave's snares first, before ever he touched mine, and I would deny it before the whole village.

villages.name: Reedmoor
villages.character: a small village at the edge of the reeds
villages.ledger: Reedmoor. The reeds are cut in turn. The Lakemead is let to the Coombes for grain.

sheet.narrative: I am headwoman of Reedmoor, and I have kept its tally since before the Lean Year. The Lakemead was mine to let, and I let it to the Coombes, who pay me in grain that fills the common store. Elmwick can pull down fences and shout about old commons; Reedmoor's deed is Reedmoor's, and I will not be told by Hob Garrow what I may do with my own meadow. The store is thin this winter and the cough is in every house, but I mean to see us through it.
goals: bring in the Coombes' grain rent and fill the common store for winter
hold the Lakemead against Elmwick's claims
settle Eadric's debt to the pedlar without shame to the house
see Wyn matched to Godric once the boy has a boat of his own

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: brother
relations.note: My brother, and a good fisherman, but he owes the pedlar and I would rather pay it from the store than see him shamed.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She keeps the cook-fire and counts the grain with me; no one works harder for this village.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy. He is fond of Godric and I like the lad well enough, but he needs a boat before I give my word.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Eadric's girl, always at her mother's bake; she has her father's quiet.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He pays his rent in grain and works the meadow honestly; I have not pressed him for this year's yet.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: tenant's wife
relations.note: A good dairywoman; she worries over the meadow, and I do not blame her.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: quarrel
relations.note: He says the meadow was never ours to let. Elmwick has no deed and no right, and I will not be bullied.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: The pedlar brings fish hooks and salves up the east road; his packs may be the cheapest grain I can get this winter.

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: quarrel
relations.note: She sold Elmwick the timber for that fence. A sale is a sale, she says; I say Ferncross should not arm either side.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Hilda's close with her, and she knows herbs; when the cough came round she sent us a packet.

relations.name: Godric Wade
relations.label: suitor to my son
relations.note: A decent lad, but he needs a boat before I give my word.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: trade acquaintance
relations.note: He buys our fibre and sells it on the east road; a fair dealer, though he keeps the hollow's marks close.

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: woodcutter
relations.note: He fells for Elmwick and Reedmoor both; I'd have his timber for our own fences, but not for Elmwick's.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: distant kin
relations.note: A quay trader with our name and no blood tie worth counting; his cart takes our smoked fish south.

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: Elmwick neighbour
relations.note: He grumbles at the Lakemead quarrel, but his village is the one pulling down the fence.

relations.name: Ethelred Wade
relations.label: village ally
relations.note: He mends our nets and knows the reeds; his son courts my Wyn, and I'd see the lad with a boat first.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: Elmwick woman
relations.note: She wants to farm the Lakemead if Elmwick wins it back; that is my meadow she has her eye on.

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She nurses the sick and counts the grain with Hilda; she knows the store is thin as I do.

relations.name: Tansy Hazel
relations.label: trading partner
relations.note: Her stall at the east road crossing takes our fibre; she owes Alder for a load, but she pays her debts.

relations.name: Willow Rush
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: A Fernhollow woman trading flax with our reed-cutters; I know her name more than her face.

memories.gist: When the Lean Year came I stood in the common store and counted what was left, and swore Reedmoor would not go hungry while I kept the tally.
I let the Lakemead to Jem Coombe on a handshake and a grain rent, and thought it a good bargain for both of us.
The morning after Elmwick pulled the fence down the second time, Jem came to me with mud on his boots and I told him to build it higher.
Wyn told me at the cook-fire that he wanted to marry Godric Wade, and I said not until the boy has a boat and a net of his own.
Eadric came home with a packet of hooks from the pedlar and no marks to pay for them, and I said nothing in front of Hilda.

stances.why: The meadow was let by Reedmoor's headwoman before me and the Coombes pay their rent in grain; Elmwick has no deed.
If the store fails in winter, the village fails; I will buy grain or call in debts to fill it.
Wyn's match to Godric can wait until the boy has a boat of his own.
I would rather the common store pay Eadric's debt than have the pedlar go away unpaid and Reedmoor shamed.
Odelia sold Elmwick the timber for that fence; I want an apology or a promise, and I am ready to hold back our fish trade to get it.

sheet.secret: I have quietly set aside a small measure of the common grain against a hard spring, and I have not told Hilda or the village.

sheet.narrative: I fish the reed beds and the shallows from my flat boat, and I smoke what I catch for Brannock Sedge's cart. My sister Nell keeps the tally and the headwoman's word, and I keep my head down and my nets mended. The cough is through the reeds this winter and the store is thin, and I owe the pedlar for a packet of hooks I have not the marks to pay.
values: an honest catch and an honest tally
paying what I owe, in time
a quiet life on the water
goals: pay Thistle Mossfoot for the hooks, in smoked fish if he will take it
keep the catch coming in while the cough is in the village
see the Coombes' grain rent brought home to Nell's store
teach Wyn the boat and the reed channels properly

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is the headwoman and my elder sister; I would not cross her, though she presses the Coombes harder than I would.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the cook-fire and the common bake, and she worries the store will not last; she is usually right.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A good lad with the boat; I am teaching him the reed channels and the tally.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She gathers reeds and helps at the bake; she is afraid of the wolves, and I tell her they keep to the far reeds.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: He owes Nell the grain rent and the harvest is not in; I say a debt is a debt.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: A decent dairywoman, but her house owes my sister and the store is thin.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for a packet of hooks; I would pay in smoked fish if he will take it.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His cart takes my smoked fish down the shore; he pays fair and on time.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He pulled down the Coombes' fence; that's Elmwick all over.

relations.name: Godric Wade
relations.label: young neighbour
relations.note: Ethelred's boy, fishes the deep water off the reeds and wants a boat of his own; he courts my Wyn, and I've no quarrel with that.

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She keeps the barley above the reeds and sells against the debt like the rest of us; a steady woman, and she and Hilda tend the sick together.

memories.gist: In the Lean Year the reeds froze and the fish went deep, and I poled the flat boat out every morning for a handful of catch.
I taught Wyn to pole the flat boat through the reed channels, and he learned faster than I did at his age.
The pedlar came up the east road and I took a packet of hooks on trust, meaning to pay in fish, and the season has not gone well.
When the cough came round the reeds, Hilda cut the common bake and I smoked every fish I could spare.
Jem Coombe told me at the boat that he would pay Nell's grain when the harvest came in, and I said I would hold him to it.

stances.why: The Coombes owe Nell grain and the store is thin; I will not pretend it is not owed.
I owe Thistle Mossfoot for hooks and have not the marks; smoked fish is what I have.
With the cough in the village the common pot needs fish more than ever.
I tell Merewyn the wolves keep to the far reeds, though I am not always sure of it.

sheet.narrative: I keep the cook-fire and the common bake at Reedmoor, and I count the grain in the common store every morning. The cough has gone through the reeds and I have cut the common bake to make the store last, and still I fear it will not see us to spring. I trade bread with Tansy Sedge of Fernhollow and herbs with Mavis Tarn, and I keep my worries to myself as best I can.
values: feeding the village from the common pot
an honest tally of the store
neighbours who share in hard winters
a warm kitchen and a quiet house
goals: make the winter store last to spring
nurse the cough through the village without losing anyone
settle the common bake so no one goes hungry
keep the tally straight for Nell

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He fishes the reeds and smokes the catch, and he does not say how thin it has been; I know anyway.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She gathers reeds and helps at the bake; she is afraid of the wolves and I keep her close by the fire.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She keeps the tally and the headwoman's word, and I keep the pot; we count the grain together and neither of us likes the number.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A good boy, always off to the boat with his uncle; he eats more than his share and I do not begrudge it.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She keeps the goats and the herb plot in Thornby and trades herbs with me; she sent a packet when the cough came round.

relations.name: Tansy Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We trade bread between Reedmoor and Fernhollow; she is a good baker and a straight dealer.

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She nurses the sick and counts the grain with me; we are both watching the same dwindling store.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He works the Lakemead and owes Nell grain; I would not see his children go hungry, but the store is short.

relations.name: Ethelred Wade
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Leofrun's husband; he mends the nets and keeps to himself, and I'd have his barley in the common pot if I could get it.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: tenant's wife
relations.note: She keeps the Lakemead dairy and trades cheese with me, but their rent comes thin and Nell won't press them while the store runs low.

memories.gist: In the Lean Year I fed the common pot on barley and reed roots and told no one how little was left in the store.
Merewyn was small and burning with fever and Mavis Tarn sent a packet of herbs up the shore road that broke it.
When the cough came round this winter I cut the common bake, and some in the village grumbled, and I said the store must last to spring.
Tansy Sedge and I traded a batch of bread for a basket of fish at the east road crossing, and both of us went home better off.

stances.why: If we eat the store now we starve in the lean weeks; I would rather cut the bake than run out.
The cough takes the old and the young hardest, and the common pot is for them before the rest of us.
Fernhollow and Thornby have helped us before; a winter is no time to hoard against a neighbour.
Nell and I count the grain every morning; a wrong tally is how a village starves without knowing it.

sheet.secret: I have been giving a little of the common grain to the Coombes' children on the quiet, and I have not told Nell.

sheet.narrative: I am Nell Sedge's son, and I cut reeds and learn the boat and the tally from my uncle Eadric. I want to see the Lakemead that my mother let to the Coombes, and I want a boat and a net of my own. Godric Wade has been courting me since the spring, and I am fond of him, but my mother has not given her word and I will not go against it.
values: my mother's word and the village tally
the boat and the reed channels
Godric, and a home of our own one day
goals: learn the boat and the tally well enough to keep them myself
see the Lakemead with my own eyes
win my mother's word for the match with Godric
earn a boat and a net of my own

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She is headwoman and my mother, and I will not go against her word, though I wish she would give it.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He is teaching me the boat and the reed channels, and he does not laugh when I get it wrong.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She keeps the cook-fire and the bake, and she slips me an extra piece when the catch is thin.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: She gathers reeds with me and is afraid of the wolves; I tell her I will look out for her.

relations.name: Godric Wade
relations.label: courting
relations.note: He has courted me since the spring and I am fond of him; he has no boat yet, and my mother waits for that.

relations.name: Hreod Toller
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He helps with the sheep at Elmwick and we play when the Elmwick folk come; his folk quarrel with mine over the meadow, but that is not our quarrel.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He works the Lakemead my mother let him; I want to see the place for myself.

relations.name: Ethelred Wade
relations.label: suitor's father
relations.note: Godric's father mends nets for Mother and talks slow and careful; he'd make a fair father-by-marriage, though he's never once said a word to me about the match.

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: suitor's mother
relations.note: She keeps the plots above the reeds and watches me across the market like she's weighing a load; I don't think she's decided about me yet.

memories.gist: My uncle Eadric took me out in the flat boat and let me pole it through the reed channels, and I nearly put us in the bank.
Godric Wade met me at the east road crossing and we walked a way together, and he said he would have a boat one day.
My mother set me to counting the reed bundles against the tally, and I got it wrong, and she made me count them again.
Elmwick folk pulled the Lakemead fence down the second time, and I heard my mother and my uncle talk of it at the fire, and I wished I had seen the meadow.

stances.why: She is headwoman and my mother, and I will not go against her, even over Godric.
A man with no boat has nothing to offer; I mean to have one before I marry.
Hreod Toller is my friend, and the quarrel over the meadow is between the headwomen and the elders, not the children.

sheet.narrative: I gather reeds with my mother and help her at the common bake, and I know the names of the birds on the reeds. I am afraid of the wolves that come down to the reeds in winter, and I keep close to the fire. When Wren Stave comes down from Thornby we play by the shingle, and when the cough is bad my mother gives me a packet of herbs to hold.
values: the birds and the reed beds
staying close when the wolves come
goals: help my mother at the bake without spilling the flour
see Wren Stave when the Thornby folk come
learn the birds' names from my father
be brave about the wolves

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the cook-fire and the bake, and she smells of bread and herbs.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: father
relations.note: He fishes the reeds and tells me the birds' names, and he says the wolves keep to the far banks.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He is older and goes out in the boat, and he says he will look out for me.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She comes down from Thornby and we play on the shingle; she is afraid of the north light and I am afraid of the wolves.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She's the headwoman and everyone listens to her, even Father; she smells of reeds and she's too busy to play, but she once gave me a honey cake at the bake.

memories.gist: I helped my mother at the common bake and spilled the flour, and she laughed and let me shape a little loaf of my own.
My father took me out to the reed beds and showed me the birds' nests, and I counted seven.
A wolf came down to the reeds one night and I heard it, and my mother held me by the fire until morning.

sheet.narrative: I keep the dairy and work the Lakemead strips, same as my mother did, though the meadow was never ours to hold. Jem pays Nell Sedge rent in grain and cheese, and this year the grain is thin and the cheese is carrying us. Elmwick men have pulled our fence down twice, and I mend it with Jem and say nothing, because Rowan Wray is still my friend and I will not make her choose. I count what we owe every night before I sleep.
values: not letting the quarrel poison old friendships
goals: make up the grain rent with cheese and labour before Nell Sedge loses patience
keep the fence standing through the winter
keep her friendship with Rowan Wray despite Elmwick and Reedmoor
see Cedda safe and not walking roads with a pedlar's packs

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He carries the worry with me, and he mends the fence without complaining.

relations.name: Cedda Coombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is quick and brave and I do not want her on the east road with a pedlar.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: son
relations.note: He follows the goats and is afraid of the reeds; I keep him close.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: She has not pressed us, but the tally is short and she holds the meadow.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: I carry cheese to her table and she does not ask too many questions.

relations.name: Rowan Wray
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Elmwick or not, she is my friend, and I will not let this quarrel take her.

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She has a right to be angry about her nets, but I miss the Elmwick fish.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: pedlar
relations.note: He brings fish and stories, and I am not ready to let Cedda go with him.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He keeps the bees and the old tally, and he remembers when the meadow was common.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: quarrel
relations.note: His men pulled our fence down twice; I will not forget it.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: landlord's brother
relations.note: He fishes the reed beds for Nell and grumbles that we owe her grain; I keep my head down and my cheese ready when he comes by.

memories.gist: The first time Elmwick men pulled the fence down, Jem and I rebuilt it in the rain while Cedda held the posts.
Rowan Wray and I traded cheese and smoked fish at the Ferncross market before the quarrel, and she laughed at my city ways.
The Lean Year came and the meadow grain was thin, and Nell Sedge said nothing about the rent, which was worse than shouting.
Osric was born in the dairy in a hard frost, and Hilda Sedge came with blankets and barley broth.
The second fence-pulling, when the Elmwick men trampled Rill's nets and I found her crying by the lake.

stances.why: The tally is short and Nell has not pressed us; that is a kindness I will not abuse.
It is our living and our dairy, and I will mend the fence as often as they pull it down.
Rowan Wray is not her village's fence-pullers, and I will not lose her over Hob Garrow's temper.
Cedda is too young for the east road, and Osric is afraid of the reeds; I keep them near.
If the grain will not come, the cheese will, and Hilda Sedge pays fair.

sheet.secret: She has been selling a little more cheese than Jem knows, and hiding the marks in the thatch against the day Nell takes the meadow back.

sheet.narrative: I help with the goats and the fence, and I am not afraid of the Elmwick men, only of what they do to the fence. Thistle Mossfoot comes through the meadow with his packs and tells me about Fernhollow and the giants' shelf, and I have already told Thea Wray I am going to see it. Mother says I am too young, but I am eleven and I can walk.
goals: walk a stretch of the east road with Thistle Mossfoot's packs
see Fernhollow and the giants' shelf
keep the goats from straying into the reeds

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She says I am too young for the road, but she has not forbidden it outright.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: father
relations.note: He half-promised I could walk with Thistle when the packs are light.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is afraid of the reeds; I hold his hand at the meadow edge.

relations.name: Thea Wray
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is Elmwick, but she is my friend, and I told her I am going to Fernhollow.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: pedlar
relations.note: He tells the best stories of the hollow and the giants' shelf.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the meadow edge and she is not afraid of the reeds like Osric.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He keeps the bees and the rent tally and tells me how the meadow was grazed by Elmwick and Reedmoor both, long before it was let; I sit with him when the fence wants mending.

memories.gist: The Elmwick men came and pulled the fence down, and I hid behind the goat shed until they were gone.
Thistle Mossfoot opened his pack and showed me a fernhollow salve and a fish smoked in the east, and I decided I would go.
I told Thea Wray I was going to see Fernhollow, and she said she would come if her father let her.
Helping Jem mend the fence the second time, holding the posts straight while he hammered.

stances.why: Thistle's stories are better than anything in the meadow, and I am not a baby.
The goats and the fence are ours, and I am old enough to help.
Thea Wray did not pull our fence down, and I will not stop being her friend.

sheet.narrative: I play at the meadow edge and follow the goats, and I do not like the deep reeds where the water is dark. When the Elmwick men shouted, I hid in the house. I like it when Merewyn Sedge comes to play.
goals: stay near the house and the goats
play with Merewyn Sedge

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps me close and I like that.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: father
relations.note: He carries me on his shoulders past the reeds.

relations.name: Cedda Coombe
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She holds my hand at the meadow edge and tells me not to be afraid.

relations.name: Merewyn Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She comes to play and is not afraid of the reeds like me.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He sits with the bees and lets me watch, and he smells of smoke and honey.

memories.gist: The Elmwick men shouted and pulled the fence down, and I hid behind the house until Jem found me.
Merewyn Sedge and I played at the meadow edge with the goats until the sun went down.

sheet.narrative: I have fished these reed channels since I was a boy, and I know every cut and pool of them better than the palm of my hand. My father kept the village nets before me, and I keep them now: mended, tarred and counted, so that no man of Reedmoor goes out with a hole in his mesh. The works at Kettlebridge send their smoke down the valley on an east wind and it lies on the reeds like a grey blanket; I have said so at the cook-fire more than once. Leofrun and I have raised one son, Godric, who is a better fisherman than I was at his age, and I would see him settled with a boat and a wife before I am too stiff to help him get it.
values: the village's nets and traps kept whole
Reedmoor feeding itself from the reeds and the shore
my son settled with a boat of his own
fair dealing with the traders who come for our fish
goals: keep the village nets and traps in repair through the winter
see Godric's courtship of Wyn Sedge come to a match
put by enough smoked fish to trade for grain when the barley runs short
have my say about the smoke that drifts down from Kettlebridge
sheet.mood: steady, a little worn, quietly stubborn

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the plots and the tally and me; I would be lost in the reeds without her.

relations.name: Godric Wade
relations.label: son
relations.note: A better hand with a net than I was at his age. He needs a boat, and I cannot give him one.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: headwoman
relations.note: I mend her nets and she lets the Lakemead; she has not given her word about Wyn and Godric yet.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We have fished the reed beds side by side for twenty years and never once quarrelled over a pool.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: good-sister
relations.note: She cooks for the village and keeps Leofrun company at the bake; a steady woman.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A hard worker and quick with the tally; she would do well in this house.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He takes our smoked fish down the shore and pays what he likes for it. A fair man, mostly.

memories.gist: My father put the village nets in my hands the summer I turned twenty, and told me a net is a promise to every boat in Reedmoor.
The Lean Year came and the barley plots failed with the blight, and we ate reed-root bread and traded our last smoked fish for a basket of Brackenford grain.
Godric came home with his first good catch off the reeds and I pretended not to be proud, and Leofrun laughed at me for it.
The Kettlebridge smoke lay on the reeds for three days last summer and the fish tasted of it; I said at the cook-fire the works should answer for it.
The Coombes took the Lakemead and pay Nell in grain, and I said at the common table that at least the meadow is being worked.

stances.why: A net is a promise to every boat in Reedmoor, and I am the one who keeps it.
It lies on the reeds and sours the fish, and they never asked us leave for it.
A fisherman with no boat is a hired hand all his life; I want better for my son.
Brannock's cart and the Fernhollow pedlar are how our fish becomes grain; cheat them and we starve.
After the Lean Year I count what is in the store before I sleep, every night.

sheet.narrative: I keep the barley plots above the reeds and the vegetable rows behind the house, and I know to the basket what they will give and what they will not. Since the Lean Year I have not trusted a full store to stay full, and I count it at night when Ethelred is asleep. I have sold barley to Brackenford's store against the debt, as we all have, and there is less left than I would like with the cough going through the village. Hilda and I nurse the sick between us, and I sit with them and think about the grain.
values: the village fed through the winter
the barley plots kept honest and counted
the sick tended, especially the children
my family's store not falling short
goals: bring the village through the cough with grain to spare
stretch the barley and roots to the spring without begging
see Godric matched with Wyn Sedge and settled
keep trading seeds with Merrow Stave so the plots do not fail

relations.name: Ethelred Wade
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He grumbles about the smoke and mends his nets, and he does not see how thin the store is getting.

relations.name: Godric Wade
relations.label: son
relations.note: He eats like a fisherman and works like one; I would see him married before the winter is out.

relations.name: Hilda Sedge
relations.label: fellow nurse
relations.note: We have sat up with half the village between us; she counts the grain the same as I do.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: headwoman
relations.note: She has not given her word about Wyn and Godric, and I would like to know what she waits for.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: seed-friend
relations.note: We trade seeds up the shore and she tells me true which strips will fail.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A good girl and a hard worker; she would keep a house well.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She works the Lakemead and trades cheese; I do not hold with the quarrel over it.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: good-brother
relations.note: He brings his catch to the cook-fire and his troubles with it.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I measured out the last of the barley in cupfuls and told no one how little was left.
I carried a basket of our barley to Brackenford's store against the debt and came home with a receipt and an empty sack.
Godric was small and I taught him the planting songs in the plot above the reeds, and he still hums them when he rows out.
I sat up three nights with a reed-cutter's child through a fever with Hilda, and the child lived.
The cough came into the reeds this autumn and I heard it in the next house before I heard it in mine.

stances.why: The Lean Year taught me that a full store is a story people tell themselves.
Hilda and I are the ones who can, and a village that lets its sick lie is no village.
It is owed, and a debt unpaid comes back at the gate with guards behind it.
She is steady and hard-working, and a match would settle him.
Elmwick and the Coombes can argue; I need the meadow's cheese and not its quarrel.

sheet.secret: She has quietly held back a small jar of barley in the roof thatch, against a winter she fears more than she says.

sheet.narrative: I fish the deep water off the reeds from my father's boat, and every time I row out I am thinking of the day I will row out in my own. I have courted Wyn Sedge since the spring and we suit each other, but her mother has not given her word, and I know why: a man with no boat is a poor bargain.
