I owe Brannock Sedge for a share of a net and I mean to pay it before I ask Nell for anything. The cough is in the village and my mother counts the grain at night; I fish harder for it.
values: the catch brought home whatever the weather
goals: save enough marks to buy a boat of my own
pay Brannock Sedge for the net share
win Nell Sedge's word for the match with Wyn
keep fishing through the winter so the house does not go short

relations.name: Ethelred Wade
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the channels and the nets; he would give me a boat if he had one to give.

relations.name: Leofrun Wade
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She counts the store at night and thinks I do not see; I fish harder for it.

relations.name: Wyn Sedge
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: We have walked the shingle since spring and I would marry her tomorrow if her mother said the word.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: headwoman
relations.note: She has not given her word, and I know it is the boat she is waiting on.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for a share of a net and he has not pressed me, which is its own kind of pressing.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: friend's father
relations.note: He has taken me out in the flat boat and shown me the reed pools; a good man to learn from.

memories.gist: My father put the oars in my hands on the reed channel the summer I turned twelve and let me row the whole way home.
The Lean Year: I was a boy and I remember the reed-root bread and my mother measuring barley in cupfuls.
I brought home my first good catch off the deep water and my father pretended not to be proud, and my mother laughed at him.
Wyn and I walked the shingle at low tide in the spring and she said she did not mind waiting for a boat, and I minded for her.
Brannock Sedge sold me a share of a net on a handshake and I have not paid him yet; it sits on me like a stone.

stances.why: A fisherman who crews for others is never his own man, and Wyn's mother knows it.
Brannock gave me the net on a handshake and I will not have it said I did not pay.
The cough is in the village and my mother counts the grain; the catch is what stands between us and a thin spring.
I will not take Wyn without her mother's blessing, however long it takes.
The deep water off the reeds is where the money is, and my father's channels only take me so far.

villages.name: Coldwell
villages.character: The old Coldwell steading in the woods by the stone road between Brackenford and Kettlebridge
villages.ledger: Coldwell. These houses were built by Hales and Coldwells. The fields beyond the beck were ours.

sheet.narrative: I am eleven and I have been coughing since the spring, so I lie by the fire most days and watch the smoke go up the chimney. I want to go out with Uncle Ned and see the road, but Mother looks at me strangely when I ask. The house is always full of people and talk, and I know the woods around Coldwell better than I know anything else.
values: the fire and the warm corner
goals: to stop coughing and be let out of the house
to go with Uncle Ned on the road one day
to see what is past the trees at the field edge

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She sits by me when the coughing is bad and her hands are cold; I wish she would not look at me like that.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He tells me about the garden before the Lean Year and lets me hold the seed basket.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He says he will take me out when I am strong, and he always smells of the road.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She keeps the pot going and puts the warmest bit in my bowl.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: the sister who nursed me
relations.note: I remember her hands and a bitter drink last winter; Mother speaks well of her.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: He is quiet and watches the road, and he showed me how to hold a stick like a sword.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She used to bring honey cakes when she visited Coldwell before, and Mother says she is my aunt and works at the inn in the town, but I have not seen her since the fever and I wonder if she would still know me.

memories.gist: The winter I had the fever, and a sister in grey came out from the town and sat with me three nights.
Before the Lean Year, running the field boundary with the dog while the men cut the last of the grain.
The day the town men came and said the fields were the store's now, and Mother stood in the door and would not move.
Lying by the fire this spring, hearing Uncle Ned and Hob Ferrier talk about the carts on the road and what they would do.

stances.why: When I am ill the fire is the only warm thing, and everyone gathers round it.
He is always out and always comes back with something.

sheet.narrative: I am Marta Hale and these are my fields, whatever the town ledger says. When the blight came we borrowed grain like everyone, and when we could not pay the Reeve took the land and set the Tolleys on it, and then called us outlaws for staying in our own houses. So we stay, and we take a share from the carriers on the stone road, and I hold this house together with what my brother and the others bring in. My son is coughing and thin and I would beg at the gate for him, but I will not be seen doing it.
values: not being made a beggar at the gate
goals: to get Robin well
to get the fields back, or a pardon, or enough to live on
to keep Ned from doing something that brings the guards down on us
to see the Tolleys off my land without harming them

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is all I have left of his father, and the cough will not let go of him.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He does the hard things for us and I am grateful, but he wants to meet the next cart with more men and I have not said yes.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: younger sister
relations.note: She brings what she can by the south gate; I do not ask her to risk more and I tell no one where it comes from.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He works the old garden patch and will not speak of the Tolleys, which suits me.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She keeps the common pot and has been leaving food at a woodpile in Ferncross; I have guessed and said nothing.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: one of mine
relations.note: A quay guard who ran from the Surge and fights better than any of us; I do not ask what he ran from.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: one of mine
relations.note: A boy who came off the works with nothing; I have taken him in as my own and I do not press him about where he came from.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He keeps us in meat and knows the woods, but he and Ned have been walking the field edge and I have told them to stay off it.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: the tenant on my land
relations.note: He farms my fields for the Guild and has asked Mercy Abbot for stone to build a wall round the yard, and the Guild has sent none.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She holds the lease of my fields and put her tenants on them, and she smiles and talks of trade.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve who outlawed us
relations.note: He took the land for the store and set the gate against us; I will not forget it.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: the sister who nursed Robin
relations.note: She came out to Coldwell in winter when no one else would, and I have sent word through Sayer asking her for medicine again.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Agnes's boy, and he has his mother's face; I would not have him know what his father's gate does to us.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: tenant's wife
relations.note: She keeps my house and works my soil and fears me for it, and I cannot say she is wrong to.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He pays the due and curses it, and he carries stone past our door; Ned has taken his loads twice and he comes armed now.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: He is my sister's husband and he takes the due at the south gate in the Reeve's name; I am civil to him for Agnes's sake and no more.

memories.gist: The Lean Year, borrowing grain from the town store against the next harvest like everyone in the north.
The day the Reeve's men read out that our fields were the store's, and the Tolleys came to look at them.
Being declared outlaw at the gate, and coming home to Coldwell and deciding we would not go.
Sister Elspeth sitting three nights with Robin through the fever last winter, and leaving herbs and a prayer.
The second time Ned and the others took a share from a carrier on the stone road by force, and the fear afterwards that the guards would come.
Walking the field boundary where the Tolleys could see me, and saying nothing.

stances.why: We were not paid for them and we will not be starved off them.
Harming the Tolleys would lose us any hope of a pardon, so I have told Ned and Hob to stay off the fields.
What the carriers give keeps the house fed, but a hard robbery will bring the guards down on us all.
She came out to us in winter when no one else in the town would.
I will ask for my son through others, but I will not stand at the gate with my hand out.

sheet.narrative: I am seventy and I have farmed this ground since before the town kept a ledger of it. My son is dead and his wife Marta holds the house now, and I do not quarrel with how she holds it; I work the old garden patch behind the house and keep the seed and the baskets. I remember the Lean Year and I will not speak of the Tolleys, and I do not say the Reeve's name in this house if I can help it. The boy is the future of the name and I mean to see him grow.
values: the name of Hale on this ground
goals: to keep the garden patch yielding
to see Robin grow strong
to live to see the fields ours again, or at least the house kept

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: She holds the house better than my son would have; I keep out of her way and work the garden.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: He is the last of the name and he is too thin; I let him hold the seed basket and tell him the old stories.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: son-in-law's brother
relations.note: Marta's brother does the hard things and I do not like the talk of carts on the road.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: Ned's wife
relations.note: She keeps the pot and is kind enough, though she is not of this house by blood.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He took the fields for the store and called us outlaws for staying in our houses; I will not say his name in this house.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: the tenant
relations.note: He walks my son's furrows; I will not speak of him.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He hunted for this steading before the Lean Year and still brings meat, but he is too fond of the road.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: daughter-in-law's sister
relations.note: She married a gate guard, but she is still Coldwell at heart and brings what she can.

memories.gist: Farming this ground with my son before the Lean Year, and the barn full at harvest.
The Lean Year, and borrowing grain from the town store like the rest of the north.
The day the Reeve's men read the fields forfeit and the Tolleys came to look them over.
My son's burial, and Marta standing at the grave with the boy in her arms.
Working the old garden patch this spring, setting seed and mending baskets, because a man must do something.

stances.why: The patch behind the house still feeds us and a man must keep doing something.
Hale blood has farmed here since before the ledger, and I will not be the one to leave.
I remember the Lean Year and I will not speak of the Tolleys or the Reeve to anyone.
Robin is the last of the name and he is too thin; everything else can wait.

sheet.narrative: I was a quay guard in Lanternquay until the Surge took the lower quay and half the people I knew. I walked away from the guard after that, and I have been at Coldwell ever since, doing what needs doing. Marta keeps us fed and Ned keeps us angry; I keep my head down and my hands ready. I fight better than the rest of them, and I do not talk about the sea.
values: keeping my word to the people I stand with
goals: see the Coldwell business settled without a hanging
keep Pell from doing something foolish
stay useful enough that nobody asks where I came from

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She took me in when I had nothing and asks no questions. I follow her, not Ned.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: brother-in-arms
relations.note: He is all noise and no plan. I will stand beside him if it comes to it, but I will not swing first for him.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: household
relations.note: She feeds us and worries about all of us. She is the only calm thing in this house.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: the boy
relations.note: He is hiding something from Kettlebridge. I have not pressed him, and I will not.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: mother
relations.note: I sent word I am alive. She will not forgive me for the worry, but she knows now.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We grew up on the same quay. If she came up the road with a cart, I would not know what to say to her.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He pays the due and hates it. He is not the enemy; the due is.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due at the south gate. He is Agnes's husband, so Marta will not touch him. I keep my distance.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: the boy
relations.note: He coughs all night; I've carried him to the fire more than once.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She'd have me up for desertion if she caught me; still, she's fair.

memories.gist: The night the surge came, I was on the lower quay and pulled two children out of the water, and could not reach a third. I have not been back to the quay since.
Walking away from the quay guard at dawn with my kit on my back, and not looking back at the lanterns.
Marta found me on the Coldwell road in the rain and gave me a bowl of Sayer's pot without asking my name.
The first time Ned took me with him to meet a cart, I talked the carter down and Ned was furious. Marta said I had done right.
Writing a few lines to my mother and giving them to a pedlar to carry south, not knowing if they would reach her.

stances.why: A fight on the road is how people get hanged, and I have seen enough hanging.
A carter will give a share sooner than he will give his life, and a share keeps us fed without a body on the road.
She took me in when I had nothing. I will not be the one who walks away from her.
The boy is young and hiding something. Whatever it is, it is not worth his neck.
I have not been back to the quay since the surge, and I do not mean to.

sheet.secret: I sent word to my mother in Lanternquay that I am alive, through a pedlar, and told no one here.

sheet.narrative: I was a Coldwell farmer before the Lean Year, and I will be one again or I will die trying. The town took our fields and let them to the Tolleys, and now the same town sends its carts past our door as if we were not here. Marta says wait; I say the carriers owe us for what was taken. I do the talking on the road, and I am not gentle about it.
values: a man who will not fight for his own is nothing
not being made a fool of
goals: stop the next cart on the stone road and take a proper share
see the Tolleys off the Coldwell fields
keep Robin alive through the winter
get a pardon, or enough to live on, on our terms

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is the eldest and she leads, but she has gone cautious since Robin's fever. Someone has to be the iron in this house.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the pot going and says little. She said the kindling came from a pedlar. I half believe her.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Marta's boy. He coughs all night and I would burn the town for him.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: brother-in-arms
relations.note: He fights better than any of us, but he talks when he should swing. Still, I would have him at my back.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: the boy
relations.note: A runaway from the foundry. He is hiding something, and I do not trust a closed mouth.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He knows the woods and he hates the Tolleys as much as I do. He has walked the field edge with me twice.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He sits in our barn and farms our fields and calls it his. He had his chance to walk away.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He pays the due and carries on. Twice we have taken from him, and twice he has come back with guards.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She married a gate guard and lives in town, and I do not hold it against her. She is still our Agnes.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He took our fields and outlawed us at the gate. I would not spit on him if he were on fire.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He's my father's brother's widower and Robin's grandsire; he still digs the old garden patch and won't say the Tolleys' name, which suits me.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He blames us for his snares and skulks at the wood edge; a soft farmer who won't come in after us, so let him bleat.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She holds the lease on our fields and set the Tolleys in our barn; she's the Reeve with a softer voice.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: farmer
relations.note: He sells grain to the town store that fed off our fields, and his brother's snare talk comes from his table.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: He's married to my sister and takes the due at the south gate; he's the town's hand on the road, and I don't forget it.

memories.gist: The day the Reeve's men came and read us outlaws at our own door, and Marta stood in the yard and would not move.
The Lean Year, when the grain came from the town store and we thought it was charity, and then the debt came due.
The first time I stopped a cart on the stone road and took a share, and the carter's face, and how easy it was.
Sitting up with Robin through a night of fever, and Sayer bringing wet cloths, and thinking he might not see morning.
Walking the edge of the old fields with Hob Ferrier and looking at the Tolleys' barn, and wanting to burn it.

stances.why: They pay the due to the town that took our fields. A share of their loads is the least we are owed.
Asking has got us nothing and Marta's caution has got us less. More men on the road will make the carters listen.
The Tolleys sit in a barn my family raised. Marta forbade me to touch them, but I have not promised to keep obeying.
Robin is sick and the winter is coming. Whatever else happens, the boy eats.
Pell keeps his own counsel, and a man who will not say what he is hiding is a risk to the rest of us.

sheet.narrative: I keep the Coldwell kitchen and the common pot, and I try to keep the peace in a house full of angry men. I was not born to the woods; I married into the Hales and I have stayed. The guards at the gate frighten me more than the wolves do, and I count the days until Robin's cough breaks. I leave a little food at a woodpile now and then, and I do not tell Ned.
goals: see Robin well again
keep Ned from doing something that gets him hanged
keep the household fed through the winter
keep my small errand to myself

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is angry at the world and I love him, but I do not tell him everything. He would mock me or worse.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: She carries the whole household and does not complain. I would do anything for her and Robin.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: He has coughed since the spring and got thin. I keep him warm and fed and I am afraid the winter will finish him.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: household
relations.note: He is quiet and steady and does not frighten me like the others do. He keeps his own counsel.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: the boy
relations.note: He is young and out of place here. I put a bowl in front of him and ask nothing.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: the sister
relations.note: She came through the snow to sit up with Robin and asked for nothing. I do not know what we would have done.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: I carried word to her at the inn. She will help if she can, but the guards must not hear of it.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He farms what was ours and has asked the Guild for a guard. I fear him less than I fear Ned meeting him.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He brings meat but he's rough, and I don't like the way he looks at the Tolley barn.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He's bent and bitter and won't say the Tolleys' name, but he still works that garden patch and he's kind to Robin; I take him his bowl and let him talk about the old days.

memories.gist: The night Sister Elspeth came through the snow to Coldwell and sat up with Robin, and I made her tea and did not know what to say.
The day we were read outlaws at the gate, and Ned's face, and knowing we would not go back inside the walls.
Carrying word to Agnes at the inn in Brackenford and being afraid the whole way that a guard would stop me.
Leaving a little bread and cheese at the woodpile of a Ferncross widow, and finding kindling at our kitchen door a few days later.
Ned asking where the kindling came from, and me saying a pedlar, and him half believing it.

stances.why: Whatever else happens, everyone in this house eats, and Robin eats first.
The gate guards frighten me more than the wolves. If they come for us, we have nowhere to run.
A little food at a woodpile costs nothing and makes the woods less cold. I do not need Ned to understand it.
He is angry enough already. I say a pedlar brought the kindling and let it lie.
Sister Elspeth came through the snow for Robin and asked nothing of outlaws. I would go to her again if I could.

sheet.secret: I have been quietly leaving food at the woodpile of a Ferncross woodcutter's widow, and she leaves kindling for our kitchen in return. Ned has noticed the kindling and I told him a pedlar brought it.

sheet.narrative: I was bound to Josiah Crane's foundry at fourteen and learned fire there — how to read a bloom, how to keep a tuyere from slagging, how a bellows breathes. A month before my indenture was out I walked off the poor terrace and kept walking until the woods took me in. Kai found me on the stone road half-starved and brought me to Coldwell, and here I am: an outlaw with a foundry in his hands and no paper to prove he was ever anything else. There is a letter sewn in my coat that I have not shown anyone, not even Kai.
values: keeping my own fire and my own name
paying back the people who took me in
never being owned by a contract again
goals: stay out of Crane's reach until the indenture is forgotten
make myself useful enough at Coldwell that nobody asks where I came from
learn to fight properly from Kai

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He pulled me off the road and never once asked what I was running from. I would stand beside him against anything.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She took me in when she had no reason to. I keep her fire and her tools and I do not make her regret it.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: household
relations.note: He is loud and rough on the road, but he is the one who taught me which end of a stave to hold.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: household
relations.note: She slips me an extra bowl when the pot is thin and never says a word about it.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: housemate
relations.note: He knows the woods like a priest knows his prayers. I go out with him for wood and keep my mouth shut.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: elder
relations.note: He talks about the old garden patch and the Lean Year and I listen. He does not ask me about Kettlebridge.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: old master
relations.note: He owns my years on paper. Every time I hear a cart on the stone road I think it is him come to collect.

relations.name: Barnaby Quill
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: The Council's scribe writes the indentures. If anyone can read me back into that foundry it is him.

relations.name: Robin Hale
relations.label: the boy
relations.note: He is small and still coughs from the winter. I keep the fire high for him.

memories.gist: The day I walked off the poor terrace with my apron still on and my hands black to the wrist, and did not look back at the works chimneys.
Kai finding me on the stone road, giving me half a loaf and saying Coldwell had room for one more.
Marta putting a mallet and a pair of tongs in my hands and telling me to keep the common fire banked through the night.
The night the letter came up the road and I read the seal by the fire and put it in my coat and said nothing.
Learning at the foundry to judge a bloom by its colour — cherry, then straw, then grey — and being proud of it.

stances.why: A written indenture made me a thing that could be fetched back; I would rather live in the woods on roots than sign another.
The common fire is the one thing I am trusted with here, and a cold hearth would send me back out on the road.
He is the only person since the foundry who wanted me for nothing.
If Marta knew Crane's people were asking after me she might send me on for the household's sake, and I have nowhere else.

sheet.secret: The letter from Barnaby Quill asking after him on the Coldwell road is sewn into his coat; he has told no one, not Kai, and the indenture paper is folded inside it.

sheet.narrative: I hunted these woods for the steading before the Lean Year, and I hunt them still — only now the meat goes into a common pot that is not mine, in a house that is not mine, on land that was. The Tolleys sleep in the barn I raised, and the Guild counts rent off my father's fields. I walk the edge of those fields so Hal Tolley can see me do it. Marta says keep off the tenants; I have kept off them so far.
values: my own hands and my own bow
not being made a beggar on my own ground
goals: see the Tolleys off the Coldwell fields one way or another
keep the household in meat through the winter
get a pardon, or a field, or at least a reckoning

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She has held us together since the fields went. I mind her word — mostly.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: hunting partner
relations.note: We hunt together and we think alike about the Tolleys. He is the only one who does not preach at me.

relations.name: Kai Ostrander
relations.label: housemate
relations.note: A quay man, but he can fight and he does not flinch. I would take him into the woods any day.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: housemate
relations.note: A foundry boy with soft hands. He is learning the woods slow, but he carries a load without complaining.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: household
relations.note: She cooks what I bring and never asks where the hides go. That is worth something.

relations.name: Aldwin Hale
relations.label: old neighbour
relations.note: He remembers the steading whole, same as me. We do not talk about the Tolleys in front of the young ones.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: tenant
relations.note: He sleeps in my barn and calls it his. He will not sleep easy while I am in these woods.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: Her Guild holds the lease on my fields and sends its tenants to farm them. She has never once come out to see what she took.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: accuser
relations.note: He says I stole his hides. His snare line was cut by someone, and it was not me, but he will not hear it.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He declared us outlaws at the gate over fields he had already taken. I would not piss on him if he were burning.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: tenant's wife
relations.note: She keeps the house that was ours and puts a wall up round the yard as if she had built it.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: Hedric's brother
relations.note: Osbert has never said a hard word to my face, but he is Hedric's brother and he farms the meadows that look down on our old fields. He believes what his brother tells him about the hides, I reckon, and he sells grain to the same store that

memories.gist: The Lean Year, when the blight took the berries and the Reeve's grain came with a ledger and a price we could not pay.
The day the Guild's men came and read us out of our fields, and the Tolleys walked in behind them with their carts.
Raising the Coldwell barn with my own hands, beam by beam, the year my father died.
Walking the field edge with Ned while Hal Tolley watched us from the barn door, and saying nothing at all.
Selling hides at Ferncross in the dark and being asked no questions, which is how I like it.
Finding Hedric Ashby's snare line cut and empty, and knowing he would put it on me before he had even looked at the ground.

stances.why: My father worked that ground and I raised its barn; no ledger makes it the Guild's.
They took a farm that was already lived in and call themselves tenants. I will not pretend otherwise.
Meat in the pot and hides at Ferncross keep us alive, and the less the road knows of it the better.
She has kept us from being taken so far, and I owe her that, even when her word galls me.
A pardon from the man who outlawed us would be a leash. I would rather be hunted than owned.

villages.name: Ashby
villages.character: Farms in the meadows near Brackenford
villages.ledger: Ashby. Farmed for the Market Guild of Brackenford.

sheet.narrative: I farm the old Coldwell fields on the Guild's lease, and I've earned every furrow. The Hales had their chance to stay and pay like the rest of us; they chose outlawry instead. Now they come to the field edge at night, and I'm done waiting for Mercy Abbot's stone. I keep my son watching from the barn and my wife behind the door.
goals: Get a stone wall built around the yard
Keep the Hales off the fields
Make the farm pay enough to keep the lease
See my children safe and settled

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: She holds the lease I farm, but she's left me to face the Hales alone.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: threat
relations.note: She wants these fields back, and I won't give them up.

relations.name: Marta Tolley
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the house and wants a wall as much as I do.

relations.name: Tib Tolley
relations.label: son
relations.note: He watches from the barn and knows the fields as well as I do.

relations.name: Nell Tolley
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's afraid of the woods, and I can't blame her.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He took the fields from the Hales and let them to the Guild; I just farm them.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good neighbour; he sells grain and keeps to his own.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: He's the one who does the threatening on the road.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: He's been at the field edge with Ned, looking at my barn.

memories.gist: The day I signed the lease with Mercy Abbot for the old Coldwell fields, thinking I'd finally have land of my own.
Seeing Ned Hale and Hob Ferrier at the edge of the field at dusk, just standing and looking.
Asking Mercy Abbot for stone to build a wall, and getting nothing but words.
The Lean Year, when the blight came and we all went hungry until the town store lent grain.
Teaching Tib to watch from the barn and count the men in the woods.

stances.why: The Guild leased them to me fair and square, and I've worked them.
They refused to give up their houses and took to the road; that makes them outlaws.
Words won't stop men at night; stone will.
My wife and children are all I've got.
I pay rent to the Guild; they should keep me safe.

sheet.narrative: I keep the wood edge for the Ashby fields, and I know every snare line on it by heart. Last week I found my best line cut and emptied, and I know whose boots have been on that path — Coldwell boots, and Hob Ferrier's besides. Osbert tells me to let it lie and keep the peace; I say a man who lets his snares be taken will lose his fields next. I carry my bow on the edge now, and I mean to have what is mine back or its worth in marks.
values: a debt unpaid is an insult
goals: Get back my snares or their value from the Coldwell people
Prove Hob Ferrier sold my hides at Ferncross
Keep the wolves and the outlaws off the Ashby fields
See Wren safe and taught to shoot straight

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He took me in and fed me; I wish he would take my side against Coldwell as readily.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is the whole of what I am keeping the wood edge for.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: good-sister
relations.note: She keeps a good table and asks no questions about the hides I bring in.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A steady lad, but he ploughs where I would hunt.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: The only man who reads a trail the way I do.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: thief
relations.note: He was at Ferncross with hides that had my snare-cuts in them.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: His people cut my line and emptied it; he can deny it to the Reeve.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: She leads them and she knows what her brother does on the road.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A Guild tenant with a barn, and no more sense of the woods than a sheep.

memories.gist: I found my best snare line cut and empty near the Coldwell boundary, the wire coiled and taken.
At Ferncross market I saw Hob Ferrier with a bundle of hides, and one had the notch of my own knife in it.
Beorn Beornson and I tracked a wolf pair along the wood edge all one cold morning and took both.
When the Lean Year came I brought in enough venison that the Ashby table never went short.
Wren asked me to teach her the bow, and I cut her a small one from a hazel stave.

stances.why: A snare line is a man's work and his meat; to cut it is to steal twice over.
Since the snare was cut I will not walk the wood edge unarmed.
They took from me and the Reeve does nothing; someone must make them answer.
Osbert is my brother and I will not shame him at his own table, whatever I think of his softness.
A girl who knows the paths and the bow will never be at a stranger's mercy.

sheet.secret: I have gone once to the Coldwell boundary at dusk with my bow, meaning to make Ned Hale speak to me, and came away without knocking. I have told no one, not even Osbert.

sheet.narrative: I live in the Ashby house with my father and my uncle's family, and I know the hens by name and the way to the wood edge by heart. Father lets me carry his spare bowstring and sometimes his snares, and I am learning to set them without tangling. Nell Tolley is my friend though she is afraid of the woods, and I tell her there is nothing in them worse than a wolf, and Father can shoot a wolf.
values: the hens must be fed before me
be brave at the wood edge
goals: Learn to set a snare as well as Father does
Make Nell Tolley not afraid of the woods
See the snare line that was cut and find out who did it

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows every path and he is never afraid, and he is teaching me the bow.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He is kind and gives me bread with honey when the hens have laid well.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She lets me help with the hens and does not scold when I drop an egg.

relations.name: Tib Tolley
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He is older and knows the fields, and he tells me stories about the barn watch.

relations.name: Nell Tolley
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is afraid of the woods, so I hold her hand when we play near them.

memories.gist: Father cut me a small hazel bow and showed me how to stand sideways to the target.
I helped Aunt Edith gather the eggs and only broke one, and she laughed instead of scolding.
Nell Tolley cried at the edge of the woods and I told her Father would shoot any wolf that came.

stances.why: He knows the woods and the bow and he says the outlaws took his snares.
Nell is afraid, so someone must not be.
Aunt Edith says the hens pay for the bread.

villages.name: Highfold
villages.character: A herders' and hunters' fold in the hills between Kettlebridge and Highshelf

sheet.narrative: I am the head of the fold, and I have kept it through thin years by my bow and my word. The shelf trusts me, or did until the cairn cutting made every human suspect. I will not crawl to Kettlebridge while Hollbrenna has closed her door, but I am not blind to the store. My father's fall has made this a hard season, and I am needed at home more than on the high pastures.
goals: See the fold through the winter without begging from Kettlebridge
Keep Hollbrenna's trust and the hide trade with Orrum
Find a way to get grain without breaking the shelf's ban
Teach Soren to hunt and Jorunn to lead

relations.name: Elska Voss
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She counts the store and I count on her; I know she wants me to go to Kettlebridge, and I cannot.

relations.name: Jorunn Voss
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has my aim and my stubbornness; she will make a fine hunter, if the fold can keep her.

relations.name: Soren Voss
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is afraid of the wolves, and I was too at his age; he will learn.

relations.name: Torek Voss
relations.label: father
relations.note: His leg is bad and he hides it; I should have been here, not on the high meadows.

relations.name: Orrum
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He counts my hides twice now and asks about my timber; the cairn cutting sits between us.

relations.name: Hollbrenna
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She has always dealt straight with me, but her ban on Kettlebridge bites the fold.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A good hunter and a straight man; I would share a fire with him any night.

relations.name: Gaudra
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Elska barters barley with her; she is fair, but the shelf is wary of us all now.

relations.name: Liv
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Jorunn learns stonework from her; a steady hand with a chisel.

relations.name: Harl
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Tavvik's brother; loyal to the elder, and I respect that.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: we ate the seed barley and I swore we would never be caught so thin again.
Hollbrenna herself named me a friend of the shelf after I carried a wounded giant down from the ridge.
Jorunn's first kill, a young roe, and the look on her face when she brought it home.
The day Orrum first counted my hides twice and asked where the timber in my roof came from.
Torek's fall in the dark, and the wolves' eyes at the goat pen.

stances.why: The shelf is our neighbour and our market; I will not trade with Kettlebridge while Hollbrenna forbids it.
My family must eat before any town's pride.
I would rather hunt harder than ask for charity.
Jorunn and Soren must know the paths and the bow if the fold is to last.

sheet.narrative: I keep the fold's plots and the goats, and I have counted the store three times: it will not last the winter. Rannoch will not go to Kettlebridge while Hollbrenna says no, and Torek's leg is going bad. I have sent word to Yrsa on the shelf for a poultice, and I am not too proud to ask Fernhollow for roots. But grain is what we need, and I will find a way to get it.
goals: Get grain before the winter
Heal Torek's leg
Keep the goats safe from wolves
Persuade Rannoch that Kettlebridge is not the only answer

relations.name: Rannoch Voss
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is a good man and a stubborn one; he will not see the store is short until it is empty.

relations.name: Jorunn Voss
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is old enough to help, and I lean on her more than I should.

relations.name: Soren Voss
relations.label: son
relations.note: He sleeps by the hearth since the wolves came; I would keep him a child a while longer.

relations.name: Torek Voss
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He says the leg is nothing, but I have seen the redness; I will not let him lose it.

relations.name: Gaudra
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She barters barley with me and knows the thin soil; she may have grain to spare.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She trades seeds from Thornby; a practical woman.

relations.name: Yrsa
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She knows poultices and herbs; I have sent to her for Torek.

relations.name: Hollbrenna
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She is wise, but her ban on Kettlebridge may starve us.

relations.name: Orrum
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He is wary of us now; I do not blame him, but I need his grain.

memories.gist: The Lean Year, when we ate the seed barley and I swore never to be short again.
Counting the store this autumn and finding it short by a third.
Torek's fall in the dark and the smell of the wound when I cleaned it.
Jorunn bringing home her first kill and Soren's eyes wide with pride.
Bartering barley with Gaudra on the shelf path, and her saying the shelf's store is thin too.

stances.why: A hungry winter kills; I will trade with anyone who will trade fairly.
Torek's leg must be saved, whatever it costs in favours.
Pride does not fill a store; I will ask Fernhollow and the shelf before I let us starve.
The goats are our milk and our wool; the wolves have taken two already.

sheet.narrative: I hunt the high pastures with my father and know every trap and path of the fold. Since the cairn cutting, the shelf folk look at us sideways, and I feel it. I have offered to help Liv dress stone without pay, to prove we are still friends. I want to see Lanternquay one day, but first I want the fold to be safe and the shelf to trust us again.
goals: Prove the fold's friendship to the shelf
Learn stonework from Liv
Help my mother get grain
See Lanternquay and the tide lanterns

relations.name: Rannoch Voss
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the bow and the paths; I would follow him anywhere.

relations.name: Elska Voss
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries about the store and Torek; I help where I can.

relations.name: Soren Voss
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is afraid of the wolves; I tell him stories to make him brave.

relations.name: Torek Voss
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: His leg is bad and he hides it; I bring him water and listen to his stories.

relations.name: Liv
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: She is teaching me to dress stone; I offered to help without pay to show the fold is a friend.

relations.name: Harl
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is loyal to the elder and uneasy about Tavvik's trade; I like him for it.

relations.name: Orrum
relations.label: elder's son
relations.note: He counts our hides twice now; I feel his coolness.

relations.name: Hollbrenna
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She is wise and slow to speak; I want her to trust us again.

relations.name: Gaudra
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She trades seeds with my mother; a steady woman.

relations.name: Vellmund
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Orrum's son; he is learning stonework too, and we talk of the ridge.

memories.gist: My first kill, a young roe, and my father's nod when I brought it home.
The day the cairn was cut, and the shelf folk turning their backs on us at the market.
Offering Liv to help dress stone without pay, and her surprise.
Soren waking from a dream of wolves and crawling to the hearth.
Harl showing me the cairn on the ridge from a distance and saying it must never be moved.

stances.why: The shelf's coolness stings; I will show them we are not like the quarrymen.
Stone is the shelf's craft, and Liv is willing to teach me.
My father, mother, brother and grandfather are my fold.
I have heard of Lanternquay and the tide lanterns, and I want to see them.

sheet.narrative: I help my father skin and smoke the catch and my mother with the goats. Since the wolves came up the track and took two goats, I am afraid to go out alone. I sleep by the hearth now, and I follow Grandfather about the yard. I dream of the shelf and the stone blocks and the giants' slow voices.
goals: Be brave like my father and sister
See the shelf and the stone blocks again
Keep the goats safe

relations.name: Rannoch Voss
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is strong and brave; I want to be like him.

relations.name: Elska Voss
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She makes the hurt better and keeps me warm.

relations.name: Jorunn Voss
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She tells me stories to make me brave.

relations.name: Torek Voss
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He tells the old stories of the shelf and lets me help with the snares.

relations.name: Vellmund
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is a giant boy who plays with me when the giants come down.

memories.gist: The wolves at the goat pen and the eyes in the dark.
Grandfather's fall and the blood on his leg.
Playing with Vellmund among the stone blocks on the shelf.

stances.why: The wolves are out there, and the hearth is safe.
I am old enough to skin and smoke and carry water.
My father is not afraid, and I want to be like him.

sheet.narrative: I am too stiff for the high hunt now, but I keep the fold's snares and tell the old stories of the shelf. I fell in the dark setting snares for the wolves and my leg is bad, though I say it is nothing. I remember the Lean Year and the wolves after it, and I fear a hungry winter more than I fear the giants' displeasure. I have said so at the table.
goals: See the fold through the winter
Heal my leg
Keep the wolves from the goats
Pass the old stories to Soren and Jorunn

relations.name: Rannoch Voss
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is a good head of the fold, but he will not see the store is short.

relations.name: Elska Voss
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: She cleans my leg and does not flinch; she is the best of us.

relations.name: Jorunn Voss
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: She has the old skill with a bow; I tell her the stories.

relations.name: Soren Voss
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: He is afraid, and I do not blame him; I was too, after the Lean Year.

relations.name: Steinar
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We are both old and stiff, and we remember the same winters.

relations.name: Hollbrenna
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She is right about the cairn, but her ban may starve us.

relations.name: Orrum
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He is wary of us now; I understand it, but it chills me.

relations.name: Gaudra
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She grows what she can on the thin soil; she may have grain.

memories.gist: The Lean Year, when the wolves came down and we ate the seed barley.
The cairn cutting, and Hollbrenna's face when she heard.
Falling in the dark while setting snares, and the shame of it.
Telling Soren the old stories of the shelf by the hearth.
Steinar and I sharing a fire on the shelf path, both too stiff to hunt.

stances.why: I have seen the Lean Year; hunger kills more than pride.
The cairns are not to be moved, and the stories must be told.
A man who cannot walk is a burden; I will not be a burden.
We need grain, and I do not care whose town it comes from.

villages.name: Sootwood
villages.character: Woodcutters and charcoal burners in the old forest above Lanternquay

sheet.narrative: I've cut oak and ash in Sootwood since I was a boy, and the slow pits have burned under my care for thirty years. The quay builders take my timber, but they pay slow and the rope and tar from Bramwell Tallow is still on my tally. I say plain what I see: that seawall will never be built while Kettlebridge sets the stone price, and I won't soften it for Ostrander Vane or anyone. Now wolves have come down the old forest and chased my Durrow to the door, and I've nights to sit up with a spear I can't spare.
goals: settle the debt to Bramwell Tallow before winter
keep the wolves from the Sootwood plots
get the woodcutting back on schedule

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the plots and the goats and puts marks aside quiet; I'd be lost without her.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She stacks the pits better than many a grown hand and dreams of the harbour mouth.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: son
relations.note: The wolves chased him to the door; he's shaken and I can't blame him.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He's patient, but he's begun to ask, and I owe him for a season of rope and tar.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: quay builder
relations.note: He took my plain words about the stone price as an insult; I only spoke truth.

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She said the same about the seawall, and she's right.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet man with a long memory for debts; we understand each other.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Maren sells her roots and eggs at her stall; a sharp trader but fair enough.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Maren's close with her from the Ferncross market; I keep my distance from Coldwell folk.

relations.name: Rook Fenner the younger
relations.label: quay friend
relations.note: Taught Tace a quay knot; a decent lad off the boats.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: neighbour's boy
relations.note: Cael and Sena's lad; he and Durrow were out at the stacks when the wolves came, and he kept his head better than my boy did. I'll take him on the felling when he's a year or two older.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: we ate thin and the charcoal pits kept us alive, but I swore I'd never be caught short again.
The day Tace first stacked a pit on her own and the burn came out clean.
When the quay builders first took my timber, I thought Sootwood had a future.
The wolves chased Durrow to the door; I heard him scream and ran with the axe.
Bramwell Tallow asked me again for his marks, patient-like, and I had nothing to give.

stances.why: Marks are scarce; a load of charcoal and timber settles what coin cannot.
The stone price is a swindle and the wall will never be built; folk should hear it.
The wolves have tasted our goats and chased my son; no child goes to the stacks alone.
The work is behind and the quay pays slow; I cannot spare nights for watching.

sheet.narrative: I keep the Sootwood plots and the goats, and carry roots and charcoal down to the quay stalls when I can. Orvin owes Bramwell Tallow for rope and tar, and I've been selling eggs and roots quietly to put marks aside before winter. The smoke from our pits drifts east and I worry it sours the Fernhollow gardens, though I'd never say so to Orvin. Since the wolves came down and chased Durrow to the door, I keep the children close and sleep light.
goals: settle Orvin's debt to Bramwell before winter
keep the children safe from the wolves
put by enough marks for the cold months

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He works too hard and worries too little about the debt; I put marks aside where he won't see.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's grown quick and brave, but I wish she'd fear the woods a little more.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: son
relations.note: Since the wolves chased him he won't go to the stacks alone, and I don't make him.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He's been patient with Orvin, and I mean to see him paid before winter.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: I sell my eggs and roots at her stall; she knows the price of everything and pays fair.

relations.name: Sayer Hale
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We met at the Ferncross market and she's a good soul; I fear for her at Coldwell.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: neighbour's child
relations.note: He hid behind the stacks when the wolves came and swears he wasn't scared; I don't believe it.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet man; his smoke and ours drift the same way.

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We share the plots and the worry about the smoke; close as sisters over a fence.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: quay trade
relations.note: Buys our timber; he took Orvin's plain words amiss and I'd mend it if I could.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: we ate thin and I learned to put by every egg and root against a hard winter.
The day Durrow was chased to the door by wolves; I held him till he stopped shaking.
Meeting Sayer Hale at the Ferncross market and finding a friend in a Coldwell woman.
Selling my first basket of eggs at Perrin Tallow's stall and putting the marks in a jar.
Watching our smoke drift east and wondering if it sours the Fernhollow gardens.

stances.why: A debt hanging over us in the cold months is worse than any hunger.
The wolves have come down and taken goats; no child goes far from the door.
Marks put by a little at a time are what keep a household through winter.
Our pits smoke east and I'd not have the Fernhollow folk think us careless.

sheet.narrative: I'm fifteen and I can stack a charcoal pit and swing an axe as well as any hand in Sootwood. I want to crew on a quay boat and see the harbour mouth, and Rook Fenner the younger taught me a quay knot I practise every night. The wolves that come down the old forest in winter scare me more than I let on. With Pell and Durrow shaken by the wolves, I keep my fears to myself and help where I can.
goals: crew on a quay boat and see the harbour mouth
learn the axe and the charcoal burn properly
keep Durrow from fretting about the wolves

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the axe and the pits, and I want to make him proud.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries about me and the wolves, but she lets me learn.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: brother
relations.note: The wolves chased him and he's still scared; I try to keep him cheered.

relations.name: Rook Fenner the younger
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He taught me a quay knot and tells me about the boats; I'd like to see them for myself.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He hid behind the stacks when the wolves came and says he wasn't scared; I like his nerve.

relations.name: Tam Sedge
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He comes up the wood road with the quay folk; a good lad to talk to.

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Fells and trims with us and keeps the tally; she says the stone should come from the ridge, and I believe her.

memories.gist: The day I stacked a pit on my own and the burn came out clean; Father nodded and said nothing, which is his way.
Rook Fenner the younger showing me a quay knot and telling me about the harbour mouth.
Hearing Durrow scream when the wolves chased him and running out with the axe myself.
The Lean Year when we ate thin; I was small but I remember the hunger.

stances.why: A woodcutter's skill is what keeps Sootwood fed, and I mean to have it.
There's a whole world past the wood road, and I mean to see it.
He's my brother and the wolves have frightened him; I won't let him fret alone.
The wolves scare me, but someone in this house has to look brave.

sheet.narrative: I carry kindling and play among the charcoal stacks, and when the quay folk come up the wood road I play with Tam Sedge. The wolves chased me to the door and I was scared; Pell hid behind the stacks and kept his head, and now he says he wasn't scared at all, but I don't believe him. I don't like the deep woods now and I won't go to the kindling stacks alone.
goals: stay close to the door
play with Tam Sedge when he comes
not think about the wolves

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: father
relations.note: He ran out with the axe when the wolves came; I feel safe when he's near.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She held me till I stopped shaking.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She ran out with the axe too and tries to cheer me up.

relations.name: Tam Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He comes up the wood road with the quay folk and we play among the stacks.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He hid behind the stacks when the wolves came and says he wasn't scared; I don't believe him.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Quiet, but he came running with his axe when the wolves took the goats.

memories.gist: The wolves chased me to the door and I screamed for Father.
Playing among the charcoal stacks with Tam Sedge when the quay folk came up the road.
Carrying kindling to Mother and feeling useful.

stances.why: The wolves came once and they could come again.
I won't be chased again.
Tam's visits are the best part of the month.

sheet.narrative: I have burned the slow pits at Sootwood for more than thirty years, and my father before me, and I do not move them for a complaint that comes up the wood road. The smoke drifts east; that is the way the wind goes and always has. I keep my axe by the door now that the wolves have come down, and I keep a tally of every load that goes out and every debt that comes in, because a burner who forgets a debt is robbed twice.
goals: keep the slow pits burning through the winter
see the east-road trade with Thistle Mossfoot stay sweet
keep Pell and Sena safe from the wolves
be paid what the quay stalls owe for charcoal
sheet.mood: steady, a little grim since the wolves came down

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: partner
relations.note: She fells and trims beside me and keeps the tally straight; I would not burn without her.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: He stacks the pits well enough, but his head is full of quay boats.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good woodcutter; the wolves took two of his goats and I keep my axe near for it.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She trades at the quay stalls and Sena thinks well of her.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: neighbour's boy
relations.note: Chased to his door by the wolves; a frightened lad, and no wonder.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade
relations.note: The small-folk pedlar brings word up the east road and buys a load now and then; his complaints about smoke I hear and let pass.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Her noodle stall takes my charcoal, but she is slow to pay and quicker to talk.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: neighbour's girl
relations.note: Orvin's daughter stacks kindling with Pell; a hard worker for her age.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: A quay builder who took offence at talk of the seawall; that is Sena's affair, not mine.

memories.gist: My father showed me how to bank a slow pit so it smoulders three days and does not flame; I have banked them the same way ever since.
Wolves took two of Orvin's goats just recently; we heard them in the night and found the blood by the plots in the morning.
A carter from Kettlebridge shorted me on a load of charcoal and laughed about it; I have not forgotten the sum or the man's face.
Pell was born in the hut between the pits in a wet autumn; Sena did not stop working until the day, and started again a week after.
The smoke from the pits has drifted east over the old forest every summer of my life; the small folk have complained before and will complain again.

stances.why: The pits are old and the wood is mine to burn; I will not move them for a complaint carried up the road.
A burner who forgets a debt is robbed twice; I keep the tally in my head and in the hut.
I have seen wolves before; when the snow comes they go back up the hills, and the axe by the door is enough until then.
Thistle Mossfoot's road brings loads and word; a soured trade costs more than a little smoke.
What Sena says to the quay builders is her business; I keep to the pits and the tally.

sheet.narrative: I fell and trim beside Cael and keep the tally of every load that goes down the wood road, and I have a tongue when the tally is questioned. I told the quay folk plain that the seawall will never be built and the stone price is a swindle, and I stand by it, but I do not want the wood road's loads turned back for my saying so. I have quietly offered Thistle Mossfoot a load of charcoal to smooth the smoke complaint, and I have not told Cael the whole of it.
values: a fair price for hard work
goals: keep the quay stalls buying Sootwood charcoal and baskets
mend things with Thistle Mossfoot before the east road sours
see the seawall stone come from the ridge and not from Kettlebridge
keep Pell from the forest edge until the wolves are gone
sheet.mood: brisk and a little worried about the road

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: partner
relations.note: He keeps the pits and I keep the road and the tally; between us it works.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: He says he is not afraid of the wolves, and I hear him not playing at the forest edge.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We keep our plots side by side and trade eggs and roots; she worries about the smoke drifting east as I do.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His goats were taken and his boy chased; he has a right to be angry.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade
relations.note: I have offered him a load of charcoal to smooth the smoke complaint; a small price for a sweet road.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: neighbour's boy
relations.note: A quiet lad who plays among the stacks with Pell; the wolves have shaken him.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Her stall takes our charcoal and our baskets; she counts her marks twice and pays once.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: quarrel
relations.note: He took my words about the seawall as Sootwood siding with Kettlebridge; I meant only what I said.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: neighbour's girl
relations.note: A good worker at the pits; she and Pell are thick as thieves.

memories.gist: I told the quay builders to their faces that the seawall will never be built and the stone price is a swindle; Ostrander Vane heard it and went cold on us.
Wolves came down to the plots and took two of Orvin's goats; Durrow was chased to his door and I have kept Pell closer since.
I sold a stack of baskets at the morning stalls on the quay and came home with more marks than Cael expected; I keep half back in the hut for a lean week.
Maren Hollis and I built the goat pen together the spring before the Surge; it has stood through two hard winters.
The small folk's complaint about the smoke came up the east road with Thistle Mossfoot; I offered him a load of charcoal to smooth it and did not make a fuss about it at home.

stances.why: The ridge is ours to quarry; paying Kettlebridge's price for stone is a swindle and I say so.
The wood road carries our loads and our living; I will not have it turned back over a quarrel.
A load of charcoal to Thistle costs less than a soured east-road trade, and Cael need not be troubled with it.
The wolves have come down and taken goats; Pell stays by the stacks until they go up again.
A load unrecorded is a load unpaid; I keep the tally and I do not let it slip.

sheet.secret: I have quietly promised Thistle Mossfoot a load of charcoal to smooth the smoke complaint, and I have not told Cael the whole of it.

sheet.narrative: I stack the pits with Da and carry water and kindling, and when the work is done I watch the smoke go up and think about the quay boats. I want to see the tide lanterns at Lanternquay more than anything. I say I am not afraid of the wolves, but I do not go to the forest edge any more, and at night I listen for them.
goals: see the tide lanterns at Lanternquay
crew on a quay boat one day
not let anyone see he is afraid of the wolves
sheet.mood: restless and a little frightened underneath

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: Da teaches me the pits and keeps his axe by the door; he does not say much.

relations.name: Sena Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: Ma keeps the tally and tells me to stay by the stacks; she worries more than she says.

relations.name: Durrow Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play among the charcoal stacks; the wolves chased him to his door and he has not been the same since.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Durrow's sister; she stacks kindling and knows a quay knot she says a boy from the harbour taught her.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Durrow's da; the wolves took his goats and he is angry about it.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: pedlar
relations.note: He tells stories of the east road and the quay.

memories.gist: Da let me bank my first slow pit by myself and it held three days; he said nothing but he nodded.
Durrow was chased to his door by the wolves and I heard him shouting; since then I stay by the stacks.
A quay man came up the wood road once and told me about the tide lanterns and the boats; I have wanted to see them ever since.

stances.why: Boats and lanterns and the harbour mouth; I will see them one day.
I say so, and I mean to make it true, but I keep by the stacks for now.

villages.name: Lakemead
villages.character: The disputed meadow farm by the southern lake

sheet.narrative: I hold the Lakemead on Nell Sedge's lease and pay her in grain, and I have rebuilt my fence twice now where Elmwick men pulled it down. I am not a quarrelsome man, but a meadow you cannot fence is no meadow at all. My father Tibbott keeps the bees and the tally and tells me the meadow was grazed by both villages once, which does not mend a post. I want the harvest in, the rent paid, and my family left to farm.
values: a lease is a promise both ways
peace with neighbours, even the ones I am at odds with
goals: get the meadow's grain in and pay Nell Sedge's rent
keep the fence standing through the summer
see Cedda safe and not walking the east road too soon

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: father
relations.note: He keeps the bees and the tally and does not say much, but he is the steadiest thing on the meadow.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the house and worries the meadow will be taken from us; I would carry the fence posts alone before I let that happen.

relations.name: Cedda Coombe
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She helps with the goats and asks after Thistle's stories; she is eleven and the east road can wait.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: son
relations.note: He follows the goats at the meadow edge and is afraid of the deep reeds; I keep an eye on him.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: She holds the lease and I pay her in grain; she has not pressed me yet, and I would rather she never had reason to.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He says the meadow was never Reedmoor's to let; he has no paper for that, and his men pulled my fence twice.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A pedlar who comes through with his packs and has always dealt fair with us; I like him, though I have not promised him Cedda's company on the road.

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She fishes the lake and her nets were trampled when Elmwick pulled my fence; I owe her for that and I have not forgotten it.

relations.name: Goda Toller
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: An Elmwick woman who wants to farm the Lakemead if it is won back; I keep my distance.

relations.name: Edric Toller
relations.label: neighbour across the quarrel
relations.note: An Elmwick man with sheep and wool and no paper for the meadow; his folk grumble with Hob Garrow, but he at least grumbles quietly.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: the blight came through and the grain was thin, and my father would not speak of the Tolleys or the taken fields.
The first time Elmwick men pulled my fence down, I found the posts in the ditch and stood there a long while before I started mending.
The second time they pulled it down, Rill Fenlake's nets were trampled where she had laid them to dry, and I helped her gather them up.
Nell Sedge walked the meadow with me when she let it, and we agreed the rent in grain and the strips I would work.
Cedda was born in the house by the meadow and Morwen would not let anyone but my father hold her first.
Thistle Mossfoot came through with his packs light one autumn and stayed the night, and the children would not let him sleep for stories.

stances.why: It is my family's living and I hold it on a lease; I will not be turned off it by men with no paper.
Nell has been fair with me and the rent is hers by right; I would be ashamed to be short without asking her leave.
I have no quarrel with Elmwick folk in the market, only with the men who pull fences; I would rather talk than fight.
Cedda and Osric are the reason for the meadow; the east road and the deep reeds can wait until they are older.
I am short of grain and ashamed to ask Reedmoor for time again, but silence will not fill the tally.

sheet.secret: I have thought of selling one of the goats to cover the rent and have not told Morwen, because she would say the meadow needs every beast it has.

sheet.narrative: I am too bent now for the heavy work, so I keep the bees and the old tally of the rent, and I remember when both Elmwick and Reedmoor grazed the Lakemead and no one thought to ask whose it was. Nell Sedge was high-handed to let it, in my view, but my son holds the lease and I will not see the Coombes turned off. Hob Garrow's talk in Elmwick sticks in my throat. I keep my bees and my own counsel.
values: an old tally is a true record
goals: see the rent tally squared without the meadow lost
keep the bees through the winter
watch the meadow's lease hold for my grandchildren

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: son
relations.note: He works the meadow and mends the fence and carries it all on his back; I keep the tally so he does not have to.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: gooddaughter
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the house and frets about the meadow; she is right to fret.

relations.name: Cedda Coombe
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: She helps with the goats and asks for stories; I tell her the old ones of the meadow.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: He follows the goats and is afraid of the deep reeds; he will learn the meadow in time.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: landlord
relations.note: She let the meadow that was never hers to let alone; the lease stands, but I do not thank her for it.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: He talks in Elmwick as though the meadow were his by right of memory; memory is not a lease.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: pedlar
relations.note: He comes through with his packs and deals fair; I have no quarrel with him.

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She fishes the lake and helped mend the fence; I trade cheese for her fish.

memories.gist: As a boy I grazed the Lakemead with Elmwick and Reedmoor folk both, and no one asked whose it was.
The Lean Year came and the grain was thin and the talk turned to fields and leases; I would not speak of the Tolleys then and I will not now.
Nell Sedge let the meadow to Jem and I watched the paper signed and said nothing, though I thought it high-handed.
I kept the bees through a hard winter when the hives nearly failed, and they came back in the spring.
My wife died and Jem took the heavy work and I took the tally and the bees.

stances.why: Whatever I think of how it was let, my son holds the meadow and the family stands on it.
The rent is paid in grain and cheese and labour, and someone must write it down honestly or the Coombes will be short and not know it.
Hob Garrow's men pulled the fence twice; talk like that ends with the Coombes turned off.
I am too bent for the heavy work and too old for loud arguments; the bees and the tally are mine to keep.

sheet.secret: I think Nell Sedge was wrong to let the meadow, and if the lease ever lapsed I would not be sorry to see it grazed common again, whatever it cost my son.

sheet.narrative: I was born on the lake's edge and I will die on it, in the old boathouse my father patched and I have patched twice since. I punt out before light with the mist on the water and I smoke what I catch in the shed behind the house; a good morning's catch keeps Gristle and me in meal and lamp oil. Nell Sedge lets me keep the boathouse for a share of the lake catch, and I pay it, though it is a lean share this year with the Coombes behind on their rent and no help coming. The Elmwick men trampled my nets when they came to pull Jem's fence down, and I have not sold a fish to anyone from Elmwick since, and I will not be talked round by soft words.
values: a fair share for a fair catch
my boathouse and my punt are mine
Elmwick folk came to fight, not to mend fences
smoke the fish clean and the buyer comes back
goals: keep the boathouse's standing with Nell Sedge paid up
get a new net made before the autumn run
see the Coombes through their thin rent without going short myself
keep Gristle off the deep water at the lake's middle
sheet.mood: sore and stubborn, with a morning's work still to do

relations.name: Gristle Fenlake
relations.label: son
relations.note: He mends the punt better than I did at his age, and he is the whole of what I have.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We trade cheese for smoked fish and neither of us has coin to spare; she worries the meadow will be taken and I know it might.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A decent man with a fence pulled down twice; I would help him mend it if I had the timber.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: landlady
relations.note: She holds the boathouse's standing over me and I owe her a share of the catch; she has not squeezed me yet, but she could.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He fishes the reeds and knows the water; we talk plain and he does not cheat on a trade.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His packs take my smoked fish east and he brings back hooks and salt; a small folk pedlar keeps his word.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: His Elmwick men trampled my nets to dry and called it a fence quarrel; I will not sell him or his a fish.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Old Tibbott keeps the bees and the rent tally and remembers when the meadow was common; he is right and it does him no good.

memories.gist: The morning I found my drying nets trampled flat in the mud where the Elmwick men had walked over them pulling Jem's fence down; a whole morning's catch spoiled and one net torn past mending.
My father teaching me to pole the punt through the shallows by the reed beds, telling me the lake gives to those who read it and takes from those who don't.
The Lean Year, when the lake still gave fish but nobody had grain to trade for it, and I smoked everything and ate smoked fish till I could not stand the smell.
The night Gristle was born in the boathouse with only Morwen Coombe to help, and the punt knocking against the step in the wind all night.
Nell Sedge coming down to the boathouse to set the terms of my standing: a share of the lake catch each season, and no argument.
Gristle, six years old, poling the punt alone across the shallows and back while I watched from the shed with my heart in my mouth.

stances.why: They trampled my nets and spoiled a catch, and called it a fence quarrel.
The boathouse is my roof and my living; if I lose the standing I lose everything.
