A clean smoke is what makes a buyer come back, and Thistle's packs carry my name east.
My father taught me the shallows and the pools, and they have never failed me entirely.
They are behind on their rent and I trade fish for cheese with them anyway; a neighbour who goes under is no good to anyone.

sheet.secret: I have been holding back a little of Nell's share of the catch these last weeks, telling myself it is against a thin season, and I have not told her or anyone.

sheet.narrative: I live in the boathouse with Mam and help her with the punt and the smoke shed. I know where the shallow pools are and where the bottom drops away, and I do not go near the middle of the lake where it is deep and dark. I play with Osric Coombe when the goats bring him down to the meadow edge, and I can mend a net as well as anyone.
values: Mam knows best about the lake
the middle is deep and I stay out of it
a mended net is a good day's work
goals: learn to pole the punt all the way to the far reeds
catch a fish bigger than my arm
not think about the deep water

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows the lake better than anyone and she is cross with Elmwick, but not with me.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He plays at the meadow edge with the goats and we skip stones in the shallows.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She brings cheese and milk and is kind to me.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Old Tibbott keeps the bees and tells me about when the meadow was common for everyone.

memories.gist: Poling the punt out to the shallows alone for the first time and Mam watching from the shed, and me not falling in.
The day the Elmwick men came and Mam shouted at them over her trampled nets, and I hid in the smoke shed till they had gone.

stances.why: The water goes dark and cold out there and I cannot see the bottom.
She works before light and I am the only one to help her.

villages.name: Saltings
villages.character: Salt pans and fish traps on the west shore below the hills: two households who keep to themselves

sheet.narrative: I keep the fish traps along the west shore and work the salt pans with my family. The smoke from Kettlebridge drifts west and sours the pans, and I grudge them for it. I owe Rook Tarn for a net and haven't paid; the pans have not yielded enough this year and I am ashamed to say so.
goals: pay off the debt to Rook Tarn
keep the traps in the channel
make the salt pans yield more
see Tarn settled with a boat

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the plot and the pans; I wish I could tell her about the debt without shame.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: son
relations.note: He works the traps well; I want him to have his own boat.

relations.name: Sedge Brine
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She knows every bird on the shore; I fear for her in winter.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for a net; he wants his marks before storm season.

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He thinks he owns the west shore; the channel is common.

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She is caught in the middle; I bear her no ill.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He takes my smoked fish to Brackenford; a fair man.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: carrier
relations.note: She carries Rook's word; I keep my distance.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: blight took the berries; we ate salt fish and barley and barely got by.
I took Rook Tarn's net and promised to pay by the next storm season, but the season passed and I still owe him.
The Surge two winters ago: waves came up the shore and we lost traps and salt pans; we rebuilt with what we had.
The day we set the first traps in the channel and Grim Tarn came down shouting that it was his family's water.
Sedge was born on a stormy night; Marra delivered her with Ebba Tarn's help.

stances.why: A man's word is his bond, and I mean to pay Rook.
The channel is common shore; Grim does not own it.
Everything I do is for Marra and the children.
Their smoke sours our pans and they care nothing for the shore.

sheet.narrative: I work the salt pans and keep the plot of roots and barley above the shore. I trade salt and barley with Tern Gannet of Thornby, and I have been putting aside marks in a hidden jar to pay Hollis's debt to Rook Tarn. Hollis does not know, and I am proud of my plan and afraid of what he will say.
goals: pay off Hollis's debt to Rook Tarn secretly
keep the winter store from running out
see Tarn settled
mend the rift with her brother Osric

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: husband
relations.note: I love him, but I keep my secret from him.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is set on Nessa Tarn; I would not have chosen her.

relations.name: Sedge Brine
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is the light of the house.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She takes my salt and barley and asks no questions.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: brother
relations.note: We have not spoken since the Lean Year; I miss him.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I mean to pay him without Hollis knowing.

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: I wish Hollis would let the trap quarrel lie.

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is caught in the middle; I bear her no ill.

relations.name: Nessa Tarn
relations.label: son's sweetheart
relations.note: A bold girl, too young and too sure of herself, and her father's quarrel sits between us; but Tarn's heart is set on her and I'll not be the one to break it.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: my brother Osric and I quarrelled over grain; we have not spoken since.
I started putting aside marks from the salt trade in a jar, meaning to pay Rook Tarn.
The Surge: we lost traps and pans; I thought we would never recover.
Tarn told me he was courting Nessa Tarn; I told him she was too young and too bold.
Sedge was born on a stormy night; Ebba Tarn helped me deliver her.

stances.why: I would do anything for my children.
Hollis's shame is my shame; I will pay Rook without telling him.
The trap quarrel does no one any good.
If the store does not last, we will not either.

sheet.secret: I have been selling salt and barley to Tern Gannet and keeping the marks in a hidden jar to pay off Hollis's debt to Rook Tarn without telling him.

sheet.narrative: I work the traps with my father and mend the boats; I want a boat of my own. I am courting Nessa Tarn, and both households know it, though her father Grim has told me not to come to the house until my father's debt to Rook Tarn is settled. I think the trap quarrel is my father's business, not mine.
goals: buy a boat of his own
settle the debt to Rook Tarn so he can court Nessa openly
marry Nessa Tarn
prove himself to Grim Tarn

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: father
relations.note: He works hard, but his quarrel with Grim Tarn stands in my way.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She disapproves of Nessa, but I know she means well.

relations.name: Sedge Brine
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is a good kid; I look out for her.

relations.name: Nessa Tarn
relations.label: courting
relations.note: I am set on her; I will buy a boat and ask for her properly.

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He says I cannot come to the house until the debt is settled.

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She is kind, but caught between the families.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: My father owes him; I wish it were paid.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Met at the Ferncross market; a good sort.

memories.gist: The first time I saw Nessa Tarn at the Thornby market, I knew I wanted her.
My father took Rook Tarn's net and promised to pay by the next storm season; the season passed and he still owes.
Grim Tarn told me I was not to come to the house until the debt was settled.
The Surge: I helped my father pull the traps out of the waves and we lost half of them.
I met Tace Hollis at the Ferncross market and we shared a jug of cider.

stances.why: I will have Nessa, whatever her father says.
A boat of my own is the only way to ask for her properly.
The trap quarrel is my father's business, not mine.
I will always stand by my family, even when they are wrong.

sheet.narrative: I help with the traps and the salt pans, and I know every bird on the shore. I play with Wren Stave when the Thornby folk come down the shore. I am afraid of the wolves that come down to the saltings in winter.
goals: see a wolf without being seen
learn to set a trap
play with Wren Stave again

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: father
relations.note: He teaches me the traps and the birds.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps me safe and tells the best stories.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is always busy with Nessa, but he still plays with me sometimes.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She comes down the shore and we look for birds together.

memories.gist: The winter the wolves came down to the saltings and I saw one from the window.
The day I learned to name every bird on the shore with my father.
Playing with Wren Stave when the Thornby folk came down the shore.

stances.why: I stay close to my family when the wolves come.
I know every bird on the shore and they never hurt me.
The shore is the best place to play.

sheet.narrative: I've fished the west shore since I could hold a line, and the salt pans behind me were my father's and his father's before him. That channel at the north end is ours by right of two generations, and I'll not have Hollis Brine pushing his traps into it and calling it free water. My boat hook was stolen by the Coldwell outlaws last winter, and I've not forgotten it. Nessa is courting a Brine boy, and while the debt to Rook Tarn stands unpaid, I'll not have him at my table.
goals: keep the north channel for my traps
see the debt to Rook Tarn settled
protect my daughter from a match I distrust
keep the salt pans working through winter

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the house and the pans; I'd be lost without her, though I don't say it.

relations.name: Nessa Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's a good hand with a spear, but she's too soft on that Brine boy.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He moved his traps into my channel and can't even pay his debts.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She's civil enough, but she's a Brine and she'll side with her husband.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: The boy's not bad, but he's a Brine and his father owes Thornby.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: We share a name and not a bloodline, but he's a good man with a net.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He buys my hides and pays fair, though he's a hard bargainer.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: Her people stole my boat hook; I've no love for outlaws.

memories.gist: My father showed me the north channel and said, 'This is ours, boy, as long as the Tarns fish it.'
The Lean Year: we ate salt fish and thin barley, and the wolves came down to the shore.
Hollis Brine moved his traps into the channel last spring, and I told him to move them back.
The Coldwell outlaws took my boat hook from the shed; I found the shed door broken.
Nessa told me she was walking out with Tarn Brine, and I told her not while the debt stands.

stances.why: The channel has been Tarn water for two generations.
They take what isn't theirs and don't pay their debts.
Blood is what holds the shore together.
A man who doesn't pay his debts is no better than an outlaw.
They stole from me once; they'll do it again if they can.

sheet.narrative: I work the salt pans and keep the goats and the herb plot, and I've set bones and dosed coughs for half the saltings. The Brines come to me when the cough takes them, and I treat them the same as anyone. I've no quarrel with Marra, but I'll not cross my husband in front of them. The winter store worries me, and the wolves come closer each year.
goals: keep the salt pans and goats through winter
see Nessa happy without breaking the household
keep the herb plot and the medicines stocked
avoid open quarrel with the Brines

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He's stubborn as the rocks, but he's a good provider.

relations.name: Nessa Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's got her father's spirit and my soft heart; I want her to be happy.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He's quarrelsome, but I'll not refuse him medicine.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She's a good woman caught in her husband's quarrel; I'd share my herbs with her.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A polite boy; I think he'd treat Nessa well.

relations.name: Mavis Tarn
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We trade salt and herbs; she's a sensible woman.

relations.name: Rook Tarn
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: Grim's friend, and a decent man.

memories.gist: My mother taught me the herb plot and the salt pans, and said, 'Heal who you can, and don't judge.'
The Surge: we lost a boat and nearly lost Grim; the sea took the lower shore.
I dosed Marra Brine's cough last winter, and she thanked me kindly.
Grim told Nessa she couldn't see Tarn Brine, and she cried in the goat shed.
The wolves came down to the saltings and took a goat; I heard them in the dark.

stances.why: A healer doesn't turn away the sick, whatever the quarrel.
The household is what keeps us through winter.
I won't defy Grim in front of the Brines, but I'll not make enemies either.
The store must last; the wolves and the cold don't wait.
I told Grim to leave Nessa and Tarn alone; they'll sort it themselves.

sheet.narrative: I help my mother with the pans and the goats and my father with the boat, and I'm a fair hand with a spear. I like Tarn Brine, and I'm angry with my father for using the debt as a gate. I meet Tarn on the shore when I can, but I'm afraid of the deep water beyond the shore and I dream of seeing Lanternquay and the tide lanterns.
goals: see Tarn Brine without my father's leave
visit Lanternquay and see the tide lanterns
keep the goats and pans well
learn to spear fish better

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: I love him, but he's being unfair about Tarn.

relations.name: Ebba Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She understands, even if she won't say it to Father.

relations.name: Tarn Brine
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He's kind and funny, and I meet him on the shore when I can.

relations.name: Sedge Brine
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She's a good friend, and she doesn't blame me for the quarrel.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He's caused trouble, but he's Tarn's father.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She disapproves of me, and I don't know why.

memories.gist: I speared my first big fish last summer, and Father clapped me on the back.
Tarn Brine gave me a shell from the north shore, and I keep it under my pillow.
Father said Tarn couldn't come to the house until the debt is settled, and I shouted at him.
I saw the tide lanterns at Lanternquay from the cliff once, and I've wanted to go ever since.

stances.why: He's kind and I want to be with him, whatever Father says.
I love my parents, but they're wrong about this.
There's more than the saltings, and I want to see it.
The sea beyond the shore is dark and cold, and I've heard stories.

villages.name: the North Light
villages.character: A light on the north cape above Thornby, kept by an old woman and her grandson
villages.ledger: The light is lit every night.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the north light for forty years, as my mother did before me, and I will not be driven off the cape by folk who have never climbed it in a gale. The sea took Osric's brother and Cuthbert's brother's boat, not my lamp, but Thornby needs someone to blame and I am convenient. I smoke my fish and trade with Simon Hollis for oil and salt, and this winter the store is short because the fisherfolk have quietly stopped selling to me. Colm is the only kin I have left, and he is a good boy, though he is afraid of the dark stair and I do not know why.
goals: keep the north light burning every night
get enough lamp oil and salt to last the winter without asking Thornby
raise Colm to be a lightkeeper
clear her name of the wrecking slander

relations.name: Colm Wray
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: The only kin I have left; he trims the wick and hauls the water, and I would not part with him.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: accuser
relations.note: He blames me for his brother's drowning, and he will not hear that the sea took him, not my lamp.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: His brother's boat was lost and he lays it at my door too; he has never climbed the cape in a gale.

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He brings me oil and salt for my smoked fish, and he does not preach at me about the wreck.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: fish-road woman
relations.note: She carries fish down the road and has not refused my trade outright, though Thornby has.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: child
relations.note: Cuthbert's girl; she comes up the cape with Colm and is not old enough to hold her father's grudge.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: child
relations.note: Osric's ward; he plays with Colm when the Thornby folk come up, and I do not hold the boy to his guardian's word.

memories.gist: My mother taught me the light when I was a girl, and I have trimmed the wick every night since she died.
The night of the great gale, I kept the lamp burning till dawn though the oil ran low and the wind shook the tower.
Osric Dunn came up the cape and called me a wrecker to my face after his brother drowned.
My daughter left Colm with me when he was small and never came back for him.
Last winter the fisherfolk stopped selling me oil, and I traded my last smoked fish to Simon Hollis for a jar.

stances.why: It is my duty and my mother's before me; without it boats would break on the cape.
I will not be called a wrecker by folk who were not here in the gale.
They have turned against me and cut off my oil; I will not beg them for anything.
He is the only kin I have, and I will keep him safe and raise him right.

sheet.narrative: I live at the north light with my grandmother, and I trim the wick and haul the water and keep the oil jars in order. The stair down to the lamp is dark and I do not like going down it, but I do because she needs me. When the Thornby children come up the cape I play with Wren and Hob, but I do not tell them what the village says about us. I saw the light burn low one night last winter, and I have not told anyone, not even her.
goals: help grandmother keep the light
not be afraid of the dark stair
play with Wren and Hob when they come up
understand why the light burned low

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She raised me and I help her with the light; I would do anything for her.

relations.name: Wren Stave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She comes up the cape with her father and we play on the shingle.

relations.name: Hob Dunn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He mends nets and plays with us when the Thornby folk come up.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: accuser
relations.note: He says Grandmother wrecked his brother's boat, and I do not understand why he is so angry.

relations.name: Cuthbert Stave
relations.label: accuser
relations.note: He says my grandmother wrecked his brother's boat, and he looks at the light as if it were a bad thing; he is kind to Wren, but I do not like the way he talks about us.

memories.gist: Grandmother taught me to trim the wick and count the oil jars when I was small.
One night last winter I saw the light burn low and I was frightened, but I did not tell anyone.
Wren and Hob came up the cape and we played on the shingle until the tide turned.
Osric Dunn shouted at Grandmother by the light, and I hid behind the oil jars.

stances.why: She needs me to keep the light, and I want to be useful.
It is dark and narrow and I do not like going down alone.
I do not know what would happen if I told, and I am afraid.

sheet.secret: I saw Grandmother's light burn low one night last winter, and I have told no one.

villages.name: Tanglewood
villages.character: A healer's cottage in the old forest near Fernhollow: a woman who left Brackenford's chapel years ago, and those who come to her

sheet.narrative: I was a chapel sister of Brackenford for thirty years, and I left over the gate-due and the silence that let it stand; the sisters heal anyone who comes, I said, so why not the ones the gate calls outlaws? Now I keep a healer's cottage in the old forest, and the sick of every settlement find the path to it, which is more than the gate would allow them. I am sixty-one, my hands are still steady, but the cottage is a long way from a surgeon's hands, and I have a letter under my herb ledger I have not answered. I say what I think about the gate-due to anyone who will listen, and I have never once gone back through that gate.
values: healing without asking who the sick are
the old forest and its gardens kept, not felled
keeping my daughter and grandson close
goals: pay Alder Rush before the first frost without asking the chapel for a mark
keep Orla from the wood road and the pits
decide what to do about Elspeth's letter
keep the salve store full through the winter

relations.name: Orla Fenwick
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Born in this cottage and too ready to walk away from it for a man I do not trust.

relations.name: Hollis Fenwick
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: Knows my herbs better than some sisters I trained; I will not have him afraid of the dark stair or the wood.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: old sister
relations.note: She writes to me still; her letter sits under my ledger and I have not the words for it yet.

relations.name: Alwin Wren
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: He taught me the charms the sisters would not, and he never once told me to go back through the gate.

relations.name: Betony Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her salves are honest and her hollow's plants are the same old forest as mine.

relations.name: Marra Brine
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Roots and barley from the saltings, and a sister's quarrel with Thornby she does not speak of.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He took my word in the spring; the debt falls due at first frost and I mean to keep my word.

relations.name: Odile Vance
relations.label: old patient's daughter
relations.note: I sat with her mother through her last winter; she sets bones well and has the sense to disapprove of that cairn.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: the burner
relations.note: Smoke and drink and a pit house; he is not taking my daughter up that road.

memories.gist: I knelt at the chapel fire and heard the Reeve's men read the Coldwell names as outlaws, and I said nothing, and I have not knelt there since.
Alwin Wren showed me the herb charms the order calls hedge-magic, and I have used them at sickbeds ever since.
I sat three nights with Odile Vance's mother in Kettlebridge and closed her eyes at the end.
Orla was born in this cottage in a hard frost, and I cut the cord myself and thought I would never be so afraid again.
Elspeth's letter came up the forest path in spring, and I read it twice and put it under the herb ledger.

stances.why: I left the order over it; a healer who asks first what a body has done is no healer.
It is taken from folk who never chose the Reeve, and the chapel kept silent about it.
The old forest is the garden and the medicine both; fallen wood serves.
A healer's credit is all she has when the salves run out.
I have seen what a pit house and a drinking man leave a woman with.

sheet.secret: Elspeth has written asking me back to the chapel before winter, with a pardon for leaving offered through the Reeve; I have told no one, and the letter lies under my herb ledger.

sheet.narrative: I was born in this cottage and I will likely die in it, but not before I have seen a little of the wood road. I keep the clearing's roots and barley and the beehives, and carry the surplus down to Ferncross and the Fernhollow stall, and that is how I came to know the Sootwood pits and Cael's nephew. My mother has forbidden him the cottage path; I go anyway when the loads are carried, and I am not a girl to be told who may walk up to my own door. The hives have been poor this year and I am short on what I promised Alder, and I have not told her how short.
values: my own choosing, right or wrong
the clearing fed and the honey sold
keeping faith with those who deal fair with me
goals: settle Alder Rush's honey before the frost
keep walking to the pits whatever my mother says
get a better year from the hives
see that Hollis is not afraid of the wood
sheet.mood: restless, fond, and quietly anxious about the honey

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She healed half the island and cannot bear that I choose a man she has not chosen.

relations.name: Hollis Fenwick
relations.label: son
relations.note: He stacks kindling better than the burner taught him, and he is the reason I keep the clearing.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: the burner
relations.note: His nephew is kind and patient with Hollis; the rest is my mother's old quarrel with smoke.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I promised him last autumn's honey and the hives failed me; I will not be a cheat.

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She punts the lake and trades fair, and she does not lecture me about the road.

relations.name: Vetch Quill
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We trade honey and barley, and we both know what a poor year the hives have had.

relations.name: Betony Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her salves go down the east road with my honey, and she never asks about the pits.

relations.name: Pell Tarn
relations.label: the burner's kin
relations.note: A boy who wants the quay boats; his cousin is the one I walk to see.

memories.gist: I carried the first full pack of honey down to the Fernhollow stall and sold every pot before noon.
Hollis was born in the cottage with my mother's hands on me, and the wolves were howling close that night.
I met Cael's nephew at the Sootwood pits when I carried honey up the wood road, and he showed me how the slow pits are stacked.
My mother forbade him the cottage path, and I took the next load up the road anyway.
The hives came out poor this summer, and I counted the pots twice and knew I was short of what I promised Alder.

stances.why: I am thirty-four and I have kept this clearing since I was a girl; I will not be told who may come up the path.
A cheat's honey does not sell twice at the Fernhollow stall.
My mother's grudge against the smoke is an old woman's quarrel; the burners have been kind to Hollis.
He is nine and the forest is his home; I will not have him frightened of his own clearing.
Ferncross and Fernhollow are the only markets that do not ask me to kneel to a gate.

sheet.secret: I am far shorter on the honey than I have told my mother, and I am thinking of selling my grandmother's silver spoon, the last thing of my father's house, to pay Alder Rush.

sheet.narrative: I live in the cottage in the clearing with my mother and my grandmother, and I know every path of it and the names of all the herbs in the garden. Grandmother is teaching me my letters from the chapel psalter, and I carry her salve packets down to the Ferncross market in a basket. I like it when Fennel and Bracken come up the path from Fernhollow, and I like the burner who taught me to stack kindling, though Grandmother's face closes when his name is said.
values: the herbs and the salve packets
goals: learn all the herb names in the garden
read the whole psalter without help
play with Fennel and Bracken when they come up the path

relations.name: Ysolde Fenwick
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She knows every herb and every charm, and her hands are warm when she sets a poultice.

relations.name: Orla Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She carries the honey down the road and always comes back before dark.

relations.name: Fennel Underbank
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He comes up the path from Fernhollow and we hunt for beetles in the woodpile.

relations.name: Bracken Rush
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He counts the packs and lets me count them too.

relations.name: Cael Tarn
relations.label: the burner
relations.note: He taught me to stack kindling so the pit draws, and he does not laugh when I ask questions.

memories.gist: Grandmother set me to name the herbs in the garden and I got eleven right before I forgot the feverfew.
I carried the salve packets down to the Ferncross market in my own basket for the first time.
The burner showed me how to stack the kindling in a cone so the slow pit draws.

villages.name: Ferncross
villages.character: Woodcutters at a crossing of tracks in the southern woods, selling timber to Elmwick and Reedmoor

sheet.narrative: I am Master woodcutter at the Ferncross, and the oak and ash of this crossing have paid my house's way for twenty years. I fell for Elmwick and Reedmoor both, and keep the charcoal pits on the side when the burn runs slow and the orders run fast. I owe Alder Rush a share of charcoal from last winter's burn and have not carried it up the road yet; the Elmwick timber paid marks in hand, and Alder can wait a little longer without the world ending. I count Orvin Hollis at Sootwood a friend, and I have not forgotten the men from Coldwell who walked off with my tools.
values: a fair price for honest work
the crossing fed before anyone else
debts paid, though not always first
keeping my word to my neighbours
goals: carry Alder Rush his charcoal share before he has to ask twice
keep the Ferncross timber trade with both Elmwick and Reedmoor
see my daughter Corliss learn the axe and the pits without hurting herself
get back the tools the Coldwell men took
sheet.mood: steady, a little pressed, keeping his worries behind his teeth

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the pot and the tally both; I would be lost at the crossing without her.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with kindling and quicker with questions; I want her to have the axe and the sense to use it.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He lent grain last winter and I owe him charcoal; he is patient but he counts.

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: fellow woodcutter
relations.note: She sold Elmwick timber for the Lakemead fence and says a sale is a sale; I say it is, but Reedmoor may not.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His barley came in light and the kitchen needs it; I would rather buy than beg.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She buys our timber and now she is cool with the crossing over a fence; I want that to blow over.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Elmwick pays on time and asks few questions; I would not want to lose his orders.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A good man with an axe and a bad word for the quay's stone price; we understand each other.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: Her people took my tools off the wood road; I have not had a good word for Coldwell since.

relations.name: Sorrel Bramblecap
relations.label: trade neighbour
relations.note: He works the hollow's grain and berry rows and grumbles about the giants' track taking timber; I sell him nothing and buy nothing, but the east road keeps us honest with each other.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the berry crop failed; I felled and burned all through it and still the crossing went hungry, and Alder Rush's grain kept us.
Two men from Coldwell stopped me on the wood road and took my tools and a load of charcoal; I walked home with empty hands.
Corliss stacked her first charcoal pit with me and never once let the fire go out.
Odelia Harrow sold a load of Elmwick timber for the Lakemead fence, and Nell Sedge heard of it and came down cold on the crossing.
I sat with Orvin Hollis at the Ferncross market and we agreed the seawall will never be built and the quay will pay dear for it.

stances.why: A man who owes and does not pay cannot ask for credit when the burn goes bad.
Nesta's pot feeds the woodcutters; whatever the orders, the crossing eats before the marks go out.
Odelia Harrow sold Elmwick timber and that was her trade to make; I will not call it treason.
Nell Sedge buys our timber and Reedmoor's fish comes up the road; a fence quarrel must not cost us that.
They took my tools on the wood road and I have not seen them since.

sheet.secret: The Elmwick order came first because it paid marks in hand, and I told Alder Rush the pits burned slow. I would not say that to his face.

sheet.narrative: I keep the Ferncross kitchen and the common pot, and there are more woodcutters at my table this winter than the plot can carry. Roderick Harrow's barley came in light and I am feeding his men as well as my own, so I am watching the store and the weather both. I trade bread and broth for fish and fibre, and I would rather owe a neighbour a kindness than see a man go hungry at my fire. The crossing holds together because somebody keeps the pot on.
values: nobody goes hungry at the crossing
a fair trade for bread and broth
goals: get Roderick Harrow to sell me barley on credit before the store runs out
keep the woodcutters fed through the winter
trade bread for fish with Tansy Sedge and Thistle Mossfoot when their packs come
see Corliss safe and warm through the cold
sheet.mood: worried and busy, with a calm face for the table

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He fells and I feed; he worries at the debts and I worry at the pot, and between us it works.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She stacks kindling and asks about the quay; I want her to see it one day, and to come home.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His barley came in light and I need it on credit; I hope he sees the kitchen is feeding his men too.

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She works the south side and keeps the tally; we share what the two houses have and watch the sky.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We met at the Ferncross market and have traded ever since; she knows what a thin store means.

relations.name: Tansy Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her bread and my broth go back and forth along the east road; she is fair with the fish.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His packs bring fish and fibre and take my bread; a small folk pedlar who pays what he says.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Bramwell owes him charcoal and he has not pressed us; I do not forget that.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She buys timber and now she is cool with the crossing; I would rather mend it over a bowl than argue.

relations.name: Mallow Bramblecap
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She feeds a hollow's common table and I feed a crossing's, so she knows what a thin store means; her people's bread and honey come up the path to me when there is any to spare.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I stretched the pot with roots and nettles and fed the woodcutters through, and I have never let the store get that low again without counting it.
Corliss was small and burned her hand on the pot hook; I salved it and she has been careful at the fire since.
Maren Hollis came down the wood road with roots and charcoal and we traded half a day's bread for it at the Ferncross market.
Roderick Harrow told me his barley came in light, and I looked at my store and knew we would be sharing thin bread before the thaw.

stances.why: The common pot is the crossing's hearth; a woodcutter who eats here works here, and no one is turned away hungry.
Roderick's barley is in his barn and my store is thin; a neighbour's credit is cheaper than a hungry winter.
The plot will not carry more woodcutters than it has before, and the cold comes early down the wood road.
Fish and fibre come up the east road and my bread goes down it; that trade keeps the pot from being only roots.
Reedmoor and Elmwick can quarrel over a meadow; I will not have it at my table when both bring fish.

sheet.secret: I have been putting a little less in each bowl so the store lasts longer, and I have not told Bramwell how thin it truly is.

sheet.narrative: I stack the kindling and learn the axe and the charcoal burn beside my father, and I am quicker at the stacks than he thinks. When the Fernhollow folk come up the path I play with Fennel Underbank, and I want more than anything to see the quay at Lanternquay and the boats. The wolves come down the wood road in winter and I do not like the sound of them at night.
values: learning the axe and the burn
goals: learn to stack a pit that does not smoke
see the quay at Lanternquay one day
keep the wolves away from the kindling stacks
sheet.mood: curious and restless, brave by day and fearful at night

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me stack the kindling and says I am quicker than he was; I want him to teach me the axe proper.

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the pot and never lets me go cold; she says the quay is a long way and I say it is not so far.

relations.name: Fennel Underbank
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He comes up the path with the Fernhollow folk and we play among the stacks; he knows every flower.

relations.name: Tamsin Harrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She helps with the goats and the garden and we play at the crossing when the work is done.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: She stacks pits at Sootwood and knows a quay knot; I want to learn it.

memories.gist: I stacked my first charcoal pit with my father and never once let the fire go out, and he said I had the hand for it.
I burned my hand on the pot hook when I was small and my mother salved it; I have been careful at the fire since.
Wolves came down the wood road in the night and I heard them from my bed; I do not go far from the stacks after dark.

stances.why: My father says the pits are the crossing's living and I want to be good at them.
The quay folk come up the wood road with fish and talk of boats; I want to see it with my own eyes.
The wolves come down the wood road and I have heard them.

sheet.narrative: I work the south side of the crossing with an axe and a hauling rope, and I keep the tally of every load that goes out of Ferncross. Bramwell fells; I trim, stack and count, and I know to the bundle what a cart will carry. Last month I sold Elmwick builders a load of timber for the Lakemead fence, and now Nell Sedge says I have taken sides in her quarrel with Hob Garrow. A sale is a sale. I owe Nell a share of that load and I will pay it, but I will not be told who I may cut for.
goals: pay Nell Sedge her share and keep selling where the price is fair
trade a load of timber to Elmwick for grain before the store runs out
keep Tamsin close and teach her the woods without letting her fear them
see the tally balanced at the end of the season

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a light barley crop and too much pride to ask for help.

relations.name: Tamsin Harrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Follows me into the woods and jumps at every shadow; I will teach her the trees one at a time.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe her a share of the load and will pay it, but she is making a quarrel out of a fence post.

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: fellow woodcutter
relations.note: We have worked the crossing together for years; he fells, I count.

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her kitchen is stretched thin and she is too anxious to say how thin.

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Punts the lake for fish and has no patience for the Elmwick men either.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Elmwick's elder buys my timber and can keep his quarrel with Reedmoor to himself.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Keeps the hollow's store and knows what a load is worth.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: neighbour's child
relations.note: Good with kindling and patient with Tamsin.

memories.gist: Selling the Elmwick load for the Lakemead fence and counting the marks into my hand.
Nell Sedge's runner coming up the wood road to say Ferncross was taking sides.
Roderick tipping out the barley sacks and the crop running light through my fingers.
Teaching Tamsin to stack kindling so the pile will not fall on her.
The Lean Year, when the woods kept us fed and the hollow sent grain up the road.

stances.why: I cut honest timber and I sell it to whoever pays; Nell Sedge does not own the road.
I owe Nell a share of that load and I will not have it said I cheated her.
A light crop means we eat thin now or starve at planting time.
Elmwick needs timber and we need grain; a straight swap beats begging.
Tamsin jumps at shadows and I would have her know the paths like I do.

sheet.secret: I have quietly set aside two bundles of good oak that I have not put in the tally, meaning to sell them on my own account.

sheet.narrative: I farm the small clearing by the crossing: barley, roots and a few goats, and I sell grain to Nesta's kitchen and to the Fernhollow pedlar when he comes up the road. This year the barley came in light, and I feel the shame of it every time I open the store. Nesta is feeding more woodcutters than her plot can carry and wants us to share out what there is; I want to help her, but I will not give away the seed for spring. Odelia says trade timber to Elmwick for grain, and she may be right, though I would rather not go asking.
values: a man provides for his own
goals: keep back enough barley seed for spring whatever else goes
see the store through to the thaw without borrowing again
help Nesta's kitchen as far as I can without beggaring my house
not be seen as the man whose harvest failed

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: Sharper about trade than I am, and not afraid to say what she has sold.

relations.name: Tamsin Harrow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Helps with the goats and the garden, and is afraid of the woods I grew up in.

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Feeds half the crossing from a plot too small for it, and asks me to share what I have.

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good woodcutter; his house and mine will sink or swim together this winter.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for a loan of grain and he has not pressed me, which is worse.

relations.name: Merrow Stave
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Trades seeds from Thornby; her barley does better than mine on poorer ground.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: Headwoman of Reedmoor, and her quarrel with Elmwick has followed us up the road.

memories.gist: Threshing the barley and watching the sacks come up half empty.
Nesta Ashdown standing in my yard asking how much we could spare for the kitchen.
Borrowing grain from Alder Rush in the Lean Year and promising to repay at the next harvest.
Tamsin carrying the seed basket and dropping half of it in the mud.
The smoke from the Kettlebridge works lying grey over the clearing for three days.

stances.why: If I eat the seed now there is no crop at all, and then we are all beggars.
Nesta feeds the men who cut our wood; a neighbour does not let a neighbour's pot go empty.
I borrowed once and have not forgotten it; I would rather sell than ask.
The barley by the wood road has done worse since the smoke started drifting east.
She counts what I cannot and I trust her tally over my own.

sheet.secret: I have already promised Nesta two sacks of barley I am not sure I can spare, and I have not told Odelia.

sheet.narrative: I help with the goats and the garden, and I follow my mother into the woods when she lets me. The trees are very tall and the wolves come down the wood road in winter, so I keep close to her. Corliss Ashdown plays with me and we stack kindling together. I want to see Lanternquay one day, where the boats are, but I would not go into the deep woods alone for anything.
goals: learn the garden and the goats properly
see the sea at Lanternquay one day
not be left alone at the edge of the woods

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows the woods and holds my hand when we go in.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is quiet since the barley came in light, and I bring him the goats to cheer him.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We stack kindling and she tells me about the quay she wants to see.

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She gives me bread from the common pot when I help in the kitchen.

memories.gist: Following mother into the south side and being told to keep behind her axe.
A wolf's howl down the wood road at dusk and running for the door.
Stacking kindling with Corliss until the pile was taller than us.

packs.name: the wolves of the low hills

stone carter.routine: carry stone on the stone road

fish runner.routine: carry cooked fish on the fish road

meat carrier.routine: carry cooked meat on the giants' track

pedlar.routine: carry fiber on the east road
